Part III · Spin qubits · Chapter 13

Singlet–triplet, exchange-only and other encoded qubits

Why you need this

A single spin is not the only way to make a qubit from electrons in dots. Encoding one qubit in the joint state of two or three spins lets you control it entirely with fast baseband voltage pulses, no microwaves at all, and makes it immune to some kinds of noise. HRL Laboratories builds its processors from exchange-only qubits, and the first open-source RFSoC spin-qubit work demonstrated exactly that kind of qubit [11]. These encodings put very different demands on the control hardware than the single-spin qubit does: fewer GHz signals, many more nanosecond-precision DC-coupled pulses.

13.1Why encode a qubit in several spins?

The LD qubit needs a microwave drive at the Zeeman frequency for every rotation. Microwaves are hard to deliver to many qubits without heating and crosstalk. Exchange \(J\), on the other hand, is controlled by voltage pulses on gates, which are fast (ns), local, and need no carrier. Exchange alone cannot rotate a single spin, because it only acts on pairs and conserves total spin. But if the qubit is defined as a property of a pair or a triple of spins, exchange becomes a full rotation tool.

13.2The singlet–triplet (S–T₀) qubit

Encoding

Take two electrons in a double dot in the \((1,1)\) charge state, in a magnetic field large enough that the polarised triplets \(T_\pm\) are split away by \(\pm E_Z\). The remaining two states with total \(S_z = 0\) form the qubit [19]:

\[ \ket{0_{ST}} = \ket S = \frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow} - \ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}, \qquad \ket{1_{ST}} = \ket{T_0} = \frac{\ket{\uparrow\downarrow} + \ket{\downarrow\uparrow}}{\sqrt2}. \]

The two control axes

In the \(\{S, T_0\}\) basis, the Hamiltonian is

\[ H_{ST} = \frac{J(\varepsilon)}{2}\,\sigma_z + \frac{\Delta E_Z}{2}\,\sigma_x \quad\text{(up to a constant)}, \]
  • Exchange \(J\) splits \(S\) and \(T_0\): rotation about z. It is switched on in nanoseconds by pulsing the detuning towards \((2,0)\) or by lowering the barrier.
  • The Zeeman energy difference \(\Delta E_Z = g\mu_B(B_{z,1} - B_{z,2})\) between the two dots mixes \(S\) and \(T_0\): rotation about x. In GaAs it comes from a difference in Overhauser fields (which fluctuates, or can be stabilised by dynamic nuclear polarisation); in silicon it comes from a micromagnet and is stable.

Note that \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) and \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\) lie on the ±x axis of this Bloch sphere. With \(J = 0\), the state precesses between \(S\) and \(T_0\) at frequency \(\Delta E_Z/h\); with \(J \gg \Delta E_Z\), it precesses around z at \(J/h\). Combining both allows any rotation.

A typical S–T₀ experiment

  1. Initialise in \(S(2,0)\) by waiting at positive detuning (two electrons in one dot form the singlet ground state).
  2. Separate: pulse to \((1,1)\). The pulse must be slow compared with \(h/t_c\), so that the electron follows the singlet branch from \((2,0)\) into \((1,1)\) without being excited across the charge anticrossing. If it is also fast compared with \(h/\Delta E_Z\), the spin state stays \(\ket S\). If instead it is slow compared with \(h/\Delta E_Z\) as well (fully adiabatic), \(S(2,0)\) maps onto the lower-energy eigenstate of the field difference, \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) or \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\).
  3. Evolve for a time \(\tau\) at a chosen detuning (sets \(J\)) to rotate.
  4. Read out by pulsing back to the PSB window: \(S\) goes to \((2,0)\), \(T_0\) stays in \((1,1)\) [38].

Every step is a baseband voltage pulse with ns-scale timing on the two plungers (or plunger and barrier). The rotation frequencies \(J/h\) and \(\Delta E_Z/h\) are typically 10 MHz–1 GHz, so the timing resolution must be well below a nanosecond for accurate gates.

Worked example

A silicon S–T₀ qubit has a micromagnet field difference of 1.5 mT between the dots. What is the x-rotation frequency, and how long is a π rotation?

\(\Delta E_Z/h = 28\ \text{GHz/T}\times1.5\ \text{mT} = 42\) MHz, so a π rotation about x takes \(1/(2\times42\ \text{MHz}) \approx 12\) ns. Timing errors of 0.1 ns give a rotation-angle error of about 1.5°. That is why baseband pulse timing, rise times and pulse distortion matter so much for this encoding.

Strengths and weaknesses

  • No microwaves; fast gates (ns); PSB readout comes naturally.
  • Insensitive to global field fluctuations, because only the difference between the dots matters.
  • Exchange is sensitive to charge noise (via \(dJ/d\varepsilon\)); \(\Delta E_Z\) cannot be switched off.
  • Leakage to \(T_\pm\) can occur if \(E_Z\) is small or near anticrossings.

13.3The exchange-only (EO) qubit

Encoding

Three spins in three dots have \(2^3 = 8\) states. Total spin and its z component are conserved by exchange, so exchange alone cannot mix states with different total spin \(S\) or \(S_z\). Group the states: one quartet (\(S = 3/2\), four states) and two doublets (\(S = 1/2\), two states each). Within, say, \(S = 1/2, S_z = +1/2\), there are exactly two states. They form the qubit [39]:

\[ \ket{0_L} = \ket{S}_{12}\ket{\uparrow}_3, \qquad \ket{1_L} = \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\ket{T_+}_{12}\ket{\downarrow}_3 - \sqrt{\tfrac13}\,\ket{T_0}_{12}\ket{\uparrow}_3 . \]

In words, \(\ket{0_L}\) has spins 1 and 2 in a singlet, \(\ket{1_L}\) has them in a triplet, combined with spin 3 to give total spin 1/2.

Control with exchange alone

Exchange \(J_{12}\) between spins 1 and 2 distinguishes singlet from triplet of that pair, so it rotates the logical qubit about the z axis. Exchange \(J_{23}\) between spins 2 and 3 acts the same way on a different pair; in the logical basis, it rotates about an axis tilted by 120° from z. Two non-parallel axes are enough for any rotation (using sequences of pulses, the same way Euler angles work). DiVincenzo and colleagues showed in 2000 that exchange alone is universal for such encoded qubits, including two-qubit gates between encoded qubits [39].

What it takes in practice

HRL Laboratories demonstrated universal logic with encoded exchange-only qubits in Si/SiGe in 2023 [40]. In 2026, HRL's open-source spinQICK work showed coherent control, state preparation and readout of a triangular EO qubit using a ZCU216 RFSoC [11]. That paper is the clearest public description of what an EO qubit needs from its controller:

  • 14 baseband DAC channels at 6.88 GSPS, plus 2 channels with DDS for the readout stimulus, all with DC-coupled amplifiers (TI LMH5401 and THS3491 stages).
  • Exchange pulses of 10 ns, digitally pre-distorted to compensate the amplifier chain's response, with about 40 ns gaps between pulses.
  • A crosstalk-compensation matrix in FPGA logic, so that each exchange pulse is accompanied by compensating pulses on neighbouring gates (virtual exchange axes).
  • PSB readout with a reference measurement every shot, a 1 MHz AC charge-sensor excitation, and real-time demodulation, with SNR of 5–6.

EO qubits are free from microwave hardware, but in return they need many fast, DC-coupled, low-noise, well-calibrated baseband channels. HRL found that noise added by the room-temperature pulse amplifiers was visible in the qubit's coherence [11].

13.4Other encodings you will meet

EncodingDots / electronsControlNotes
Resonant exchange (RX) qubit3 dots, 3 electronsAlways-on exchange + microwave on a gate (RF at the qubit splitting, ~GHz)An EO variant with resonant driving
Hybrid qubit2 dots, 3 electronsBaseband or microwave at GHzMixes spin and charge states for speed; more charge-noise sensitivity
Charge qubit2 dots, 1 electronDetuning pulses or microwaves at \(2t_c/h\)Fast but coherence of ns; used for coupling to resonators
Flopping-mode spin qubit2 dots, 1 electronMicrowave EDSR near the interdot transitionLarge drive at low power
Hole spin qubits (Ge, Si)1 dot per qubitEDSR via intrinsic spin–orbit, often at low fieldsNo micromagnet; anisotropic g-factor [12]
Donor qubits (P in Si)1 donorESR (electron) and NMR (nucleus)Extremely long nuclear coherence

13.5Comparing the main encodings

Loss–DiVincenzoSinglet–tripletExchange-only
Dots per qubit123
Single-qubit controlMicrowave (ESR/EDSR) at 2–40 GHzBaseband exchange + static ΔBzBaseband exchange only
Fast DAC channels neededOne microwave line per few qubits + baseband for readout and two-qubit gates2 baseband per qubit3+ baseband per qubit
ReadoutElzerman or PSB (with a partner)PSB (natural)PSB on one pair
Main noise sensitivityCharge noise via micromagnet gradientCharge noise in J; ΔBz noiseCharge noise in J; hyperfine (if not purified)
Fit with the 4x2Good for microwaves and readout; needs DC-coupled pulses for PSBNeeds 2 DC-coupled fast channels: exactly the 4x2's DAC count, after modificationNeeds more channels than the 4x2 has
On the 4x2

For a singlet–triplet qubit, the 4x2's two DACs are just enough to pulse two gates (P1 and P2, or a plunger and a barrier), but the pulses must be DC-coupled. The board's baluns block DC (Chapter 29). If you modify the outputs (remove the balun, add DC-coupled differential amplifiers, as the QICK-DAWG and spinQICK hardware do for inputs and outputs respectively [41, 10]), you still need a separate readout source, because both DACs are busy with gate pulses. One solution is to use the readout as an AC excitation through an ADC-side circuit, or to add a second board. For exchange-only qubits, a ZCU216 (16 DACs) or several synchronised boards are the realistic route.

Check yourself

1. Why can exchange alone not rotate a single-spin (LD) qubit, but can rotate an S–T₀ qubit?

Show answer
Exchange \(J\,\vec S_1\cdot\vec S_2\) conserves total spin and total \(S_z\); it cannot flip one spin's \(S_z\) on its own. An LD qubit's states differ in \(S_z\). The S–T₀ qubit's states have the same \(S_z = 0\) but different total spin, which exchange does split.

2. In an S–T₀ qubit, what happens if \(\Delta E_Z = 0\)?

Show answer
Only z rotations (exchange) are available; you cannot rotate between S and T₀ from the poles. Universal control needs a second axis, so a field difference (micromagnet or nuclear polarisation) is essential, or an alternative such as resonant exchange driving.

3. Count the fast DC-coupled channels a single EO qubit needs at minimum, and compare with the 4x2.

Show answer
At least two exchange (barrier) gates, J₁₂ and J₂₃, plus usually plunger pulses for initialisation and PSB readout: in practice 3–6 fast channels per EO qubit. The 4x2 has 2 DACs, both AC-coupled, so it cannot run an EO qubit alone.
Summary
  • Encoded qubits use the joint state of several spins so that exchange, switched by baseband pulses, provides rotations.
  • S–T₀: two spins, axes J (z) and ΔEZ (x); natural PSB readout; ns pulses on two gates.
  • EO: three spins, two or three exchange axes 120° apart; universal with exchange alone; demonstrated by HRL, including with spinQICK on a ZCU216.
  • These encodings trade microwave hardware for many fast, DC-coupled, low-noise baseband channels.

Part III · Spin qubits · Chapter 14

Two-qubit gates and multi-qubit devices

Why you need this

A quantum computer needs entangling gates. For spins they all come from the exchange interaction, switched on for tens of nanoseconds by a barrier-gate pulse while single-qubit microwave pulses correct phases and rotate targets. Programming a two-qubit gate means synchronising a shaped baseband pulse, one or more microwave bursts and a readout, all to within a nanosecond, which is the most demanding thing you will ask of a controller. This chapter explains the physics behind the three standard gates and what their pulses look like.

14.1Two spins with exchange and different Zeeman energies

Two LD qubits in neighbouring dots, with Zeeman energies \(E_{Z1}\) and \(E_{Z2}\) (different, thanks to the micromagnet), coupled by exchange \(J\):

\[ H = \frac{E_{Z1}}{2}\sigma_z^{(1)} + \frac{E_{Z2}}{2}\sigma_z^{(2)} + \frac{J}{4}\big(\vec\sigma^{(1)}\cdot\vec\sigma^{(2)} - 1\big). \]

Write \(\Delta E_Z = E_{Z1} - E_{Z2}\). Two regimes give two different kinds of gate:

  • \(J \ll \Delta E_Z\): the flip-flop part of exchange (\(\sigma_x\sigma_x + \sigma_y\sigma_y\)) connects \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) and \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\), which differ in energy by \(\Delta E_Z\). It is strongly off-resonant and has almost no effect. What remains is the Ising part \(\tfrac J4\sigma_z\sigma_z\): a controlled phase.
  • \(J \gg \Delta E_Z\): exchange dominates and swaps the two spins: a SWAP gate.

Silicon micromagnet devices typically have \(\Delta E_Z/h\) of tens to hundreds of MHz and operate in the first regime.

14.2The CZ (controlled-phase) gate

In the regime \(J\ll\Delta E_Z\), the four computational states stay (nearly) product states, and their energies are

\[ E_{\uparrow\uparrow} = \bar E_Z,\quad E_{\downarrow\downarrow} = -\bar E_Z,\quad E_{\uparrow\downarrow} = \tfrac{\Delta E_Z}{2} - \tfrac{J}{2},\quad E_{\downarrow\uparrow} = -\tfrac{\Delta E_Z}{2} - \tfrac{J}{2}, \]

with \(\bar E_Z = (E_{Z1}+E_{Z2})/2\). The antiparallel states are lowered by \(J/2\) each. Over a pulse during which exchange is on, the four states pick up phases; subtracting the single-qubit parts (which a virtual Z on each qubit can undo) leaves a conditional phase

\[ \phi_{CP} = \frac{1}{\hbar}\int J(t)\,dt . \]

When \(\phi_{CP} = \pi\), the gate is CZ = diag(1, 1, 1, −1) up to single-qubit Z rotations. For a constant \(J\), the gate time is \(t_{CZ} = h/(2J)\).

Worked example

With \(J/h = 5\) MHz during the pulse, \(t_{CZ} = 1/(2\times5\ \text{MHz}) = 100\) ns. With \(\Delta E_Z/h = 100\) MHz, \(J/\Delta E_Z = 0.05\): small enough that the swap-like error is small, provided the pulse is turned on and off smoothly. Silicon experiments typically use CZ gates of 50–200 ns.

Why the pulse shape matters

Turning \(J\) on suddenly excites unwanted transitions between \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) and \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\), because the eigenstates change abruptly. A smooth envelope (for example a cosine or Hann window) keeps the evolution adiabatic with respect to \(\Delta E_Z\), so the states follow the slowly changing eigenstates and only acquire phase. The silicon experiments that crossed 99% two-qubit fidelity all used carefully shaped barrier pulses and calibrated the single-qubit phase corrections [14, 15, 22]. A further subtlety: the barrier pulse also shifts the dot potentials slightly through cross-capacitance, so the plungers are compensated with virtual-gate pulses at the same time.

14.3The CROT (conditional rotation) gate

While \(J\) is on, the frequency of qubit 2 depends on the state of qubit 1: from the energies above, qubit 2's transition is at \(f_2 \pm J/(2h)\). The spectrum splits into four lines.

A microwave π pulse at one of the four frequencies, long enough to resolve the \(J\) splitting (pulse bandwidth smaller than \(J/h\)), flips the target only for one control state. This is a CROT, equivalent to a CNOT up to single-qubit phases. It needs exchange on during a frequency-selective microwave pulse, so both baseband and microwave channels must be synchronised.

14.4The SWAP gate

When \(J \gg \Delta E_Z\), the eigenstates of the two spins become singlet and triplets, and a pulse with \(\int J\,dt/\hbar = \pi\) exchanges the two spin states: \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\to\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\). The √SWAP (half the pulse area) is entangling and universal together with single-qubit gates. SWAP gates are also useful to move quantum information along a chain without moving electrons. They need large, fast exchange pulses, and residual \(\Delta E_Z\) causes errors unless the pulse is short or the field difference is small.

14.5Where the field stands

In 2022, three groups demonstrated two-qubit gates in silicon above 99% fidelity: Delft (Xue et al.), RIKEN (Noiri et al.) and Princeton (Mills et al.), all in Si/SiGe with micromagnets [14, 15, 22]. Delft operated a six-qubit processor with universal control the same year [16]. HRL demonstrated universal logic between exchange-only encoded qubits [40]. The open questions now are mostly about scale: uniformity of many qubits, crosstalk, calibration effort, wiring and control electronics. That last point is exactly where open-source RFSoC controllers come in.

14.6Scaling beyond nearest neighbours

  • Linear arrays: 4–12 dots in a line, each with plunger and barrier gates, read by sensors at the sides [16].
  • 2D arrays: 2×2 and larger, with more complex gate stacks.
  • Shuttling: moving electrons coherently along a channel with a travelling potential, to link distant qubit regions. Shuttling with "conveyor-belt" gates uses several phase-shifted sinusoids at MHz frequencies on a set of gates, a natural task for multi-channel DACs.
  • Spin–photon coupling: coupling spins to a superconducting microwave resonator, for long-range interactions.
On the 4x2

A minimal CZ or CROT experiment on two LD qubits needs at least:

  • one microwave channel (EDSR for both qubits, frequency-multiplexed),
  • one DC-coupled fast baseband channel for the barrier (exchange) pulse, plus plunger compensation,
  • one or two baseband channels for the PSB readout pulse on the plungers,
  • one readout carrier and one ADC.

That is three to five DAC channels; the 4x2 has two, both AC-coupled. Realistically, a two-qubit experiment uses the 4x2 for readout and microwaves together with a DC-coupled AWG for the gate pulses, or moves to a larger board. Chapter 44 discusses how to synchronise them and what the 4x2 can still contribute, such as real-time feedback and calibration loops.

Check yourself

1. Why does a CZ gate require \(J \ll \Delta E_Z\), while a SWAP requires \(J\gg\Delta E_Z\)?

Show answer
When \(\Delta E_Z\) dominates, the flip-flop term is off-resonant, so exchange only adds a state-dependent energy shift (an Ising coupling), giving a controlled phase. When \(J\) dominates, the flip-flop term is resonant and exchanges the spin states.

2. \(J/h = 2\) MHz. How long is the CZ gate? How long must a CROT π pulse be, at least, to resolve the J-split lines?

Show answer
\(t_{CZ} = 1/(2\times2\ \text{MHz}) = 250\) ns. For the CROT, choose the Rabi frequency so that the unwanted line (detuned by \(J/h\)) completes a whole number of full rotations while the wanted line gets exactly π. For a square pulse this "synchronisation" condition gives \(f_R = (J/h)/\sqrt{3} \approx 1.15\) MHz (π pulse ≈ 430 ns) or, with more margin, \(f_R = (J/h)/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.52\) MHz (π pulse ≈ 1 µs).
Summary
  • All spin two-qubit gates use exchange \(J\), switched by barrier-gate pulses.
  • \(J\ll\Delta E_Z\): CZ with \(\phi_{CP} = \int J\,dt/\hbar = \pi\); smooth pulses keep it adiabatic.
  • With exchange on, qubit frequencies split by \(J/h\): a selective microwave π pulse makes a CROT (CNOT).
  • \(J\gg\Delta E_Z\): SWAP and √SWAP.
  • Silicon passed 99% two-qubit fidelity in 2022; scaling now depends heavily on control electronics.
PreviousChapter 13 · Singlet–triplet, exchange-only and other encoded qubitsNextChapter 15 · Tuning a device: from first cooldown to a working qubit

Part III · Spin qubits · Chapter 15

Tuning a device: from first cooldown to a working qubit

Why you need this

Most of the time in a spin-qubit lab is not spent running elegant gate sequences. It is spent getting a new device from "a chip with wires" to "a qubit that can be measured": checking gates, forming dots, finding the last electron, setting up readout, finding the resonance. This chapter walks through that sequence in the order labs actually do it, with the measurement used at each step, how long it typically takes, and which steps the RFSoC 4x2 speeds up. It ties together everything in Parts II and III.

15.1Step 1: at room temperature

Before cooling, measure each gate's leakage to every other gate and to the 2DEG contacts (should be open circuit, above GΩ), and each ohmic contact's resistance to the others (usually kΩ–MΩ at room temperature through the substrate, which disappears at low temperature in undoped wafers). Record a bond map linking every device pad to a fridge line and a breakout-box pin. Ground all lines while handling: nanometre-scale gates are destroyed by electrostatic discharge, and one zap can kill a device.

15.2Step 2: cooldown checks

A dilution refrigerator cooldown takes about 1–3 days (Chapter 16). At base temperature, repeat the leakage checks, verify that every line works, and record the fridge temperatures and the attenuation of RF lines. Many problems later on (noisy readout, hot electrons, missing pulses) come from a line that was never tested.

15.3Step 3: turn-on and pinch-off

In an undoped Si/SiGe device, nothing conducts until gates pull in electrons. A global turn-on ramps all accumulation, plunger and barrier gates together while measuring current between two ohmic contacts with a small bias (say 100 µV) and a lock-in. Current appears at the turn-on (threshold) voltage, typically somewhere between 0.5 and 2 V depending on the stack. Then, with the channel conducting, sweep each barrier down individually: a pinch-off curve shows the voltage at which it closes the channel. Pinch-off voltages tell you which gates work and their useful ranges. Hysteresis or sudden jumps indicate charge traps.

Common mistake

Ramping gates quickly or to too high a voltage. Large voltages can push charge into the oxide or break it down. Labs set software limits on every gate and ramp rates (for example 10–50 mV/s), and keep a log of the maximum voltage each gate has seen.

15.4Step 4: the charge sensor

Form the sensor dot with its own plunger and barriers, find its Coulomb peaks, and measure diamonds to get its lever arm and charging energy (Chapter 7). Then set up RF reflectometry: sweep the carrier frequency to find the tank resonance, check how deep the dip is (matching), and sweep the carrier power to find the highest power that does not broaden the Coulomb peaks. Finally, park the sensor on the steepest flank of a peak.

On the 4x2

This is the first step where the 4x2 does the measuring. A frequency sweep of the reflected signal is a short QICK program (or even a simple PYNQ loop) with the DAC as source and the ADC with QICK's demodulator as receiver. Power sweeps use the generator gain. Chapter 39 gives the procedure and code.

15.5Step 5: forming the qubit dots

Using the sensor, take charge stability diagrams in pairs of plunger voltages. Find the charge transitions of each qubit dot, then empty the dots until the last transition is found. Measure the slopes of the lines to build the virtual-gate matrix (Chapter 8), then re-measure in virtual coordinates. Adjust barriers to set tunnel rates to the reservoirs (for loading and Elzerman readout, typically 10 kHz–1 MHz) and the interdot tunnel coupling.

A slow DC-sensor CSD of 100×100 points at 10 ms per point takes almost 2 minutes; with RF readout and a fast raster ("video mode", Chapter 40), the same map can be taken in under a second and refreshed continuously while you turn knobs. This difference changes how tuning feels: from waiting to watching.

15.6Step 6: spin readout

For PSB, scan the readout point near the \((1,1)\)–\((2,0)\) transition with a pulse sequence that alternately prepares singlets and mixed states, and look for the triangle where the signal depends on the spin state (Chapter 11). For Elzerman readout, find the plunger voltage where the Fermi level sits between the spin-split levels. Then record single-shot histograms, set a threshold and estimate readout fidelity. Measure \(T_1\) with load–wait–read.

15.7Step 7: finding the resonance

Now the magnetic field is set and microwaves are applied. Because the micromagnet adds an unknown field (often 50–300 mT), you do not know exactly where the resonance is. Labs use long, strong bursts (or frequency chirps that adiabatically invert the spin over a wide band) and sweep frequency against magnetic field. The resonance appears as a line whose slope gives \(g\mu_B/h\). Two lines mean two qubits. This search over GHz with MHz-wide lines can take hours, so efficient spectroscopy matters.

15.8Step 8: coherent control and calibration

With the resonance found: Rabi oscillations (sets π time and confirms coherent driving), a Rabi chevron (refines the frequency), Ramsey (precise frequency and \(T_2^*\)), Hahn echo (\(T_2\)), and AllXY (pulse calibration). This is the point where you can say you have a qubit.

15.9Steps 9 and 10: benchmarking and two-qubit gates

Randomised benchmarking gives single-qubit gate fidelities. For two qubits, calibrate exchange (measure \(J\) versus barrier voltage, often with "fingerprint" plots of exchange oscillations versus pulse amplitude and detuning, as in the spinQICK EO work [11]), then the CZ or CROT gate, then Bell-state tomography.

15.10Keeping it working

A tuned device does not stay tuned. Charge noise drifts the qubit frequencies, a single charge trap can jump and shift a dot by a fraction of a millivolt, and the sensor's working point wanders. Labs therefore schedule recalibrations (Ramsey frequency checks every few minutes, sensor re-centring, readout threshold updates) and log every parameter. Automating these tasks is an active research area [27]. HRL's spinQICK includes experiments for electrostatic tune-up (charge stability, gate action, global turn-on) as well as qubit calibrations [10].

In the lab

Realistic timescales for a well-equipped group with a known device design: steps 1–3 take a day or two after cooldown; steps 4–6 one to several weeks; finding and calibrating the first qubit another week or more. A new device design or a new heterostructure can take months. Fast readout and automation shorten every step after step 3.

Check yourself

1. Why is the charge sensor tuned before the qubit dots?

Show answer
All later steps (finding transitions, the last electron, readout) are measured with the sensor, because qubit dots are too opaque for transport. Without a working sensor you cannot see the qubit dots at all.

2. A 200 × 200 CSD takes how long at 10 ms per point (DC) versus 5 µs per point (RF raster)?

Show answer
40 000 points: 400 s (almost 7 minutes) with DC readout, 0.2 s with RF raster readout, ignoring overheads.
Summary
  • Tuning goes: room-temperature checks → cooldown checks → turn-on and pinch-off → sensor → qubit dots → spin readout → resonance → coherent control → benchmarking → two-qubit gates.
  • Early steps use DC instruments; from the sensor onward, fast RF readout and pulsed control dominate.
  • Devices drift, so recalibration and logging are part of normal operation.

Part IV · The lab · Chapter 16

The dilution refrigerator and its wiring

Why you need this

Every signal from your RFSoC reaches the qubit only after travelling a metre or more through a dilution refrigerator, through attenuators, filters and bias tees that change its amplitude, shape and noise. If you do not know what is in the lines, you cannot predict the pulse amplitude at the gate, you cannot tell why your electrons are hot, and you can easily heat the mixing chamber with too much microwave power. This chapter explains how the refrigerator works and how its lines are designed, with numbers you can use to plan power levels.

16.1How a dilution refrigerator reaches 10 mK

A modern "dry" dilution refrigerator cools in stages, each a copper plate hanging below the previous one inside nested radiation shields and a vacuum can [42]:

  1. Pulse-tube cryocooler (no liquid helium bath): a closed-cycle helium gas cooler driven by a compressor. Its first stage cools a plate and shield to about 40–60 K; its second stage reaches about 3–4 K with roughly 1 W of cooling power.
  2. The dilution unit uses a mixture of helium-3 and helium-4. Below about 0.87 K the mixture separates into a 3He-rich phase floating on a 3He-poor (dilute) phase. In the mixing chamber, 3He atoms crossing from the rich to the dilute phase absorb heat, like evaporation. The still (about 0.7–1 K) pumps 3He out of the dilute phase, which is then recondensed and returned through heat exchangers. This cycle reaches about 10 mK at the mixing chamber.

Cooling power falls steeply with temperature: roughly a watt at 4 K, a few tens of milliwatts at the still, hundreds of microwatts at 100 mK, and only around 10–20 µW at 20 mK. Every watt of heat you bring down with wiring or microwaves counts against these budgets [43].

StageTypical temperatureCooling power (order of magnitude)What sits there
50 K plate40–60 Ktens of Wfirst thermal anchors, radiation shield
4 K plate3–4 K~1 Wcryogenic (HEMT) amplifiers, first attenuators, magnet
Still0.7–1 K~10–40 mWattenuators, filters
Cold plate~100 mK~100 µWattenuators
Mixing chamber (MXC)~10 mK~10–20 µW at 20 mKsample, final filters, bias tees, couplers

A cooldown from room temperature takes one to three days; warming up takes about a day. Changing a sample therefore costs several days, which is why labs test devices carefully before cooling and plan wiring changes well in advance.

16.2The magnet

Spin experiments need a static field of 0.1–2 T. It comes from a superconducting solenoid (or a vector magnet with two or three coils) mounted on the 4 K plate around the sample. For Si/SiGe devices with micromagnets, the field is usually applied in the plane of the chip. Magnets can be put in persistent mode, where a superconducting switch closes the loop and the current circulates without the power supply, giving a very stable field. Field ramps are slow (minutes), so the field is usually changed rarely.

16.3Why the lines need attenuators: thermal noise

Every resistor at temperature \(T\) emits thermal (Johnson) noise with power \(k_BT\) per unit bandwidth into a matched load. A coaxial line connected to room-temperature electronics therefore carries 300 K of noise down to your device, even when the instrument is "off". That noise heats the electrons and drives unwanted transitions.

An attenuator reduces both signal and incoming noise by its factor \(A\) (for example \(A = 100\) for 20 dB), but as a resistive component at temperature \(T_{\text{att}}\) it adds its own thermal noise. The output noise temperature is

\[ T_{\text{out}} = \frac{T_{\text{in}}}{A} + \Big(1 - \frac1A\Big)T_{\text{att}} . \]

So each attenuator replaces most of the incoming noise with noise at its own, lower temperature. Placing attenuators at successively colder stages steps the noise temperature down.

Worked example: noise temperature of a readout input line

A line has −20 dB at 4 K, −10 dB at the still (0.8 K) and −20 dB at the mixing chamber (20 mK). Starting from 300 K:

  • After 4 K: \(300/100 + 0.99\times4 = 6.96\) K.
  • After the still: \(6.96/10 + 0.9\times0.8 = 1.42\) K.
  • After the MXC: \(1.42/100 + 0.99\times0.02 = 0.034\) K = 34 mK.

The noise reaching the sample is equivalent to 34 mK, close to the base temperature. Total attenuation is 50 dB. A −10 dBm source then gives −60 dBm at the coupler; add the coupler's −20 dB and the sample sees −80 dBm. For reflectometry you would add about 20–30 dB more to reach −100 to −110 dBm.

16.4The different kinds of lines

LineTypical constructionBandwidth at the deviceTypical attenuation / filtering
DC gate lines (many, 24–100)twisted pairs of resistive wire (constantan, phosphor bronze), thermally anchored at every stageDC to ~10 Hz–100 kHzRC low-pass and metal-powder or "Ag-epoxy" filters at the MXC to block RF noise
Fast gate lines (baseband pulses)coax: stainless steel or CuNi above 4 K, often superconducting NbTi belowDC (via bias tee: ~Hz) to a few GHz−10 to −30 dB total, low-pass filters; kept low so pulses stay large
Microwave drive (EDSR)coax as aboveup to 20–40 GHz−20 to −40 dB total
Readout inputcoax100 MHz–1 GHz (reflectometry)−40 to −60 dB plus a directional coupler
Readout outputcoax, superconducting between MXC and 4 Ksameno attenuation; cryogenic amplifier at 4 K (sometimes circulators or a parametric amplifier first)

Values are typical for spin-qubit setups and vary between labs [43, 29].

Combining DC and fast signals: bias tees and adders

A gate often needs both a precise DC voltage (from the DC source, through a heavily filtered line) and fast pulses (from an AWG, through a coax). A bias tee on the sample PCB combines them: the DC arrives through a large resistor (for example 1–10 MΩ), the pulses through a capacitor (for example 10–100 nF). This RC network passes pulses above its cut-off \(1/(2\pi RC)\), typically well below 1 Hz to a few Hz, so pulses of microseconds to milliseconds pass with little droop. Some groups instead use resistive "adder" circuits, which are DC-coupled for the fast signal as well; HRL's spinQICK setup used a room-temperature voltage divider combined with a resistive bias tee at the mixing chamber [11].

Common mistake

Forgetting that a bias tee is a high-pass filter for the pulse path. A long square pulse through an RC bias tee with time constant \(\tau_{RC}\) droops exponentially, and any pulse sequence with a non-zero average shifts the gate's DC level over time. For \(\tau_{RC} = 0.1\) s, a 1 ms pulse droops by 1%. The 4x2's own outputs add a second high-pass, from the board's baluns, at a much higher frequency (Chapter 29).

16.5The sample PCB

The device chip is glued and wire-bonded to a printed circuit board mounted on the cold finger of the mixing chamber. The PCB carries the bias tees, RC filters on DC lines, the reflectometry inductor and sometimes varactors for tuning the match, and connectors to the fridge wiring. Parasitic capacitance of its traces and bond pads sets the reflectometry resonance (Chapter 9), so PCB design is part of readout design.

16.6Electron temperature, grounding and other enemies

  • Electron temperature is usually 30–150 mK even when the MXC is at 10 mK. Causes: insufficient filtering of DC lines, noise on fast lines, poor thermalisation of the PCB, and heating by microwaves. Measure it from Coulomb-peak widths (Chapter 7).
  • Ground loops between instruments, fridge and PC inject mains-frequency (50/60 Hz) noise. Use a single grounding point, isolation transformers or DC blocks, and battery- or isolated-powered DC sources.
  • Pulse-tube vibrations at about 1.4 Hz and harmonics can appear as noise, through moving cables (triboelectric charge) or microphonics.
  • Microwave heating: EDSR drive power dissipated in attenuators and in the device warms the MXC and the electrons. Long bursts at high power can warm the MXC by several mK.

16.7Hot qubits

Silicon spin qubits have been operated at temperatures around 1 K, where the cooling power is a thousand times larger. Readout then relies on PSB (which tolerates temperature) and coherence is shorter. This research direction matters for integrating cryogenic control electronics next to the qubits in the future [7].

On the 4x2

The 4x2 sits at room temperature, next to the fridge. Use these rules when connecting it:

  • Know the attenuation and filtering of every line before connecting a DAC output. Write a power budget from DAC output to device (Chapter 18).
  • Keep the board's ground and the fridge's ground connected at one point only. Use DC blocks or isolators on SMA lines if you see mains-frequency pickup.
  • The ADC input must never see more than its maximum rated power. After a HEMT (+35 dB) and a room-temperature amplifier (+30 dB), a −100 dBm readout signal becomes about −35 dBm, comfortably within range; but a large DAC signal leaking through the coupler could be amplified far above that. Add a limiter or extra attenuation while setting up (Appendix B).
Check yourself

1. Why are attenuators placed at several stages instead of one big attenuator at the mixing chamber?

Show answer
An attenuator dissipates the power it removes. Removing the large thermal noise and signal power at the 4 K stage (with ~1 W cooling) is cheap; doing it all at the MXC (~µW) would heat it. Stepping down also reduces the noise temperature progressively.

2. A fast gate line has −20 dB total attenuation. You want a 5 mV pulse at the gate. What amplitude must the source produce (ignoring other losses)?

Show answer
−20 dB in voltage is a factor 10, so 50 mV. (Remember that a 50 Ω source driving a high-impedance gate through a matched line can double the voltage at an unterminated end; real setups need calibration of the actual amplitude at the device, for example with photon-assisted tunnelling or by measuring pulse-induced shifts of charge transitions.)
Summary
  • A dry dilution refrigerator uses a pulse tube to ~4 K and 3He/4He dilution to ~10 mK, with cooling power falling from ~1 W (4 K) to ~10 µW (20 mK).
  • Attenuators at successive stages reduce thermal noise; \(T_{\text{out}} = T_{\text{in}}/A + (1-1/A)T_{\text{att}}\).
  • DC lines are heavily filtered; fast lines are lightly attenuated coax; readout outputs have a cryogenic amplifier at 4 K.
  • Bias tees on the sample PCB combine DC and pulses but act as high-pass filters for the pulses.
  • Electron temperature, grounding and microwave heating are the common practical problems.

Part IV · The lab · Chapter 17

The traditional instrument rack, box by box

Why you need this

To judge what an RFSoC 4x2 can do for your lab, you need to know what it replaces. A spin-qubit setup has grown out of a rack of separate instruments, each solving one problem: DC sources, current amplifiers, lock-ins, AWGs, microwave sources, mixers, digitisers. Commercial "qubit controllers" bundle several of them. This chapter describes each box, what its key specifications mean, and which jobs the 4x2 with QICK can take over, which it can share and which it cannot do.

17.1The boxes in a typical spin-qubit rack

Multi-channel DC voltage sources

One channel per gate, often 24–48 channels or more, with very low noise (µV-level), high resolution (20–25 bits over ±5–10 V), and slow, smooth ramping. Examples in the community include the QDevil QDAC and the Basel "LNHR" DAC. They set the electrostatic landscape and must not add noise, because voltage noise on a gate is charge noise. Some can step quickly when triggered, which allows coarse raster scans for CSDs. HRL's spinQICK setup used a custom 20-bit DC source, and a 32-channel 20-bit DAC add-on ("QuACK") designed to be triggered by QICK is in development [11, 10].

Current preamplifier and lock-in amplifier

For transport (Coulomb peaks, diamonds, pinch-offs) and DC charge sensing: a transimpedance amplifier converts nA–pA currents to volts (bandwidth kHz at high gain), and a lock-in amplifier applies a small AC excitation (Hz–kHz) and measures the response at that frequency with a narrow bandwidth, rejecting noise. Digital lock-ins (Stanford Research, Zurich Instruments) are standard.

Arbitrary waveform generator (AWG)

For fast baseband gate pulses: DC-coupled outputs with 1–2.5 GSa/s and 12–16 bits, waveform memories of millions of samples, sequencing and marker outputs for triggers. Key specifications: rise time (sub-ns), amplitude range (±1 V or more), noise, and whether it is DC-coupled. A typical spin experiment needs 4–16 such channels.

Microwave source and IQ modulation

For EDSR drive: a low-phase-noise source at 2–40 GHz (the local oscillator, LO) combined in an IQ mixer with two baseband waveforms (I and Q) from AWG channels. The mixer output is \(I(t)\cos\omega_{LO}t - Q(t)\sin\omega_{LO}t\), which lets the AWG control the amplitude, phase and fine frequency of the microwave burst (Chapter 20). Many vector signal generators include the IQ modulator internally.

Digitiser and demodulator

For reflectometry and single-shot readout: an ADC card or instrument (hundreds of MSa/s to GSa/s) and demodulation, either analog (an IQ mixer driven by the carrier, then a slow digitiser) or digital (in an FPGA). Real-time integration and thresholding inside the instrument avoid sending raw data to the PC.

Trigger and timing hardware

Everything above must stay synchronised to a few nanoseconds. Labs distribute a 10 MHz reference clock to all instruments and use one instrument (often the AWG) as the master that triggers the others. Jitter between instruments and the latency of triggering are recurring pain points.

Measurement and test equipment

Oscilloscope (check pulse shapes), spectrum analyser (check microwave power and spurs), vector network analyser (find resonator frequencies, measure line attenuation), multimeters.

Cryogenic and magnet electronics

Superconducting magnet power supply, temperature controller, HEMT amplifier bias supply. These are not replaced by any qubit controller.

17.2Integrated qubit controllers

Since about 2019, several companies sell integrated controllers that combine AWG, microwave and digitiser functions with an on-board real-time processor: for example Quantum Machines (OPX family), Zurich Instruments (HDAWG, SHFQC and related products), Qblox (Cluster modules) and Keysight (QCS). Their main advantages for spin qubits are many synchronised channels, DC-coupled baseband outputs, built-in IQ upconversion to tens of GHz, low-latency feedback and polished software. Their main disadvantage is cost, typically tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars for a multi-qubit setup. Many leading spin-qubit groups use them; the 2026 FPGA feedback demonstration on a silicon double dot used an OPX [21].

Open-source RFSoC controllers (QICK, QubiC, and the spinQICK extension) target the same functions at a fraction of the price, about $1000 per high-speed DAC channel according to HRL [11], with the trade-off that you assemble the analog front end and maintain the software yourself. Several companies now sell RFSoC boxes with front ends designed for QICK [44].

17.3What the 4x2 with QICK can take over

Rack function4x2 + QICKNotes
Readout carrier source (100 MHz–1 GHz)YesOne DAC channel with DDS, phase-coherent with the readout
Digitiser + demodulator + integratorYesADC + QICK readout blocks; I/Q per shot, decimated traces, DDR4 buffer for long records
Pulse sequencer and timing masterYestProcessor with ~2.4 ns timing; loops, branching, feedback
Trigger outputs to other instrumentsYes8 PMOD digital outputs controlled by the tProcessor
Microwave drive up to ~5 GHzYesDirect synthesis, first Nyquist zone
Microwave drive 5–10 GHzPartlySecond Nyquist zone with reduced, frequency-dependent power
Microwave drive >10 GHzWith external mixer + LOThe 4x2 provides the IF waveform

Lock-in at kHzNoBaluns block low frequencies
DC gate voltagesNoNeed a DC source (can be triggered by PMOD outputs)
Many channelsNo2 DACs, 4 ADCs (2 used by QICK standard firmware)

Board facts from the board documentation and the QICK firmware [1, 2, 3].

In the lab

A sensible way to bring a 4x2 into an existing lab is as a readout and timing engine: it generates the reflectometry carrier, demodulates the sensor signal in real time, and triggers the AWG and DC source with its PMOD outputs. Microwave drive can be added on its second DAC (directly or with a mixer). This uses the board's strengths and leaves the baseband pulsing to a DC-coupled instrument until you decide whether to modify the board or move to a larger RFSoC.

Check yourself

1. Which instruments in a spin-qubit rack add noise directly to the qubit's electrostatic environment, and why does that matter?

Show answer
The DC gate sources and the fast-pulse AWG (and any amplifiers after them). Their voltage noise on gates moves the dots' potentials, which is indistinguishable from charge noise and dephases the qubits.

2. Why are integrated controllers attractive compared with separate instruments?

Show answer
Synchronisation and latency: all channels share one clock and one real-time processor, so pulses, readout and feedback happen within nanoseconds without external triggering, and one program describes the whole experiment.
Summary
  • A rack contains DC sources, current amplifiers and lock-ins, AWGs, microwave sources with IQ mixers, digitisers, timing hardware and test equipment.
  • Commercial integrated controllers combine many of these with real-time processors at high cost; RFSoC-based open-source controllers aim at the same functions cheaply.
  • The 4x2 + QICK can replace the readout source, digitiser, demodulator, sequencer, triggers and microwave drive up to a few GHz; it cannot replace DC sources, kHz lock-ins or DC-coupled baseband AWGs without modification.

Part V · Signals and software-defined radio · Chapter 18

Signals, power, decibels and impedance

Why you need this

From here on, the book moves from physics to electronics. Every cable you connect to the RFSoC carries a signal described by amplitude, frequency and phase, measured in dBm, flowing through 50 Ω coax into components with gains and losses in dB. If you can do power budgets in your head, you can predict what reaches the device, avoid damaging the ADC, and understand data sheets. This chapter covers the vocabulary every RF engineer uses, following the fundamentals chapters of AMD's SDR book [5] and standard microwave engineering [30].

18.1Sine waves: amplitude, frequency and phase

The basic signal of RF engineering is the sinusoid

\[ v(t) = A\cos(2\pi f t + \phi) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi). \]
  • \(A\) is the amplitude (peak voltage). The peak-to-peak value is \(2A\) and the RMS value is \(A/\sqrt2\).
  • \(f\) is the frequency in Hz; its inverse \(T = 1/f\) is the period; \(\omega = 2\pi f\) is the angular frequency in rad/s.
  • \(\phi\) is the phase in radians or degrees: a shift of the wave along the time axis by \(\phi/\omega\).

Why sinusoids? Because linear systems (cables, filters, amplifiers in their linear range) do not change the frequency of a sinusoid; they only change its amplitude and phase. Any signal can be written as a sum of sinusoids (Fourier analysis, Chapter 21), so knowing a system's effect on each frequency tells you its effect on everything.

18.2Power, decibels and dBm

The average power a sinusoid delivers into a resistance \(R\) is

\[ P = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R} = \frac{A^2}{2R} . \]

RF power spans enormous ranges (from watts to below a femtowatt), so it is expressed logarithmically. A ratio of powers in decibels is \(10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1)\). For voltages (or currents) across the same resistance, power goes as voltage squared, so the voltage ratio in dB is \(20\log_{10}(V_2/V_1)\). The unit dBm is power relative to 1 mW:

\[ P_{\text{dBm}} = 10\log_{10}\frac{P}{1\ \text{mW}} . \]
PowerdBmRMS voltage in 50 ΩAmplitude in 50 Ω
1 W+307.07 V10 V
10 mW+10707 mV1 V
1 mW0224 mV316 mV
1 µW−307.07 mV10 mV
1 nW−60224 µV316 µV
10 fW−1100.71 µV1 µV

Rules of thumb: +3 dB doubles power, +10 dB multiplies it by 10, +6 dB doubles voltage, +20 dB multiplies voltage by 10. Gains and losses in a chain simply add in dB, which is why engineers love them. Related units you will meet:

  • dBc: power relative to the carrier (for spurs and harmonics, e.g. "−60 dBc").
  • dBFS: power relative to a converter's full-scale signal (for ADC/DAC specs).
  • dBm/Hz and dBFS/Hz: noise power per hertz of bandwidth.

18.3Impedance

For sinusoidal signals, resistors, capacitors and inductors are all described by a complex impedance \(Z = V/I\) (engineers write \(j\) for \(\sqrt{-1}\)):

\[ Z_R = R, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L . \]

A capacitor blocks DC (infinite impedance at \(\omega = 0\)) and passes high frequencies; an inductor does the opposite. That is the whole idea behind bias tees, filters and the reflectometry tank circuit of Chapter 9.

Worked example

A 100 nF DC-blocking capacitor in series with a 50 Ω load forms a high-pass filter with cut-off \(f_c = 1/(2\pi RC) = 1/(2\pi\times50\times10^{-7}) \approx 32\) kHz. Below 32 kHz, the capacitor's impedance exceeds 50 Ω and the signal is increasingly blocked. That is why AC-coupled paths cannot pass slow signals or long flat pulses. The 4x2's SMA paths contain two 100 nF capacitors and a balun (Chapter 29); the balun limits the low-frequency end far more than the capacitors do.

18.4Transmission lines and why everything is 50 Ω

At high frequencies, a cable longer than a small fraction of a wavelength is not a simple wire. It is a transmission line: signals travel along it as waves at about two-thirds of the speed of light (roughly 5 ns per metre in typical coax), and the ratio of voltage to current in a travelling wave is the line's characteristic impedance \(Z_0\), fixed by its geometry. Almost all RF equipment uses \(Z_0 = 50\) Ω, a historical compromise between low loss and high power handling in air-filled coax.

When a wave meets a load with impedance \(Z \ne Z_0\), part of it reflects, with reflection coefficient \(\Gamma = (Z - Z_0)/(Z + Z_0)\) (Chapter 9). Three cases matter for your lab:

  • Matched load (\(Z = 50\) Ω): no reflection. Instruments and attenuators are designed for this.
  • Open end (\(Z\to\infty\)), for example a fast gate line ending on a tiny gate capacitance: \(\Gamma = +1\). The voltage at the open end is twice the incident wave's voltage, and the reflected wave travels back up the line.
  • Short (\(Z = 0\)): \(\Gamma = -1\); the voltage at the end is zero.
Common mistake

Assuming the pulse amplitude at the gate equals the source's nominal 50 Ω amplitude. A gate at the end of a coax is essentially an open circuit at pulse frequencies, so the voltage there is up to twice the incident amplitude (after the line's attenuation), and reflections bounce between gate and source, ringing the pulse. Many groups put a 50 Ω termination or a resistive divider on the sample PCB, or calibrate the real amplitude with the qubit or with charge transitions. Always calibrate pulse amplitude at the device.

18.5Differential signals and baluns

The RFSoC's converters are differential: each DAC output and ADC input is a pair of pins (P and N) carrying opposite voltages, and the signal is their difference. Differential signalling rejects noise that appears equally on both pins. Lab equipment, however, is single-ended: one coax centre conductor relative to ground. A balun (balanced–unbalanced transformer) converts between the two. Transformer baluns are coupled magnetically, so they cannot pass DC, and they work only over a specified frequency range. On the 4x2, each SMA connector reaches the chip through decoupling capacitors and a MACOM MABA-011118 balun rated from 10 MHz to 10 GHz [2]. This one component explains most of the 4x2's limits for spin qubits.

18.6Power budgets

A power budget follows the signal from source to destination, adding gains and subtracting losses in dB. Do one for every new setup.

18.7Thermal noise and noise temperature

A resistor at temperature \(T\) delivers thermal noise power \(P_n = k_BTB\) into a matched load in a bandwidth \(B\). At 290 K this is −174 dBm per hertz, a number worth memorising: in a 1 MHz bandwidth, −174 + 60 = −114 dBm. Amplifiers add noise, described by a noise temperature \(T_N\) (the temperature of a resistor at the input that would produce the same added noise). For a chain of amplifiers with gains \(G_i\) and noise temperatures \(T_i\), the total is given by the Friis formula:

\[ T_{\text{sys}} = T_1 + \frac{T_2}{G_1} + \frac{T_3}{G_1G_2} + \dots \]

The first amplifier dominates when its gain is large. That is why a cryogenic HEMT (\(T_1\) of a few K, \(G_1\) about \(10^3\)–\(10^4\)) at 4 K makes a room-temperature amplifier's 100 K or more nearly irrelevant, and why the HEMT sets the readout SNR [30].

Worked example: readout SNR in 1 µs

The sensor's signal at the device is a change of −110 dBm in reflected power between charge states (a 10 fW difference). The HEMT has \(T_N = 4\) K. Noise power in a bandwidth of 1 MHz (about a 1 µs integration) is \(k_BT_NB = 1.38\times10^{-23}\times4\times10^6 = 5.5\times10^{-17}\) W = −132.6 dBm. The SNR in power is \(-110 - (-132.6) = 22.6\) dB, a factor of about 180 in power, or about 13 in amplitude. Plenty for single-shot readout, which is why a good HEMT at 4 K is essential.

On the 4x2
  • All four ADC and two DAC SMA ports are 50 Ω single-ended (through the baluns) [2].
  • DAC output power is set by the DAC's current mode (QICK's printout for the 4x2 reports "20 mA" mode) and by the digital amplitude (QICK gain, 0 to 1). The maximum output of a Gen3 RF-DAC is of order 0 dBm, and on Gen3 devices it can be adjusted in fine steps with Variable Output Power (VOP) [5, 3]. Measure the actual power at your frequency with a spectrum analyser before relying on a number.
  • The ADC full-scale input is of order +1 dBm; Gen3 ADCs also include a digital step attenuator in front of the converter [5]. Check DS926 for your device's absolute maximum ratings [45].
Check yourself

1. Convert −40 dBm into amplitude in a 50 Ω system.

Show answer
−40 dBm = 100 nW. \(V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{PR} = \sqrt{10^{-7}\times50} = 2.24\) mV, amplitude \(= 3.16\) mV.

2. A chain has a DAC at 0 dBm, −20 dB, −20 dB, −10 dB attenuators and a −20 dB coupler. What power reaches the device?

Show answer
0 − 20 − 20 − 10 − 20 = −70 dBm.

3. Why does a balun block DC?

Show answer
It is a transformer: energy is transferred between windings by a changing magnetic flux, which requires a changing current. A constant (DC) current produces no changing flux, so nothing is coupled.
Summary
  • A sinusoid has amplitude, frequency and phase; power into \(R\) is \(A^2/2R\).
  • dB for ratios (10 log power, 20 log voltage), dBm relative to 1 mW; 0 dBm = 316 mV amplitude in 50 Ω.
  • Capacitors block DC, inductors block high frequencies; transmission lines have a characteristic impedance (50 Ω) and reflect at mismatches; an open gate sees up to twice the incident voltage.
  • The RFSoC's differential converters reach the 4x2's SMA ports through baluns, which block DC.
  • Thermal noise is −174 dBm/Hz at 290 K; the first amplifier (HEMT) sets the system noise.

Part V · Signals and software-defined radio · Chapter 19

Sampling, quantisation and Nyquist zones

Why you need this

The RFSoC is a direct RF-sampling device: its ADCs and DACs work directly at GHz frequencies, without the analog mixers older radios needed. To use it well, you must understand what sampling does to a signal: which frequencies the DAC can produce, where its unwanted images appear, which input frequencies an ADC confuses with each other, and how many effective bits you get. When QICK asks for nqz=1 or nqz=2 when you declare a generator, this chapter tells you what you are choosing [5].

19.1Sampling a signal

An ADC measures the input voltage at regular instants \(t_n = nT_s\), where \(T_s = 1/f_s\) is the sampling period and \(f_s\) the sample rate. The result is a list of numbers \(x[n] = x(nT_s)\). A DAC does the reverse: it turns a list of numbers into a voltage that changes at each sample instant.

The sampling theorem (Nyquist–Shannon) says: a signal containing only frequencies below \(f_s/2\) is completely determined by its samples. The frequency \(f_s/2\) is the Nyquist frequency. Conversely, frequencies above \(f_s/2\) cannot be told apart from frequencies below it.

19.2Aliasing

Sample a cosine at frequency \(f\) and another at \(f' = f_s - f\). At the sample instants,

\[ \cos(2\pi f' nT_s) = \cos(2\pi n - 2\pi f nT_s) = \cos(2\pi f n T_s), \]

so the two produce identical samples. More generally, all frequencies \(|f \pm kf_s|\) for integer \(k\) produce the same samples. This is aliasing.

The frequency axis is divided into Nyquist zones of width \(f_s/2\): zone 1 from 0 to \(f_s/2\), zone 2 from \(f_s/2\) to \(f_s\), zone 3 from \(f_s\) to \(3f_s/2\), and so on. After sampling, every zone folds onto zone 1. Even zones are mirrored (frequency increasing in zone 2 appears decreasing in zone 1).

Worked example: where does it fold?

The QICK readout on the 4x2 samples at \(f_s = 4423.68\) MSPS, so the Nyquist frequency is 2211.84 MHz. An input at 3000 MHz is in zone 2 and appears at \(4423.68 - 3000 = 1423.68\) MHz. An input at 5000 MHz is in zone 3 and appears at \(5000 - 4423.68 = 576.32\) MHz. If your readout carrier is at 576 MHz, a stray 5 GHz signal (for example leakage from a microwave line) would land on top of it. This is why analog filters before ADCs matter.

Using aliasing on purpose: RF sampling

Aliasing is not always bad. If you know your signal is in, say, zone 2, and you filter out everything else, the ADC can digitise it directly and the folding is just a known frequency mapping. This is RF sampling (or undersampling), and it is how the RFSoC's ADCs can digitise signals above their Nyquist frequency, up to their analog input bandwidth (about 6 GHz for the 4x2's ADCs [2]). For reflectometry at a few hundred MHz you do not need it: you work in zone 1.

19.3The DAC side: zero-order hold, sinc roll-off and images

A DAC holds each sample's voltage for one sample period. Mathematically, the output is the ideal sampled signal convolved with a rectangular pulse of width \(T_s\). In frequency, convolution becomes multiplication, and the Fourier transform of a rectangle is a sinc. So the DAC's output spectrum is the ideal spectrum multiplied by

\[ |H(f)| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi f/f_s)}{\pi f/f_s}\right| = |\operatorname{sinc}(f/f_s)| . \]

Two consequences [5]:

  • Roll-off: output power falls with frequency, by about 3.9 dB at \(f_s/2\). Inverse-sinc digital filters can compensate in zone 1.
  • Images: a DAC playing a tone at \(f\) also produces images at \(f_s - f\), \(f_s + f\), \(2f_s - f\), …, weighted by the sinc. These must be filtered if they could reach the device.

Gen3 RF-DACs also offer mix-mode: each sample period is split into two halves of opposite sign, which moves the output response's maximum into zone 2. Normal mode is best in zone 1, mix-mode in zone 2 [5].

On the 4x2

In QICK, declare_gen(ch, nqz=1) tells the firmware and library that you will play frequencies in zone 1 (0 to 4915 MHz at the 4x2's 9830.4 MSPS DAC rate); nqz=2 sets the RF-DAC's Nyquist-zone mode to 2, which (as the QICK source notes, referring to AMD's PG269) increases output power in the 2nd and 3rd Nyquist zones; this is the mix-mode described above [3, 46]. Zone 2 spans 4915 to 9830 MHz. Expect lower and frequency-dependent power in zone 2, and measure it. The DAC rate of 9830.4 MSPS is 20 times the 491.52 MHz reference clock, and the ADC rate of 4423.68 MSPS is 9 times it [3].

19.4Quantisation: how many bits you really get

An \(N\)-bit converter represents the voltage with \(2^N\) levels. The step between levels is one LSB \(\Delta = V_{\text{FS}}/2^N\). Rounding to the nearest level adds a quantisation error between \(-\Delta/2\) and \(+\Delta/2\). For a busy signal this error behaves like white noise with power \(\Delta^2/12\).

For a full-scale sinusoid, the ratio of signal power to quantisation noise power is

\[ \text{SNR}_{\text{ideal}} = 6.02N + 1.76\ \text{dB}. \]

A 14-bit converter could reach 86 dB. Real converters fall short because of thermal noise, clock jitter and nonlinearity; the effective number of bits is defined by inverting the formula with the measured SNR: \(\text{ENOB} = (\text{SNR} - 1.76)/6.02\). RF-sampling converters are usually specified by their noise spectral density instead (Chapter 22).

Processing gain: more bits by filtering

Quantisation and thermal noise spread over the whole Nyquist band \(f_s/2\). If you only care about a narrow bandwidth \(B\) (for example 1 MHz around your readout carrier), filtering away the rest removes most of the noise. The improvement is the processing gain

\[ G_p = 10\log_{10}\frac{f_s}{2B}. \]

At \(f_s = 4.42\) GSPS and \(B = 1\) MHz, \(G_p = 33\) dB. This is why integrating a readout signal in the FPGA gives much better SNR than the raw 14 bits suggest, and why the demodulate-and-integrate step (Chapter 23) is so powerful.

19.5Clock jitter

If the sampling instants wobble by a random time \(\sigma_t\) (jitter), a signal of frequency \(f\) acquires a voltage error of order \(2\pi fA\sigma_t\). The resulting SNR limit is

\[ \text{SNR}_{\text{jitter}} = -20\log_{10}(2\pi f\sigma_t). \]

With \(\sigma_t = 100\) fs at 1 GHz, the limit is 64 dB; at 5 GHz it is 50 dB. High-frequency sampling needs very clean clocks, which is why the 4x2 has dedicated jitter-cleaning clock chips (Chapter 30).

Check yourself

1. A DAC at 9830.4 MSPS plays a 1200 MHz tone. Where are the first two images?

Show answer
At \(f_s - f = 8630.4\) MHz and \(f_s + f = 11030.4\) MHz, attenuated by the sinc response (and by the board's analog path).

2. What is the ideal SNR of a 12-bit converter? How much processing gain do you get filtering a 4 GSPS stream to 100 kHz?

Show answer
\(6.02\times12 + 1.76 = 74\) dB. \(G_p = 10\log_{10}(4\times10^9/2\times10^5) = 43\) dB.

3. Why does the even Nyquist zone appear mirrored?

Show answer
A frequency \(f\) in zone 2 aliases to \(f_s - f\); as \(f\) increases, \(f_s - f\) decreases, so the spectrum is reversed.
Summary
  • Sampling at \(f_s\) represents frequencies up to \(f_s/2\); higher frequencies alias into zone 1 at \(|f - kf_s|\).
  • DAC outputs roll off as sinc(\(f/f_s\)) and produce images at \(kf_s\pm f\); mix-mode favours zone 2.
  • On the 4x2 with QICK: DAC 9830.4 MSPS (zone 1 up to 4915 MHz), ADC 4423.68 MSPS (Nyquist 2212 MHz).
  • Ideal SNR is \(6.02N+1.76\) dB; filtering to a narrow bandwidth adds processing gain \(10\log(f_s/2B)\).
  • Clock jitter limits SNR at high frequency.

Part V · Signals and software-defined radio · Chapter 20

I/Q signals, mixing, NCOs and digital up/down-conversion

Why you need this

"I and Q" appear everywhere in qubit control: the readout returns I/Q values, microwave pulses are built from I/Q envelopes, and IQ mixers shift waveforms to GHz. The reason is that a sinusoid of a given frequency has two independent knobs, amplitude and phase, and I/Q is the cleanest way to handle both. This chapter builds the idea from complex numbers, then explains mixers, numerically controlled oscillators (NCOs) and the digital up- and down-converters inside the RFSoC and QICK. It follows the SDR book's chapters on quadrature modulation and SDR architectures [5].

20.1A sinusoid as a rotating arrow

Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\) lets us write any sinusoid as the real part of a rotating complex number:

\[ A\cos(\omega t + \phi) = \Re\big\{A e^{i\phi}\,e^{i\omega t}\big\}. \]

The complex number \(\tilde A = Ae^{i\phi}\) is the phasor. It contains everything about the signal except its frequency. If the amplitude and phase change slowly over time, \(\tilde A(t)\) is called the complex envelope.

Write the phasor in Cartesian form, \(\tilde A = I + iQ\), with \(I = A\cos\phi\) and \(Q = A\sin\phi\). Expanding the cosine:

\[ A\cos(\omega t+\phi) = I\cos\omega t - Q\sin\omega t . \]

So any sinusoid at frequency \(\omega\) is a sum of a cosine with weight \(I\) (the in-phase component) and a sine with weight \(Q\) (the quadrature component, 90° shifted). Amplitude is \(\sqrt{I^2+Q^2}\), phase is \(\operatorname{atan2}(Q, I)\).

20.2Mixing: multiplying signals shifts frequencies

A mixer multiplies two signals. From \(\cos a\cos b = \tfrac12[\cos(a-b) + \cos(a+b)]\), multiplying a signal at frequency \(f_{IF}\) (the intermediate frequency) by a local oscillator at \(f_{LO}\) produces two outputs, at \(f_{LO} - f_{IF}\) and \(f_{LO}+f_{IF}\). These are the lower and upper sidebands. Usually you want only one; the other is the image.

Single-sideband (IQ) upconversion

An IQ mixer contains two mixers driven by copies of the LO 90° apart. Feed it baseband I and Q signals at the IF:

\[ I(t) = \cos\omega_{IF}t,\quad Q(t) = \sin\omega_{IF}t \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; I\cos\omega_{LO}t - Q\sin\omega_{LO}t = \cos\big((\omega_{LO}+\omega_{IF})t\big). \]

The image cancels exactly, leaving only the upper sideband. Swapping the sign of Q selects the lower sideband. Real mixers are imperfect: unequal gains and a phase error of a degree or so leave an image at −25 to −40 dBc, and a small DC offset on I or Q lets the LO leak through. Both are calibrated by adjusting small offsets and amplitude/phase corrections while watching a spectrum analyser. IQ upconversion is how commercial controllers produce qubit drive at 10–20 GHz [47].

20.3Downconversion and demodulation

The reverse operation recovers I and Q from a received signal \(r(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)\). Multiply it by \(\cos\omega t\) and by \(-\sin\omega t\):

\[ r(t)\cos\omega t = \tfrac{A}{2}\cos\phi + \tfrac{A}{2}\cos(2\omega t + \phi), \qquad -r(t)\sin\omega t = \tfrac{A}{2}\sin\phi - \tfrac{A}{2}\sin(2\omega t+\phi). \]

A low-pass filter removes the \(2\omega\) terms, leaving \(I/2\) and \(Q/2\). In complex notation this is a single multiplication by \(e^{-i\omega t}\) followed by filtering. This is the core of every reflectometry receiver, lock-in amplifier and qubit readout chain.

20.4Numerically controlled oscillators

In digital hardware, the reference sinusoids are generated by a numerically controlled oscillator (NCO), also called direct digital synthesis (DDS). Each clock cycle, an \(N\)-bit phase accumulator adds a frequency word \(W\):

\[ \theta[n+1] = \theta[n] + W \pmod{2^N}, \qquad f = \frac{W}{2^N}f_{\text{clk}} . \]

The accumulator value is converted to \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) (by a lookup table or a CORDIC circuit). The frequency resolution is \(f_{\text{clk}}/2^N\), and the phase stays continuous when \(W\) changes, which is exactly what qubit control needs.

Worked example: QICK frequency resolution

QICK's generators use 32-bit DDS running at the DAC sample rate. On the 4x2, \(9830.4\ \text{MHz}/2^{32} = 2.29\) Hz. The QICK documentation quotes 2.3 Hz for the generator and 20.6 Hz for the common step that both a generator and a readout can hit exactly [4]. A 9 Hz mismatch between them would rotate the demodulated phase once every 0.1 s, which is why QICK provides frequency matching (Chapter 36).

20.5Digital up- and down-conversion in the RFSoC

The RFSoC's data converters contain hardened digital up-converters (DUC) and digital down-converters (DDC): interpolation or decimation filters, a complex mixer with an NCO (a 48-bit fine mixer, plus a coarse mixer for fixed shifts like \(f_s/4\)), and quadrature-error correction. In Gen3 devices, interpolation and decimation factors from 1× to 40× are available [5, 46]. A 5G radio uses them to move low-rate baseband data to GHz without burdening the FPGA.

QICK takes a different approach on the 4x2. Its standard firmware sets the DACs to 1× interpolation and the ADCs to 1× decimation, and does the frequency synthesis and down-conversion in the FPGA fabric itself [3]:

  • Each signal generator computes 16 output samples per fabric clock cycle (614.4 MHz × 16 = 9830.4 MSPS), multiplying its envelope by its own DDS, so the output frequency, phase and amplitude can change from one pulse to the next under tProcessor control.
  • Each readout takes the full-rate ADC stream, mixes it with its own DDS, filters and decimates by 8 (to 552.96 MSPS on the 4x2), and accumulates over the readout window.

Doing it in fabric gives QICK precise, per-pulse control and phase coherence between generators and readouts, at the cost of FPGA resources. Chapter 33 describes these blocks in detail.

20.6Upconversion options for EDSR with the 4x2

OptionHardwareFrequenciesDACs usedPros / cons
Direct, zone 1noneup to ~4.9 GHz1Simplest, phase-coherent, clean; needs a low-field operating point
Direct, zone 2band-pass filter recommended~4.9–9.8 GHz1No mixer; lower, frequency-dependent power; images and spurs to check
DSB mixer + filterLO source, mixer, band-pass filterany (LO ± IF)1Leaves the second DAC free for readout; IF must be large (≥1 GHz) for easy filtering
IQ mixer (SSB)LO source, IQ mixerany2Clean single sideband after calibration; uses both DACs, so readout needs another source
Common mistake

Forgetting that the external LO is a separate oscillator. Its phase is not locked to the RFSoC unless both share a 10 MHz reference. Without a shared reference, the qubit drive phase drifts relative to QICK's timing, and Ramsey or echo experiments with long sequences lose phase coherence. Lock the LO and the 4x2 (via its external reference input, Chapter 30) to the same 10 MHz clock.

Check yourself

1. A signal has I = 0.3, Q = −0.4. What are its amplitude and phase?

Show answer
Amplitude \(\sqrt{0.09+0.16} = 0.5\); phase \(\operatorname{atan2}(-0.4, 0.3) \approx -53°\).

2. With an LO at 14 GHz and an IF of 600 MHz into a simple mixer, where are the outputs? How far apart are wanted and image?

Show answer
13.4 and 14.6 GHz, 1.2 GHz apart (\(2f_{IF}\)). Filtering one out needs a sharp filter; an IF of 1.5 GHz would separate them by 3 GHz.

3. Why must the phase accumulator be continuous when the frequency word changes?

Show answer
So that the oscillator's phase, which is the qubit's reference frame, does not jump. A phase jump would rotate the effective drive axis and corrupt subsequent gates.
Summary
  • A sinusoid at known frequency is a phasor \(I + iQ\): amplitude and phase.
  • Mixers multiply signals, producing sum and difference frequencies; IQ mixers cancel the image for single-sideband output.
  • Demodulation multiplies by \(e^{-i\omega t}\) and low-pass filters, giving I and Q.
  • NCOs (DDS) generate phase-continuous sinusoids with resolution \(f_{\text{clk}}/2^N\); QICK uses 32-bit DDS (2.3 Hz steps on the 4x2).
  • QICK synthesises and demodulates in FPGA fabric; external mixers and an LO extend the 4x2's range for EDSR.
