Part V · Signals and software-defined radio · Chapter 21

Spectra, filters, decimation and interpolation

Why you need this

The shape of a qubit pulse in time decides which frequencies it contains, and therefore which neighbouring qubits or transitions it disturbs. The readout chain filters and decimates billions of samples per second down to one number per shot. Cables and amplifiers distort baseband pulses, and you correct them with digital pre-distortion filters. All three are applications of a small set of ideas from signal processing: the Fourier transform, filters, and changing the sample rate. This chapter explains them with the qubit applications in mind [5].

21.1Time and frequency are two views of one signal

The Fourier transform decomposes a signal into sinusoids:

\[ X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-i2\pi f t}\,dt . \]

\(|X(f)|^2\) tells you how much power the signal has at each frequency. One general rule matters more than any formula: short in time means wide in frequency. A pulse of duration \(\tau\) occupies a bandwidth of order \(1/\tau\). A 10 ns exchange pulse spans about 100 MHz; a 100 ns microwave burst about 10 MHz around its carrier.

The shape matters as much as the duration. A square pulse has a sinc-shaped spectrum with slowly decaying side lobes (−13 dB for the first, then falling as \(1/f\)). A Gaussian pulse has a Gaussian spectrum with no side lobes at all.

21.2The discrete Fourier transform and FFT

For \(N\) samples at rate \(f_s\), the discrete Fourier transform gives \(N\) frequency bins spaced by the resolution \(\Delta f = f_s/N\). The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes it in \(N\log N\) operations. Two practical points:

  • Spectral leakage: a sinusoid that does not fit an integer number of periods into the record spreads into neighbouring bins. Multiplying the record by a smooth window (Hann, Blackman) before the FFT reduces leakage.
  • Noise per bin: white noise is spread over all bins, so longer records (more bins) lower the noise level per bin, while a sinusoid stays in one bin. A spectrum analyser's displayed noise floor depends on its resolution bandwidth for this reason.

The SDR book's Notebook Set C builds a spectrum analyser on the RFSoC; it is an excellent first hands-on exercise for seeing aliasing, images and spurs on your own board [5].

21.3Filters

A filter passes some frequencies and attenuates others. In the digital world there are two families:

  • FIR filters compute each output as a weighted sum of the last \(N\) inputs, \(y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} h_k\,x[n-k]\). The weights \(h_k\) are the taps (the impulse response). FIRs are always stable, can have exactly linear phase (all frequencies delayed equally), and map efficiently onto FPGA multipliers.
  • IIR filters also feed back past outputs. They achieve sharp responses with few coefficients but have nonlinear phase and can be unstable if designed carelessly. A single-pole IIR is the digital version of an RC circuit.

Analog filters are just as important in the lab: low-pass filters on DC lines, band-pass filters before the ADC to stop aliasing, and filters after mixers to remove images. Commercial coaxial filters (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass) are cheap and should be part of every RFSoC setup.

21.4Changing the sample rate

Decimation

To reduce the sample rate by a factor \(M\), first low-pass filter to below the new Nyquist frequency \(f_s/(2M)\), then keep every \(M\)th sample. Skipping the filter lets out-of-band noise and signals alias into the band. Decimation is what makes real-time readout possible: the ADC produces 4.4 billion samples per second, but you want one I/Q number per shot. QICK's readout on the 4x2 decimates by 8 after down-conversion, giving 552.96 MSPS "decimated" data that can be recorded as a trace, and then accumulates over the readout window for the per-shot result [3].

Interpolation

To increase the sample rate by \(L\), insert \(L-1\) zeros between samples and low-pass filter to remove the resulting images. Interpolation lets a waveform be stored at a lower rate (saving memory) and played at the full DAC rate. QICK's interpolated generator (sg_int4_v2, used on the ZCU216) stores envelopes at a quarter of the DAC rate for this reason [4].

21.5Pre-distortion: undoing the cables

A baseband pulse travelling through amplifiers, cables, bias tees and filters arrives distorted: edges are rounded (low-pass behaviour), long pulses droop (high-pass behaviour, from AC coupling and bias tees), and reflections add ringing. If the chain is linear, its effect is a filter with some impulse response \(g(t)\). You can measure \(g(t)\) (with a fast oscilloscope at room temperature, or with the qubit itself) and apply an inverse filter digitally to the waveform before playing it, so that what arrives at the gate is the shape you wanted. This is pre-distortion.

HRL's spinQICK exchange-only experiments fitted the room-temperature chain (ZCU216 → LMH5401 → THS3491 → low-pass filter) with two single-pole IIR filters and pre-distorted their 10 ns exchange pulses accordingly [11]. For long sequences that exceeded waveform memory, they pre-distorted a short repeating unit and played it in a loop.

Worked example: correcting AC-coupling droop

A high-pass path with time constant \(\tau\) turns a step into \(e^{-t/\tau}\). Its inverse adds back the integral of the past signal: \(v_{\text{pre}}(t) = v(t) + \frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^t v(t')\,dt'\). For a 1 µs square pulse of 10 mV through a path with \(\tau = 20\ \mu\)s, the pre-distorted pulse ramps up linearly from 10 mV to 10.5 mV during the pulse. But for \(\tau = 10\) ns (comparable to the 4x2's balun response at its low-frequency end), the correction would need a ramp of 100 times the pulse height, impossible. Pre-distortion can fix small droop, not a missing DC path.

Check yourself

1. What frequency resolution does an FFT of 16 384 samples at 4423.68 MSPS have?

Show answer
\(4423.68\times10^6/16384 = 270\) kHz per bin.

2. Why must you filter before decimating?

Show answer
After decimation by \(M\), all frequencies alias into the new, narrower Nyquist band. Without filtering, noise and signals from the whole original band fold in, adding noise and spurs.

3. Why does pre-distortion fail to fix a balun-coupled output for millisecond pulses?

Show answer
The balun's high-pass time constant is short (of order nanoseconds to tens of ns at a 10 MHz corner). Holding a level for milliseconds would require the pre-distorted waveform to grow without bound, far beyond the DAC's range.
Summary
  • Short pulses are spectrally wide; smooth shapes (Gaussian) avoid the side lobes of square pulses.
  • The DFT/FFT has resolution \(f_s/N\); windows reduce leakage.
  • FIR filters are weighted sums of past inputs; IIR filters feed back outputs.
  • Decimation (filter then downsample) turns GSPS ADC streams into per-shot results; interpolation saves waveform memory.
  • Pre-distortion cancels known, modest distortions of the pulse chain; it cannot create a DC path that does not exist.
PreviousChapter 20 · I/Q signals, mixing, NCOs and digital up/down-conversionNextChapter 22 · Noise, converter figures of merit and frequency planning

Part V · Signals and software-defined radio · Chapter 22

Noise, converter figures of merit and frequency planning

Why you need this

A real DAC does not output a perfect sine, and a real ADC does not record one perfectly. Both add noise and spurious tones ("spurs") at predictable frequencies. If a spur lands on your readout carrier, your readout signal fluctuates; if broadband DAC noise reaches a gate, it acts like charge noise; if a clock's phase noise is high, your qubit drive's phase wanders. This chapter teaches you to read a converter data sheet, to recognise the usual spurs in a measured spectrum, and to choose frequencies so the spurs land where they do no harm. It follows the SDR book's figures-of-merit and frequency-planning chapter and its notebooks [5].

22.1The figures of merit

NameDefinitionWhat it tells you
SNRSignal power / noise power over the Nyquist band (excluding harmonics)Random noise level
SINADSignal / (noise + distortion)Overall quality; gives ENOB
SFDRCarrier / largest spur, in dBcHow clean the spectrum is
HD2, HD3Power of 2nd and 3rd harmonics, dBcNonlinearity
IMD3Third-order intermodulation products of two tones at \(2f_1 - f_2\), \(2f_2 - f_1\)Matters when several tones share one output (multiplexed readout or drive)
NSDNoise power per Hz relative to full scale, dBFS/HzNoise in any bandwidth you choose

For RF-sampling converters with GHz Nyquist bands, NSD is the most useful noise specification. The noise in a bandwidth \(B\) is

\[ P_{\text{noise}}\ (\text{dBFS}) = \text{NSD} + 10\log_{10}B . \]

The SDR book quotes typical NSD for first-generation RF-ADC tiles of −150 dBFS/Hz at 240 MHz input and −146 dBFS/Hz at 2.4 GHz [5]; Gen3 devices are of a similar order (see DS926 for the exact values [45]).

Worked example

With NSD = −150 dBFS/Hz and a readout integration bandwidth of 1 MHz (about 1 µs), the ADC's own noise is −150 + 60 = −90 dBFS. If your amplified readout signal reaches the ADC at −35 dBm and full scale is about +1 dBm, the signal is at −36 dBFS, so the ADC adds noise 54 dB below the signal. The amplifier chain's noise (Chapter 18) is usually far larger. In a well-designed chain, the ADC is not the limit; the HEMT is.

22.2Where spurs come from

  • Harmonics at \(2f, 3f, \dots\) from nonlinearity. Above the Nyquist frequency they alias back into zone 1 at predictable places.
  • Interleaving spurs: GHz ADCs are built from several slower sub-ADCs taking turns. Small mismatches between them create spurs at \(f_s/M \pm f\) (with \(M\) the number of sub-converters). The RFSoC calibrates these in the background, but residues remain.
  • Clock and fabric spurs at fixed frequencies related to the reference and fabric clocks (for example \(f_s/8\), \(f_s/16\)), from digital activity coupling into the analog parts.
  • DAC images at \(f_s \pm f\) (Chapter 19) and harmonics of the DAC output.
  • Phase noise: random phase fluctuations of the sample clock or LO spread the carrier into "skirts" around it, measured in dBc/Hz at an offset frequency.

22.3Frequency planning

Frequency planning means choosing your frequencies so that the predictable spurs fall outside the bands you use. The SDR book's Notebook Set F includes an interactive RFSoC frequency planner that plots where harmonics, images and interleaving spurs land for a given sample rate and signal frequency [5].

Worked example: choosing a readout frequency

On the 4x2 with QICK, the ADC runs at 4423.68 MSPS (Nyquist 2211.84 MHz). Candidate readout carrier: 500 MHz.

  • HD2 = 1000 MHz, HD3 = 1500 MHz, HD4 = 2000 MHz: all in zone 1, away from 500 MHz. Fine.
  • HD5 = 2500 MHz, in zone 2, aliases to 4423.68 − 2500 = 1923.68 MHz. Fine.
  • \(f_s/8 = 553\) MHz and \(f_s/4 = 1106\) MHz are possible fixed spurs. 500 MHz is 53 MHz from \(f_s/8\): fine if your readout bandwidth is a few MHz, but avoid carriers within a few MHz of such frequencies.
  • If the 4x2 also drives EDSR at, say, 3.9 GHz on the other DAC, any leakage of that tone into the ADC aliases to 4423.68 − 3900 = 523.68 MHz, only 24 MHz from your readout. Move the readout to, for example, 350 MHz, or filter the ADC input.

Write such a table every time you choose frequencies. It takes ten minutes and can save days of chasing "noise".

22.4Noise that matters for qubits

  • DAC noise on gate lines: broadband noise from a DAC (or AWG) at the device's gates is indistinguishable from charge noise. Attenuating the line by 20 dB lowers it by 20 dB, together with the signal, so large-amplitude needs and low noise conflict. HRL measured that their room-temperature amplifier chain, not the RFSoC itself, dominated the high-frequency noise seen by their qubit [11].
  • Phase noise of the drive: phase fluctuations of the microwave drive are rotations of the qubit's drive axis. Use a low-phase-noise LO and a common 10 MHz reference.
  • Spurs near the qubit frequency: a weak, constant spur close to resonance drives the qubit slowly all the time, causing errors that look like reduced \(T_1\) or extra decoherence.
  • Readout carrier leakage: the readout carrier and its harmonics can reach other lines through crosstalk on the PCB or in the fridge. Turn the readout off during manipulation when possible (QICK pulses it only during readout).
In the lab

Before connecting the board to the fridge, connect each DAC to a spectrum analyser and record the spectrum for the frequencies you plan to use, from 10 MHz to 10 GHz. Then loop a DAC back into an ADC through attenuators and look at the ADC's FFT (with QICK's decimated or raw capture). You will learn your board's actual spurs, and you will have a reference to compare against if something changes.

Check yourself

1. NSD is −147 dBFS/Hz. What is the noise level in a 10 MHz bandwidth?

Show answer
−147 + 70 = −77 dBFS.

2. A 1300 MHz readout tone is sampled at 4423.68 MSPS. Where does its 2nd harmonic appear?

Show answer
2600 MHz is in zone 2 and aliases to 4423.68 − 2600 = 1823.68 MHz.
Summary
  • Converters are characterised by SNR, SINAD/ENOB, SFDR, harmonic distortion, intermodulation and NSD.
  • Noise in a bandwidth \(B\) is NSD + 10 log B (dBFS).
  • Spurs come from harmonics (aliased), interleaving, clocks and DAC images; phase noise spreads carriers.
  • Frequency planning places carriers away from predictable spurs; check every new configuration with a spectrum analyser.
  • For qubits, gate-line noise, drive phase noise and spurs near resonance matter most.
PreviousChapter 21 · Spectra, filters, decimation and interpolationNextChapter 23 · From waveform to qubit result: demodulation, integration and thresholds

Part V · Signals and software-defined radio · Chapter 23

From waveform to qubit result: demodulation, integration and thresholds

Why you need this

This chapter connects everything in Part V to the readout of your qubit. The ADC delivers billions of samples per second; you want, for every shot, one bit: spin up or down. In between are down-conversion, filtering, choosing the right time window, integrating, rotating the IQ plane and thresholding. On the RFSoC, almost all of this happens in FPGA logic in real time, which is why the RFSoC can make decisions (feedback) within a microsecond of a measurement. Understanding each step lets you set QICK's readout parameters sensibly and squeeze the most fidelity out of your sensor.

23.1The readout pipeline

23.2Step 1: down-conversion

The readout's DDS generates \(e^{-i\omega t}\) at the carrier frequency. Multiplying turns the reflected carrier into a slowly varying complex number, \(s(t) = I(t) + iQ(t)\), proportional to the reflection coefficient \(\Gamma\) of the tank circuit, plus noise. Because the generator that produced the carrier and the readout's DDS run from the same clock and (with frequency matching) the same frequency, \(s(t)\) is constant in time for a constant \(\Gamma\), shot after shot [4].

23.3Step 2: filtering and decimation

A low-pass filter removes the \(2\omega\) component and noise outside the band; then the stream is decimated. On the 4x2, QICK's readout decimates by 8, from 4423.68 to 552.96 MSPS [3]. These decimated samples can be recorded directly: QICK's acquire_decimated() returns the averaged I/Q trace versus time, which is how you see the carrier arrive, check the timing, and look at the sensor's response during a pulse.

23.4Step 3: choosing the readout window

The signal does not appear at the ADC at the moment the DAC starts the carrier. It takes time to travel: cables down and up a fridge (several metres, about 5 ns/m), amplifiers, filters, and the converters' own pipelines. This delay is the time of flight, typically 0.2–1 µs in total. The tank resonator also takes time to ring up: its response time is about \(Q/(\pi f_0)\), where \(Q\) is its quality factor. For \(Q = 30\) at 200 MHz, that is about 48 ns.

So: measure the time of flight once with a decimated trace (Chapter 36), then start the readout window after the signal has arrived and settled. In QICK this is the trigger time of the readout relative to the pulse, plus a calibrated offset.

23.5Step 4: integration

Summing the decimated samples over a window of length \(T\) gives one complex number per shot. For white noise, the signal grows as \(T\) and the noise as \(\sqrt T\), so SNR grows as \(\sqrt T\) until something else (relaxation, drifts) intervenes. QICK accumulates the samples in hardware and returns either every shot's sum or the average over shots.

Weighted integration

If the signal changes during the window, for example because a triplet relaxes to a singlet during PSB readout, equal weights are not optimal. The SNR-optimal linear filter for distinguishing two known average traces \(\bar s_0(t)\) and \(\bar s_1(t)\) in white noise is the matched filter, with weights \(w(t) \propto \bar s_1(t) - \bar s_0(t)\). If the difference decays because of relaxation, the weights decay too, trusting early samples more.

23.6Step 5: the IQ plane, rotation and threshold

Plot each shot's integrated \((I, Q)\) as a point. Shots from the two states form two clouds. The direction joining the cloud centres carries the information; the perpendicular direction only adds noise. Rotate the plane by the angle \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta Q, \Delta I)\) of the separation vector, so that all the signal is on the new \(I'\) axis, and discard \(Q'\). Then set a threshold on \(I'\) between the clouds.

Worked example: from traces to SNR

Your averaged decimated traces for the two charge states differ by 40 ADC units in \(I'\) during a 2 µs window; single decimated samples have a noise standard deviation of 400 units. At 552.96 MSPS, 2 µs contains about 1106 samples. Summing them (and dividing by the count) reduces the noise by \(\sqrt{1106} \approx 33\), to about 12 units. The single-shot SNR is \(40/12 \approx 3.3\), giving about 5% error per state (Chapter 5). To reach SNR 6 you would need about \((6/3.3)^2 \approx 3.3\) times longer: 6.6 µs, if relaxation allows.

23.7Averaged versus single-shot data

  • Averaged: average I/Q over many shots, then rotate and scale to a probability using calibration points (prepared 0 and 1). Robust and simple, but SPAM and readout errors blend into the result.
  • Single-shot: threshold each shot, then count. Gives true probabilities (after correcting for readout errors) and correlations between qubits. Required for feedback, error correction and many benchmarking protocols.

23.8The same pipeline as a lock-in

If you replace the GHz carrier with a lower-frequency excitation (HRL used 1 MHz through the charge sensor, read with a 20 kΩ current-to-voltage resistor [11]), the same mix–filter–integrate chain is a digital lock-in amplifier. On the 4x2 such a low frequency is below the baluns' 10 MHz rating, so expect strong attenuation unless you bypass them; reflectometry at hundreds of MHz avoids the problem.

On the 4x2

The 4x2's QICK readouts provide, per channel, an accumulated buffer of 16 384 entries (one per shot or per sweep point) and a decimated buffer of 4096 samples (7.4 µs at 552.96 MSPS). A 1.07-billion-sample DDR4 buffer (1.94 s) can record long continuous traces, useful for watching tunnelling events, and a multi-rate buffer captures raw 8192-sample stretches [3]. These numbers come from the firmware's configuration printout; print soc to see your own firmware's values.

23.9What the 4x2 can demodulate

Demodulation on the 4x2 is just arithmetic in the FPGA, so the board can demodulate any signal that reaches its ADC cleanly. What decides that is the analog path in front of the ADC. Each ADC input passes through two 100 nF capacitors and a balun rated for 10 MHz to 10 GHz (Chapter 29) [2]. The ADC then samples at 4423.68 MSPS in the standard QICK firmware, so the first Nyquist zone ends at 2211.84 MHz [3].

SignalTypical frequencyUnmodified 4x2?Notes
RF reflectometry carrier (SET or QPC sensor)100 MHz – 1 GHzYesThe intended use. One DAC makes the carrier and one ADC reads it back (Chapter 39).
Gate-based (dispersive) sensing100 MHz – 1 GHzYesThe same chain. The charge signal shows up mostly as a phase shift instead of an amplitude change.
Any carrier in the first Nyquist zone10 MHz – 2.2 GHzYes, directlyPut a low-pass filter at the ADC input to stop higher zones folding in.
Carriers above the first zone2.2 GHz and upPossibleRF sampling in a higher Nyquist zone with a band-pass filter. The signal folds to a known alias (Chapter 19). Check the ADC's analog input bandwidth in DS926 [45].
The qubit's own microwave (EDSR at 10–20 GHz)10 – 20 GHzNot neededSpin qubits are read through the charge sensor, not by listening to the drive. To check the drive chain, mix it down externally first.
Lock-in excitation through the sensorkHz – a few MHzNoBelow the balun's 10 MHz rating. A few MHz is strongly attenuated; kHz does not get through.
DC transport currentDCNoThe coupling capacitors block DC completely.

Why there is a lower limit. A balun is a small transformer. At low frequency its winding inductance has a low impedance and shorts the signal, so the transformer stops coupling energy across. The series capacitors add a second high-pass corner and block DC entirely. Together they set the 10 MHz floor. This is the same reason the board cannot output DC gate pulses (Chapter 29).

What to do with low-frequency signals:

  • Keep a lock-in amplifier for DC and kHz transport during the first cooldowns (Coulomb diamonds, pinch-offs). Most groups do this anyway.
  • Move to RF reflectometry. It gives the same charge information at a carrier of hundreds of MHz and is much faster (Chapter 9).
  • Modify the ADC input to make it DC-coupled, as the QICK-DAWG team did with an LMH5401 amplifier [41]. Then the same demodulation chain works as a digital lock-in at kHz–MHz.

Other limits to know.

  • Number of tones. The standard firmware has two readout channels, each on its own ADC input, and each demodulates one frequency at a time. The frequency can change between shots. Reading several sensors on one line by frequency multiplexing needs multiplexed firmware or a second readout channel (Chapters 9 and 33).
  • Signal level. The reflected signal from a tank circuit is tiny. It needs cryogenic and room-temperature amplification to sit well above the ADC's noise floor (Chapter 22).
  • Bandwidth is not a limit. After decimation the demodulated signal has 552.96 MSPS, so it can follow changes on nanosecond scales. The tank circuit, with a bandwidth of a few MHz, is always the slower part.
Check yourself

1. Your two IQ clouds are centred at (100, 20) and (40, 100). By what angle should you rotate so that the separation lies along +I?

Show answer
The separation vector is (40 − 100, 100 − 20) = (−60, 80), at angle atan2(80, −60) ≈ 126.9°. Rotating by −126.9° puts it along +I (or by 53.1° to put it along −I; either works if the threshold is placed accordingly).

2. Why does integration time stop improving fidelity beyond a certain point?

Show answer
During longer windows more excited states relax (or the charge state changes for other reasons), so the classes overlap more. Slow drifts and 1/f noise also stop averaging down as \(\sqrt T\).

3. Your lab measures the sensor dot with a 77 Hz lock-in excitation. Can you connect that signal to a 4x2 ADC input and demodulate it there?

Show answer
No. 77 Hz is far below the 10 MHz lower limit of the ADC input's balun and capacitors, so the signal does not reach the converter. Keep the lock-in for this measurement, or measure the same sensor with RF reflectometry at hundreds of MHz, which the 4x2 handles directly.

4. A colleague's tank circuit resonates at 3.0 GHz. Can the 4x2 demodulate it, and at what frequency does the signal appear after sampling at 4423.68 MSPS?

Show answer
Yes, by RF sampling in the second Nyquist zone (2211.84–4423.68 MHz) with a band-pass filter around 3 GHz. The signal folds to 4423.68 − 3000 = 1423.68 MHz. In the second zone the spectrum is reversed, so the IQ plane is mirrored (Q changes sign) and phase shifts appear with the opposite sign. Thresholding still works; just account for the sign when you interpret phases. The DAC can generate 3.0 GHz directly because it is inside the DAC's first zone (up to 4915.2 MHz).
Summary
  • Readout: mix with the carrier, filter and decimate, integrate over a window, rotate, threshold.
  • Start the window after the time of flight and resonator ring-up.
  • SNR grows as \(\sqrt T\) for white noise; matched (weighted) filters do better when the signal decays.
  • Single-shot thresholding gives bits and enables feedback; averaging gives probabilities with calibration.
  • QICK does mixing, decimation and accumulation in the FPGA, with buffers for shots, traces and long records.
  • The 4x2 demodulates any carrier from about 10 MHz to 2.2 GHz directly, and higher ones with band-pass filtering. kHz lock-in signals and DC are blocked by the AC-coupled input unless the input is modified.
PreviousChapter 22 · Noise, converter figures of merit and frequency planningNextChapter 24 · Digital logic and FPGA fabric

Part VI · FPGAs and the RFSoC chip · Chapter 24

Digital logic and FPGA fabric

Why you need this

QICK's signal generators, readouts and tProcessor are not programs running on a CPU. They are digital circuits configured into the RFSoC's FPGA fabric. You can use QICK without ever designing such circuits, but you need to understand what they are to read the documentation, interpret timing limits ("2.4 ns clock", "16 samples per cycle"), judge what a firmware change would involve, and talk to engineers. This chapter starts from bits and ends with the building blocks of a modern FPGA.

24.1Numbers in hardware

Digital hardware stores numbers as bits. An \(N\)-bit unsigned integer covers 0 to \(2^N - 1\). Signed integers almost always use two's complement, where the top bit has negative weight: a 16-bit value covers −32768 to +32767. ADC samples on the RFSoC are 14-bit (padded into 16-bit words), and QICK's gain values are signed integers scaled so that 1.0 corresponds to the largest positive value.

Fractions are handled with fixed-point arithmetic: an integer with an implied binary point. In "Q1.15" format, a 16-bit word represents values from −1 to \(1 - 2^{-15}\) in steps of \(2^{-15}\). Fixed point is cheap in hardware but you must track how many bits each operation needs: multiplying two 16-bit numbers gives 32 bits; summing 1024 of them needs 10 more bits to avoid overflow. This is why QICK's accumulators are wide and why its I/Q results are large integers that the Python library rescales.

24.2Combinational logic, registers and clocks

Digital circuits are built from two kinds of element:

  • Combinational logic (AND, OR, NOT, adders, multiplexers): outputs depend only on current inputs, after a short propagation delay.
  • Sequential elements: a flip-flop captures its input at the rising edge of a clock and holds it until the next edge. A group of flip-flops is a register.

A synchronous design alternates registers and combinational logic. At each clock edge, registers capture the results computed since the previous edge. The clock period must exceed the longest combinational delay between two registers (the critical path) plus setup times. Tools check this automatically ("timing closure"). At 614.4 MHz, the clock used by QICK's 4x2 generators, the period is only 1.63 ns, so each step of the logic must be very short.

Pipelining and parallelism

Two tricks let FPGAs process GHz data with sub-GHz clocks:

  • Pipelining: split a long calculation into stages separated by registers. Each stage is short, so the clock can be fast; the result appears several cycles later (latency), but a new input can enter every cycle (throughput).
  • Parallelism: process several samples per clock cycle. A 9.8304 GSPS DAC fed by a 614.4 MHz fabric clock needs 16 samples per cycle. QICK's signal generator computes 16 DDS outputs and 16 envelope samples in parallel every cycle, a 256-bit wide data path [4].
Worked example

The 4x2's ADCs run at 4423.68 MSPS and the readout fabric at 276.48 MHz. How many samples arrive per fabric cycle? \(4423.68/276.48 = 16\). After QICK's decimation by 8, the rate is 552.96 MSPS, which is 2 samples per cycle at 276.48 MHz.

24.3What an FPGA is made of

A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is a chip full of generic digital building blocks and programmable wiring between them. Loading a configuration file (the bitstream) sets every block's function and every connection, creating a custom circuit. The main resources in an AMD UltraScale+ FPGA, as in the RFSoC, are:

  • Lookup tables (LUTs): a 6-input LUT is a tiny 64-entry memory that can implement any Boolean function of 6 inputs. LUTs are the "logic gates" of an FPGA.
  • Flip-flops: registers next to each LUT.
  • Block RAM (BRAM): 36 Kbit dual-port memories, for waveform tables, FIFOs and buffers. QICK's envelope memories and readout buffers are made of BRAM.
  • UltraRAM: larger 288 Kbit blocks for bigger memories.
  • DSP slices: hardened multiply-accumulate units (27×18-bit multiplier plus a 48-bit accumulator) running at hundreds of MHz. Every multiplication in a DDS, mixer or filter uses them.
  • Clocking: PLLs and MMCMs (mixed-mode clock managers) generate and phase-align the many clocks a design uses.

The XCZU48DR in the 4x2 contains roughly 930 000 logic cells, about 4 000 DSP slices and tens of megabits of block RAM and UltraRAM (see AMD's product tables for exact numbers). That is enough for QICK's full design with room to spare, and the same fabric resources exist in the ZCU216's ZU49DR: the boards differ mostly in their RF front ends [4].

24.4How designs are described

FPGA circuits are written in hardware description languages (HDLs) such as Verilog or VHDL, which describe registers and logic rather than sequential instructions. Higher-level tools exist: high-level synthesis (HLS) compiles C++ into circuits, and IP blocks (ready-made circuits such as the RF data converter interface, DMA engines and FIFOs) are connected graphically in a block design. QICK's firmware is a mix of custom Verilog/VHDL blocks (the tProcessor, generators, readouts) and AMD IP, assembled in a Vivado block design (Chapter 27).

24.5Why an FPGA, not a fast CPU?

  • Determinism: a circuit does exactly the same thing on every clock cycle. No operating system, caches or interrupts can delay a pulse.
  • Bandwidth: processing 16 samples per cycle per channel on several channels in parallel exceeds what any CPU can do in real time.
  • Latency: a decision computed from a measurement can affect the next pulse within hundreds of nanoseconds, which is essential for feedback.

The price is development effort: changing a circuit means re-running synthesis and implementation (hours) and verifying timing. That is why QICK separates fixed firmware (circuits) from flexible software (programs for the tProcessor, written from Python).

Check yourself

1. What is the largest value of a 14-bit two's-complement number, and the smallest?

Show answer
\(+8191\) and \(-8192\).

2. A design must process 4.4 GSPS with a 276.48 MHz clock. What does that force the designer to do?

Show answer
Process 16 samples in parallel every clock cycle (a wide data path), and pipeline every operation so that each stage fits in 3.6 ns.

3. Why would summing 10 000 16-bit samples overflow a 16-bit register, and how many bits are needed?

Show answer
The sum can reach 10 000 × 32767 ≈ 3.3 × 10⁸, which needs about 29 bits plus sign (16 + log₂10 000 ≈ 16 + 13.3). Accumulators must be wider than their inputs.
Summary
  • Hardware uses two's-complement integers and fixed-point fractions; bit growth must be managed.
  • Synchronous logic alternates registers and combinational logic; the critical path sets the clock rate.
  • Pipelining and parallel samples per cycle let sub-GHz fabric handle GSPS converters (16 samples per cycle in QICK on the 4x2).
  • FPGAs contain LUTs, flip-flops, BRAM, UltraRAM, DSP slices and clock managers connected by programmable routing.
  • FPGAs give determinism, bandwidth and low latency, at the cost of slow design iterations.

Part VI · FPGAs and the RFSoC chip · Chapter 25

Zynq UltraScale+: processing system, programmable logic, AXI and DMA

Why you need this

The RFSoC is a system-on-chip: a full computer (ARM processors, memory controller, Ethernet, USB) and an FPGA on the same piece of silicon, talking to each other through standard on-chip buses. When your Python code writes a QICK program to the tProcessor, or reads back a buffer of I/Q values, it travels across these buses. Knowing how they work explains where data-transfer limits come from, why some operations are fast and others slow, and what the terms in QICK's and PYNQ's documentation ("AXI-Lite register", "DMA", "MMIO", "AXI-Stream") mean.

25.1Two halves of one chip

The processing system (PS)

The processing system contains four ARM Cortex-A53 application cores (QICK's 4x2 firmware sets them to 1.2 GHz [3]), two Cortex-R5F real-time cores, a DDR4 memory controller and the usual computer peripherals. On the 4x2 it boots Linux from the micro-SD card and runs PYNQ and Jupyter. The PS is a normal (if modest) computer: running Python on it is convenient but not fast, which is why heavy analysis is usually done on your lab PC.

The programmable logic (PL)

The programmable logic is the FPGA fabric of Chapter 24 plus hardened blocks: the RF-ADCs and RF-DACs, SD-FEC decoders, high-speed transceivers and Ethernet MACs. On the 4x2, the PL also has its own 4 GB of DDR4 memory, which QICK uses as a long capture buffer [2, 3].

25.2AXI: how the halves talk

All communication between PS and PL, and between blocks inside the PL, uses ARM's AMBA AXI protocols. Three flavours matter:

ProtocolUsed forExample in QICK
AXI4-LiteReading and writing individual 32-bit registers at memory addresses ("memory-mapped I/O")Setting a readout's frequency register, starting the tProcessor
AXI4 (full)Burst transfers to and from memoryDMA engines copying buffers to PS DDR4
AXI4-StreamContinuous one-way data flow, no addressesADC samples into readouts; tProcessor commands to generators; generator samples to DACs

The valid/ready handshake

AXI4-Stream (and the channels of AXI4) move data with a simple handshake: the sender raises TVALID when it has data; the receiver raises TREADY when it can accept; a transfer happens on every clock edge where both are high. This lets fast and slow blocks connect safely: a receiver that is busy just holds TREADY low.

25.3Memory-mapped I/O and DMA

From Linux, PL registers appear at physical addresses. PYNQ's MMIO class lets Python read and write them like elements of an array (Chapter 32). Each access takes of order a microsecond from Python, fine for configuration but far too slow for moving data.

For bulk data, a DMA (direct memory access) engine in the PL copies blocks of data between a stream and PS memory by itself, at hundreds of MB/s to GB/s, while the CPU waits or does other work. QICK uses DMA engines to load programs into the tProcessor, upload waveform envelopes into generators, and read back readout buffers [3]. PYNQ allocates the contiguous memory buffers DMA needs.

Worked example: data rates

One readout returns one complex I/Q pair (two 32-bit integers, 8 bytes) per shot. 16 384 shots make 128 KiB, transferred by DMA in well under a millisecond. Raw ADC data is another story: 4423.68 MSPS × 2 bytes = 8.8 GB/s per channel. No PS–PL path can stream that continuously to Linux, which is why decimation and accumulation must happen in the PL, and why the long DDR4 capture buffer sits on the PL side.

25.4Interrupts and timing

The PL can signal the PS with interrupts (for example "buffer full"), but Linux's response time is microseconds to milliseconds and not deterministic. Anything that must happen at a precise time, such as a pulse after a measurement, must therefore be done in the PL. That is the design principle behind QICK: the PS prepares and collects, the PL acts in real time.

On the 4x2
  • PS: quad Cortex-A53, 4 GB DDR4, Gigabit Ethernet, USB 3.0, micro-SD, Mini DisplayPort [1].
  • PL: 8 RF-ADCs and 8 RF-DACs on the chip (4 ADCs and 2 DACs wired to SMA connectors), 4 GB PL DDR4, a QSFP28 cage for up to 100 Gb/s Ethernet, PMOD and SYZYGY connectors [1, 2].
  • The 100G QSFP28 port could stream large amounts of data to a PC, but QICK's standard firmware does not use it; data reaches the PC through the PS and Gigabit Ethernet.
Check yourself

1. Why can't the tProcessor be replaced by a Python loop on the ARM cores?

Show answer
Linux and Python give no timing guarantees: interrupts, scheduling and garbage collection cause delays of microseconds to milliseconds, and each register access takes about a microsecond. Pulses need nanosecond-precise, deterministic timing, which only logic in the PL provides.

2. What is the difference between AXI4-Lite and AXI4-Stream?

Show answer
AXI4-Lite reads and writes single registers at addresses (control). AXI4-Stream moves a continuous flow of data from one block to the next without addresses (data paths such as ADC samples).
Summary
  • The RFSoC combines a processing system (ARM cores, DDR4, peripherals, Linux) with programmable logic (fabric, RF converters, hardened blocks).
  • AXI4-Lite carries register accesses, AXI4 burst transfers, AXI4-Stream continuous data, all with a valid/ready handshake.
  • MMIO is for configuration; DMA is for bulk data; real-time actions must be in the PL.
  • GSPS raw data cannot be streamed to Linux, so QICK reduces it in the PL.
PreviousChapter 24 · Digital logic and FPGA fabricNextChapter 26 · Inside the RFSoC data converters

Part VI · FPGAs and the RFSoC chip · Chapter 26

Inside the RFSoC data converters

Why you need this

The RF data converters are the part of the RFSoC that touches the analog world. They are organised into tiles with their own clocks and PLLs, they have built-in mixers, filters and calibration engines, and they are configured from software through an interface called the RF Data Converter (RFDC) driver. QICK sets them up for you, but when you check power levels, debug a missing signal, add an external clock, or read a QICK printout that says "DAC tile 2, blk 0 is DAC_A", you need this map. This chapter summarises the SDR book's three data-converter chapters and AMD's PG269 product guide for the parts that matter to you [5, 46].

26.1Tiles and blocks

The converters are grouped into tiles. Each tile has its own clock input and PLL, and contains two or four converter blocks, each with its own digital signal-processing pipeline. In AMD's naming, ADC tiles are numbered 224–227 and DAC tiles 228–231. In software (PYNQ's xrfdc and QICK) the same tiles are numbered 0–3 within each type.

On the RFSoC 4x2, the XCZU48DR has 8 ADCs and 8 DACs, of which the board brings out 4 ADCs and 2 DACs [2]:

Board labelTile (AMD)Tile index (software)QICK standard firmware use
DAC_ADAC tile 230DAC tile 2, block 0generator 1
DAC_BDAC tile 228DAC tile 0, block 0generator 0
ADC_A, ADC_BADC tile 226ADC tile 2not used by the standard tProc v1 firmware printout
ADC_CADC tile 224ADC tile 0, block 2readout 1
ADC_DADC tile 224ADC tile 0, block 0readout 0

The QICK column comes from the configuration printout of the 4x2 standard firmware in QICK's demo notebooks [3]; check your own firmware's printout, because firmware versions differ. QICK's quick-start guide confirms "DAC_B and ADC_D ... will be generator 0 and readout 0" [4].

26.2The RF-ADC pipeline

  • Input buffer and digital step attenuator (DSA): Gen3 devices can attenuate the input in steps before conversion, useful if your signal is too strong.
  • The ADC core: 14 bits at up to 5 GSPS on Gen3, built from interleaved sub-converters with background calibration (Chapter 22).
  • Threshold detectors: flag over-range inputs.
  • Complex mixer: a coarse mixer (shifts by \(f_s/4\), \(f_s/2\)) and a fine mixer with a 48-bit NCO, converting real input to complex baseband.
  • Decimation filters: 1× to 40× on Gen3.
  • FIFO and AXI-Stream: hand the samples to the fabric at the fabric clock rate.

26.3The RF-DAC pipeline

26.4Clocks and PLLs

Each tile needs a sampling clock. It can come from an external clock pin directly, or from the tile's internal PLL multiplying a lower reference. On the 4x2, external LMX2594 synthesisers feed the tiles (Chapter 30), and the QICK firmware configures the tiles with a 491.52 MHz reference, generating 9830.4 MSPS for the DACs and 4423.68 MSPS for the ADCs [3]. Because different tiles have different PLLs, their sampling clocks can have different phases after power-up. AMD's multi-tile synchronisation (MTS) feature aligns tiles to each other, and QICK's documentation describes how clocks are grouped ("Groups of related clocks: [tProc clock, DAC tile 0, DAC tile 2], [ADC tile 0]" in the 4x2 printout) [3].

26.5Configuration from software

The RFDC is configured through the xrfdc driver, which PYNQ exposes in Python: you can read and set Nyquist zones, mixer frequencies, decimation and interpolation, DSA and VOP settings, and check PLL lock status. QICK wraps the settings it needs, for example set_nyquist() (Chapter 19) and the DAC current mode, and leaves the rest at the firmware's defaults. Changing a converter's sampling rate is possible but involves reprogramming clocks; QICK's documentation has a dedicated page on it [4].

Common mistake

Changing RFDC settings directly with xrfdc while a QICK program runs, or changing them behind QICK's back. QICK caches some settings (Nyquist zone, mixer frequency) and assumes it controls them. Make changes through QICK's methods, or reload the firmware afterwards.

Check yourself

1. A QICK printout says "ADC tile 0, blk 0 is ADC_D". Which AMD tile number is that, and which SMA connector?

Show answer
ADC tile 224 (software index 0), the SMA labelled ADC_D on the board.

2. Why does QICK not use the converters' built-in mixers and decimators on the 4x2?

Show answer
It needs per-pulse, phase-coherent control of frequency and phase by the tProcessor, and several independent readout configurations. Doing synthesis and down-conversion in the fabric gives that flexibility; the hardened DUC/DDC are configured from software and are less suited to changing every pulse.
Summary
  • Converters are grouped into tiles with their own clocks and PLLs; ADC tiles 224–227, DAC tiles 228–231 (software 0–3).
  • On the 4x2: DAC_A = tile 230, DAC_B = tile 228, ADC_A/B = tile 226, ADC_C/D = tile 224; QICK standard firmware uses DAC_B, DAC_A, ADC_D, ADC_C.
  • ADC path: buffer/DSA, ADC, threshold, QMC, mixer, decimation; DAC path: interpolation, mixer, QMC/IMR/inverse sinc, DAC, output mode.
  • QICK sets 1× rates and does DSP in fabric; tile clocks are aligned with multi-tile synchronisation.
PreviousChapter 25 · Zynq UltraScale+: processing system, programmable logic, AXI and DMANextChapter 27 · The design flow: Vivado, bitstreams and overlays

Part VI · FPGAs and the RFSoC chip · Chapter 27

The design flow: Vivado, bitstreams and overlays

Why you need this

QICK ships ready-made firmware files for the 4x2, so you can do a great deal without ever opening an FPGA tool. Sooner or later, though, you may want something the standard firmware does not have: all four ADCs, a different sample rate, a custom real-time filter, a crosstalk matrix like spinQICK's. Then you need the design flow. This chapter explains what the files are, what each tool does, how long it takes, and what a QICK firmware project looks like, so you can judge when a change is a Python change and when it is a firmware change [5].

27.1From block design to bitstream

  • Vivado is AMD's FPGA tool suite. Its IP Integrator lets you assemble a block design from IP blocks (the Zynq PS, the RF Data Converter, DMAs, custom blocks) and connect them with AXI interfaces; the design can be saved and recreated as a Tcl script.
  • Synthesis converts HDL into a netlist of device primitives.
  • Implementation places the primitives on specific sites and routes the connections, then performs static timing analysis. If any path is too slow for its clock, the design "fails timing" and must be changed (pipelining, different placement, lower clock).
  • The bitstream (.bit) configures the PL. The hardware handoff (.hwh) is an XML description of the block design: which IP blocks exist, their names, addresses and parameters.

27.2Overlays: PYNQ's name for firmware

In PYNQ, an overlay is a bitstream plus its .hwh. When Python loads it, PYNQ programs the PL and parses the .hwh so that every IP block becomes a Python object with its registers mapped at the right address [49]. QICK builds on this: QickSoc('qick_4x2.bit') loads the overlay, discovers the generators, readouts and buffers from the hardware description, and builds the configuration you see when you print soc [3]. Swapping overlays takes seconds, so you can keep several firmware variants on the SD card.

27.3A QICK firmware project

The QICK repository contains, under firmware/projects/, one directory per board and processor version, for example qick_tprocv1_4x2_standard and qick_tprocv2_4x2_standard. Each holds [3]:

  • proj.tcl: creates the Vivado project and adds sources;
  • bd_2023-1.tcl: recreates the block design (for Vivado 2023.1);
  • ios.xdc, timing.xdc: pin assignments and timing constraints;
  • out/: the pre-built qick_4x2.bit and .hwh.

The custom IP (tProcessor, signal generators, readouts, buffers) lives in firmware/ip and firmware/hdl, with testbenches for simulation. Reading the block-design Tcl file is the most reliable way to see what a firmware contains. For example, the 4x2 tProc v2 standard design instantiates two axis_signal_gen_v6 generators, three axis_dyn_readout_v1 readouts, two averaging buffers, a weighted buffer, a DDR4 buffer, a multi-rate buffer and a time tagger [3].

27.4When do you need to rebuild firmware?

ChangePython onlyNew firmware
New pulse sequence, sweep, feedback logic in the tProcessor program✓
Different frequencies, phases, gains, envelopes✓
Readout window length, number of shots✓
Nyquist zone, DAC current mode✓ (through QICK/RFDC)
Using ADC_A/ADC_B as additional readouts✓
Different converter sample rates or clock plansometimes (clock reprogramming)often
Real-time crosstalk matrix, custom filters, ML inference✓
Longer waveform memories, more generators per DAC✓
In the lab

Before building your own firmware, ask on the QICK community channels and check the QICK and spinQICK repositories: many variants already exist, for example spinQICK's 16-output ZCU216 firmware and its crosstalk-compensation build [10]. Building QICK firmware needs a Linux or Windows workstation with Vivado installed (tens of GB) and several hours per build. Check that your Vivado edition supports the XCZU48DR device: large RFSoC devices typically need a paid licence edition, and AMD's University Program can help academic users with licences.

Check yourself

1. What two files make a PYNQ overlay, and what does each contain?

Show answer
The .bit bitstream (the PL configuration) and the .hwh hardware handoff (an XML description of the IP blocks, addresses and parameters that Python uses to build drivers).

2. You want the tProcessor to apply a crosstalk matrix to two DAC outputs in real time. Python change or firmware change?

Show answer
Firmware: real-time arithmetic on output samples needs new logic in the generator data path (as in spinQICK's crosstalk firmware). With only two outputs you could instead precompute compensated waveforms in Python, which is a Python-only change.
Summary
  • Vivado turns HDL, IP and block designs into a netlist (synthesis), a placed and routed design (implementation, with timing checks), and a bitstream.
  • A PYNQ overlay is .bit + .hwh; QICK reads the .hwh to discover its blocks.
  • QICK firmware projects are Tcl scripts per board; pre-built 4x2 bitstreams are included.
  • Most experiment changes are Python changes; new hardware features need a firmware rebuild.
PreviousChapter 26 · Inside the RFSoC data convertersNextChapter 28 · A tour of the RFSoC 4x2 board

Part VII · The RFSoC 4x2 board · Chapter 28

A tour of the RFSoC 4x2 board

Why you need this

This chapter is the reference for your hardware: every connector, chip, LED and switch on the RFSoC 4x2 that matters for qubit work, with what it does and where its limits are. Keep it open the first time you set up the board. All facts come from the RFSoC-PYNQ board pages and Real Digital's reference manual (revision A6) and schematic [1, 2].

28.1The board in one paragraph

The RFSoC 4x2 was developed by the AMD PYNQ team with Real Digital as a low-cost academic RFSoC platform. It is built around a Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC Gen3 XCZU48DR-1FFVG1517E with a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 processing system and UltraScale+ programmable logic. The chip has 8 RF-ADCs and 8 RF-DACs; the board brings out 4 ADCs (5 GSPS) and 2 DACs (9.85 GSPS) on SMA connectors through baluns, hence the name "4x2". It has 8 GB of DDR4 (4 GB for the PS, 4 GB for the PL), a QSFP28 port, Gigabit Ethernet, USB 3.0, a micro-SD boot card, PMOD and SYZYGY expansion connectors and a small OLED display. It is sold only to universities and research institutes, through the AMD University Program, at an academic price of $2,499 (2026) [1]. Its schematics, bill of materials and PCB files are open source.

28.2RF connectors

Six SMA connectors carry the RF signals: DAC_A, DAC_B (outputs) and ADC_A–ADC_D (inputs). Each passes through decoupling capacitors and a MACOM MABA-011118 balun, under an RF shield, with no active components in the path [2]. Practically:

  • All ports are single-ended 50 Ω and AC-coupled. The balun is rated 10 MHz–10 GHz; below 10 MHz transmission falls off.
  • The ADCs have a 6 GHz RF input bandwidth according to Real Digital [2]; the DACs run up to 9.85 GSPS.
  • There is no on-board amplification, filtering or protection. External attenuators, filters, amplifiers and DC blocks are your responsibility.

Chapter 29 treats the analog front end in depth, including how others have modified it.

28.3Clocking hardware

A Skyworks Si5395 jitter-attenuating clock multiplier, driven by a 48 MHz crystal, generates most PS and PL clocks. A TI LMK04828 jitter cleaner, using a 10 MHz clock from the Si5395 and a 160 MHz VCXO, drives two TI LMX2594 RF synthesisers, which produce the ADC and DAC sampling (reference) clocks. PYNQ programs the LMK and LMXs at start-up. SMA inputs for an external reference clock (CLK IN) and a synchronisation signal (SYNC IN) go to the LMK, and a PPS (pulse-per-second) input is provided [2]. Chapter 30 explains how to lock the board to a lab 10 MHz reference.

28.4Memory and storage

  • PS DDR4, 4 GB, 64-bit, 2400 MT/s: Linux, Python, your data.
  • PL DDR4, 4 GB, 64-bit, 2400 MT/s: available to FPGA designs; QICK uses it for a capture buffer of about 1.07 billion samples (about 1.94 s at the decimated rate) [3].
  • micro-SD card (16 GB or more): holds the PYNQ Linux image, boot files and your notebooks. Set the BOOT switch to "SD" to boot from it.

28.5Communication ports

  • Gigabit Ethernet (TI DP83867 PHY on the PS): the normal link to your lab network or PC; supports IEEE 1588 time stamping [2].
  • Micro-USB 3.0 device port: the board appears to a PC as a USB network adapter ("Ethernet gadget") at 192.168.3.1, useful for a first connection without a network [1].
  • Micro-USB 2.0 "PROG UART": an FTDI chip providing a serial console (to watch Linux boot) and JTAG for Vivado debugging.
  • QSFP28: up to 100 Gb/s Ethernet from the PL transceivers; unused by standard QICK, but a path for high-throughput streaming in custom designs.
  • Two USB 3.0 host ports (for keyboards, storage, USB instruments) and Mini DisplayPort.

28.6User I/O: PMOD, SYZYGY, buttons and LEDs

The Pmod+ header is a 30-pin, 100-mil connector with 22 FPGA signals (routed as differential pairs), 4 ground and 4 supply pins. Two standard 12-pin PMOD modules (PMOD A and B) fit in marked positions, or the whole connector can be used. Signals are rated up to about 50 MHz [2]. QICK uses PMOD0_0–PMOD0_7 as tProcessor-controlled trigger outputs and PMOD1_0 as an external start input [3].

Common mistake

Assuming PMOD outputs are 3.3 V or 5 V TTL. The manual states that FPGA I/O uses the LVCMOS18 standard unless noted otherwise, and the PMOD pins carry no exception, so treat them as 1.8 V logic [2]. Many instruments' trigger inputs expect TTL thresholds and need a level shifter; spinQICK's hardware list includes a PMOD level shifter "to buffer the trigger pulses for improved stability" [10]. Never connect a 5 V signal to a PMOD pin.

The SYZYGY port is a 40-pin Samtec connector with 32 differential FPGA signals (up to 500 MHz), a clock, I²C and supplies, for plug-in boards such as fast DACs or ADCs. The board also has 5 PL push-buttons, 4 slide switches, 4 white LEDs and 2 RGB LEDs on the PL, one push-button and two LEDs on the PS, and a 16×2 OLED display that shows the IP address after boot.

28.7Power, heat and status LEDs

Power comes from a 12 V, 10 A supply (included). An LM25069 protection circuit switches on only between 10.7 and 13.3 V and shuts down on over-power (about 110 W). The RFSoC can dissipate more than 20 W, so a heatsink and fan are mandatory; a yellow "FAIL" LED indicates a stuck fan and a red "OVER TEMP" LED a die over-temperature, which resets the chip [2]. Nine INA220 monitors measure the critical supply rails and are readable over I²C.

The converter supplies come from switching regulators followed by low-dropout regulators (LDOs) to keep the ADC and DAC rails quiet [2]. Even so, a board next to sensitive measurements should have its own clean power and a single, well-defined ground connection to the rest of the setup.

28.8First boot

  1. Write the latest RFSoC 4x2 PYNQ image to the micro-SD card (or use the supplied card), insert it, set BOOT to SD.
  2. Connect the micro-USB 3.0 cable to your PC (or Ethernet to your network) and the 12 V supply; switch on.
  3. All ten power LEDs light; after about 40 seconds the DONE and INIT LEDs turn green; the four white user LEDs flash and stay on; the OLED shows the network address.
  4. Browse to http://192.168.3.1/lab (or the IP shown) and log in with the password xilinx.

These steps follow the official getting-started guide [1]. Note that QICK recommends specific PYNQ image versions for each board (for the 4x2, PYNQ 3.0.1 at the time of writing) and does not yet support PYNQ 3.1 [4, 3]. Chapter 31 covers PYNQ itself, and Chapter 34 installs QICK.

Check yourself

1. Which four facts about the 4x2's RF ports most affect spin-qubit use?

Show answer
Only 2 DAC and 4 ADC ports are available; every port is AC-coupled through capacitors and a balun (10 MHz–10 GHz); there is no on-board amplification, filtering or protection; outputs are single-ended 50 Ω.

2. You need to trigger a DC source that expects a 3.3 V TTL trigger. What do you connect?

Show answer
A level shifter (for example a PMOD level-shifter module) between a QICK PMOD trigger output (1.8 V logic) and the instrument's trigger input, with a shared ground.
Summary
  • XCZU48DR Gen3 RFSoC; 4 ADC (5 GSPS) and 2 DAC (9.85 GSPS) SMA ports through 10 MHz–10 GHz baluns.
  • Si5395 + LMK04828 + 2 × LMX2594 clocking with external reference and sync inputs.
  • 4 GB PS + 4 GB PL DDR4; micro-SD boot; Gigabit Ethernet, USB 3.0 gadget, UART/JTAG, QSFP28.
  • Pmod+ (QICK triggers on PMOD0_0–7, 1.8 V logic), SYZYGY, LEDs, OLED; 12 V/10 A power with a mandatory fan.
  • Board at 192.168.3.1 over USB, password xilinx; QICK recommends PYNQ 3.0.1 for the 4x2.
PreviousChapter 27 · The design flow: Vivado, bitstreams and overlaysNextChapter 29 · The analog front end: baluns, limits, protection and modifications

Part VII · The RFSoC 4x2 board · Chapter 29

The analog front end: baluns, limits, protection and modifications

Why you need this

The few millimetres of circuit between each SMA connector and the RFSoC chip decide what the 4x2 can and cannot do for spin qubits. They make the board excellent for RF and microwave signals and unable to produce DC levels or long baseband pulses. This chapter explains that circuit, shows what it does to typical gate pulses, lists the ways around it (from external instruments to board modifications that others have published), and covers how to protect the converters.

29.1What is between the SMA and the chip

Each of the six RF ports has the same passive network: decoupling capacitors and a MACOM MABA-011118 transformer balun, under an RF shield, with no active components [2]. For the ADC inputs, the QICK-DAWG team identified the parts as the balun plus two 100 nF capacitors (C302 and C303 on the schematic for one channel), together forming a high-pass filter [41].

What the balun's rating means

A transformer balun couples energy magnetically, so it has a lower frequency limit set by its winding inductance and an upper limit set by parasitic capacitance and the length of its windings. Its rated band, 10 MHz to 10 GHz for this part, is where insertion loss and amplitude/phase balance meet the manufacturer's specifications; outside the band, the response degrades smoothly rather than stopping abruptly. The QICK-DAWG documentation describes the stock ADC path as having a "1 GHz high-pass" behaviour for its purposes [41], which disagrees with the 10 MHz rating in Real Digital's manual [2]. The rated part number supports the 10 MHz figure; the difference may come from how "too much attenuation" was defined for their kHz-range photodiode signals. Measure your own board: a swept tone from a DAC into an ADC (or a VNA on each port) gives the real transfer function in a few minutes.

29.2What AC coupling does to pulses

As a first approximation, treat the port as a first-order high-pass with a 10 MHz corner, time constant \(\tau = 1/(2\pi\times10\ \text{MHz}) \approx 16\) ns. A step in voltage becomes a spike that decays with \(\tau\); a pulse becomes a positive spike at its start and a negative spike at its end; any signal with no frequency components below ~10 MHz passes nearly unchanged.

Consequences for the signals of Chapter 1:

SignalThrough a stock 4x2 port
Readout carrier (100 MHz–1 GHz) and reflected signalPasses. Ideal use.
Microwave EDSR bursts (GHz carrier)Passes, up to the DAC's useful frequency range.
Fast exchange pulses (~10 ns)Distorted: droop and undershoot of tens of percent. Partially correctable by pre-distortion; not ideal.
Detuning and readout-level pulses (µs–ms)Do not pass: only edges get through.
DC gate voltages, slow rampsBlocked.
Lock-in excitation at kHz–MHzStrongly attenuated below ~10 MHz.

29.3Ways around the AC coupling

1. Keep baseband pulses on another instrument

Use a DC-coupled AWG for gate pulses, triggered by a QICK PMOD output (through a level shifter), with both instruments locked to the same 10 MHz reference. The 4x2 does readout, microwaves and timing. This needs no modification and is the recommended starting point (Chapter 38). The cost is trigger jitter and latency between the two instruments, which you must calibrate.

2. Use signals that survive AC coupling

Some useful baseband experiments only need signals without a slow component:

  • Fast charge-stability maps with sinusoidal or triangular sweeps at tens of MHz superimposed on DC gate voltages (through bias tees on the PCB), with the readout synchronised to the sweep phase (Chapter 40).
  • Photon-assisted tunnelling and lever-arm calibration with microwaves on a gate.
  • Charge noise spectroscopy and sensor characterisation at high frequency.
  • Short, balanced (zero-mean) pulse pairs, for example a +A pulse immediately followed by a −A pulse of equal area, which suffer less droop.

3. Modify the board

Others have removed the balun and capacitors from 4x2 ports to make them DC-coupled:

  • ADC inputs (published): the QICK-DAWG team removed the balun and replaced the two capacitors with 0 Ω resistors or wire, then drove the ADC's differential input with a TI LMH5401 fully differential amplifier evaluation board. The ADC's input common-mode voltage must be set correctly: they used \(V_{cm} = 0.7\) V for the 4x2 (the same as the ZCU216; the ZCU111 needs 1.2 V), with amplifier supplies of +3.2 V and −1.8 V [41].
  • DAC outputs (not documented for the 4x2 in the sources used here): on the ZCU216, whose DAC outputs are brought out differentially, HRL's spinQICK setup uses LMH5401 modules to convert the differential DAC outputs to DC-coupled single-ended signals, followed by THS3491 amplifiers [10, 11]. Doing the same on a 4x2 requires removing the output balun and capacitors and providing the RF-DAC outputs with the DC termination and bias they need (RF-DAC outputs are current-mode outputs whose termination and supply requirements are specified in AMD's PG269 and DS926). Get this wrong and you can damage the DAC. Study the schematic and AMD's documentation, and ideally ask the Real Digital, PYNQ or QICK communities before attempting it.
Common mistake

Modifying the board without measuring first. Rework under RF shields on a 1517-ball BGA board is delicate, can damage pads, and is irreversible in practice. Before any modification, measure each port's transfer function and noise, keep the measurements, and practise the soldering on a scrap board. Consider whether option 1 or a different board meets your needs.

4. Use a board designed for it

The ZCU216 brings out its 16 DACs and 16 ADCs through connectors to which you attach either baluns or DC-coupled networks; QICK's documentation notes that the ZCU216 "allows for flexibility in AC- or DC-coupling your signals" [4]. The QICK Box (an RF front end with DC-coupled and RF modules for the ZCU216) [44] and spinQICK's recommended QICK Box configuration with "DC In" and "DC Out" modules [10] are built for exactly this. Chapter 45 compares the options.

29.4Protecting the converters

  • Never exceed the ADC's absolute maximum input power, given in DS926 [45]. Full scale is of order +1 dBm; inputs well above it can cause permanent damage. When looping a DAC into an ADC, or connecting an amplified readout signal, start with 10–20 dB of attenuation.
  • Watch for amplifier oscillations and switching transients: a room-temperature amplifier that oscillates, or the connection of a charged cable, can deliver far more than the steady-state power.
  • ESD: the SMA centre pins connect (through passives) to the chip. Discharge yourself and cables before connecting, and use DC blocks and limiters at inputs exposed to unknown equipment (Appendix B).
  • Do not apply DC to the SMA ports. The capacitors block it in steady state, but switching a DC voltage on or off produces a step that passes through.
In the lab

A useful first-week exercise: (1) connect DAC_B to a spectrum analyser and record output power versus frequency from 10 MHz to 10 GHz at fixed gain, in Nyquist zones 1 and 2; (2) connect DAC_B through a 20 dB attenuator to ADC_D and measure the loopback transfer function and its phase; (3) send a 1 µs square pulse into an oscilloscope (50 Ω input) and record what comes out. You will then know your board's front end better than any data sheet can tell you.

Check yourself

1. A 1 µs plunger pulse of 20 mV is played through a stock 4x2 DAC port. What arrives at the gate, roughly?

Show answer
A positive spike of up to 20 mV at the start, decaying within a few tens of ns, near-zero during the pulse, and a negative spike at the end. The intended 1 µs level is lost.

2. Why is removing a DAC output balun riskier than removing an ADC input balun?

Show answer
The RF-DAC is a current-mode output that needs a specific DC termination and bias; the stock output network provides part of that. Removing it without providing the correct termination can stress or damage the DAC. ADC inputs need a correct common-mode voltage, which is easier to supply with a differential amplifier, and that modification has been published.
Summary
  • Each RF port has DC-blocking capacitors and a 10 MHz–10 GHz balun; the result is AC coupling with a corner near 10 MHz (measure your board).
  • RF readout and microwave bursts pass; µs–ms baseband pulses and DC do not; 10 ns pulses are distorted.
  • Workarounds: external DC-coupled AWG; AC-compatible signals; board modification (published for ADC inputs with LMH5401 and \(V_{cm}\) = 0.7 V); or a ZCU216/QICK Box.
  • Protect the converters: respect DS926 maximum ratings, attenuate first, avoid ESD and DC steps.

Part VII · The RFSoC 4x2 board · Chapter 30

Clocks, references, synchronisation and triggers

Why you need this

A qubit experiment is a timing problem. The phase of every microwave pulse, the start of every readout window and the trigger of every external instrument must be fixed relative to each other, shot after shot, to well below a nanosecond and a degree. Inside the RFSoC this is easy, because everything runs from one clock tree. Between the 4x2 and the rest of your lab (an external LO, an AWG, a DC source, a second board) it takes deliberate work. This chapter explains the board's clock tree, how to lock it to a lab reference, how QICK keeps time, and how to trigger and synchronise other instruments.

30.1The clock tree on the 4x2

Because the DACs, ADCs and fabric all derive from one reference, a generator and a readout on the same board are always frequency-locked and keep a fixed phase relationship while the board is running. QICK's documentation calls this "an advantage of the RFSoC": all converter clocks are synthesised from a common reference and are always phase-locked with respect to each other [4]. After each power-up, though, the fixed phase offsets between different tiles and between generator and readout can change, which is why phase-sensitive experiments calibrate them after every boot (Chapter 36).

QICK programs the clock chips the first time you create a QickSoc after power-on. On the 4x2, four LEDs labelled "CLOCK STATUS" light up and should stay on steadily [4].

30.2Locking to a lab reference

Use an external reference when you need better frequency stability (QICK's documentation notes that touching the on-board oscillator's can shifts a DAC tone by hundreds of Hz) or when the 4x2 must be phase-locked to other instruments, such as the LO for EDSR upconversion [4]. On the 4x2:

  • Feed a 10 MHz reference into the CLK IN SMA and create the SoC with QickSoc(..., external_clk=True) [3].
  • The input goes without attenuation to an AC-coupled single-ended LMK04828B input. The LMK data sheet asks for roughly 0.35–2.4 V peak-to-peak; QICK's documentation suggests 0 to +10 dBm as a safe range [4].
  • The usual lab setup: a rubidium or OCXO 10 MHz distribution amplifier feeding the 4x2, the microwave LO, the AWG and any other instrument that must stay phase-locked.
Common mistake

Locking the 4x2 and the EDSR local oscillator to different references, or one of them to nothing. Two free-running oscillators drift relative to each other by Hz to kHz. The upconverted drive's phase then wanders relative to QICK's virtual-Z bookkeeping, which shows up as decaying Ramsey or echo contrast that looks like decoherence but is not.

30.3How QICK keeps time

The tProcessor schedules every event (pulse starts, readout triggers, PMOD outputs) at an absolute time on a counter that runs from a fabric timing clock. In tProc v2 this is a 48-bit absolute time counter shared by all outputs [4]. The 4x2 standard firmware's printout reports a tProc timing clock of 409.6 MHz (2.44 ns per tick) [3]. Events are placed on this grid; within one generator, pulse waveforms themselves are defined sample by sample at the full DAC rate (0.1 ns), so fine delays can be built into the envelope.

Different outputs have different fixed latencies through their data paths. QICK and spinQICK provide calibrations for these offsets; measure them once with an oscilloscope or a loopback, and correct in software (Chapter 36).

30.4Triggers to and from other instruments

  • Outputs: QICK drives 8 PMOD pins (PMOD0_0–PMOD0_7) as timed digital outputs from the tProcessor, with the same timing grid as the pulses [3]. Use them to trigger AWGs, DC sources, oscilloscopes, or a laser. They are 1.8 V logic (Chapter 28): add a level shifter for 3.3 V/5 V inputs.
  • Input: an external start pin (PMOD1_0 in the 4x2 firmware) can start a tProcessor program on an external event [3].
  • Latency and jitter: a trigger from the 4x2 to an external AWG has a fixed delay (cables, the AWG's trigger latency, often tens to hundreds of ns) and some jitter. Lock both instruments to the same 10 MHz to reduce jitter, measure the delay with a scope, and shift the QICK timeline to compensate.

30.5Synchronising several boards

Larger experiments need more channels than one board has. QICK supports multi-board operation: a SYNC input on the 4x2's LMK allows clock-divider synchronisation across boards (the manual notes that LMK outputs OUT1 and OUT5 must be enabled for this) [2], and QICK's tutorials cover multi-board synchronisation and the XCOM system, a full-mesh synchronisation and low-latency communication network between QICK boards [4, 50]. Multi-board synchronisation is more mature on the ZCU216-based systems that large QICK users run.

Check yourself

1. Why is the phase between a QICK generator and readout stable within a session but possibly different after a reboot?

Show answer
Both derive from one reference and are phase-locked while running, but tile PLLs, dividers and data-path FIFOs can start in different states at each power-up, giving a new fixed offset. Hence recalibration after boot.

2. What do you connect, and how do you call QICK, to lock the 4x2 to your lab rubidium standard?

Show answer
A 10 MHz output of the standard (0 to +10 dBm) into CLK IN, and QickSoc(..., external_clk=True).
Summary
  • Si5395, LMK04828 and two LMX2594s generate all clocks from one reference; converters and fabric are always mutually phase-locked.
  • Lock to a lab reference with 10 MHz on CLK IN and external_clk=True; lock the LO and other instruments to the same reference.
  • QICK schedules events on a ~2.44 ns tProcessor grid (4x2 standard firmware); waveforms are sample-accurate at 0.1 ns.
  • PMOD0_0–7 are timed trigger outputs (1.8 V); PMOD1_0 can start programs; measure and compensate trigger latencies.
  • Multi-board synchronisation uses SYNC IN and QICK's synchronisation tools such as XCOM.
PreviousChapter 29 · The analog front end: baluns, limits, protection and modificationsNextChapter 31 · PYNQ: Linux, Jupyter, overlays and first boot

Part VIII · PYNQ · Chapter 31

PYNQ: Linux, Jupyter, overlays and first boot

Why you need this

PYNQ is the software layer that makes the 4x2 usable from Python. It boots Linux on the ARM cores, runs a Jupyter server you open in your browser, loads FPGA designs at run time, and gives Python objects for every hardware block. QICK is a Python package built on top of it. Understanding PYNQ means you can set up the board on your network, install software, move files, recover from mistakes, and know which problems belong to Linux, which to PYNQ and which to QICK [49, 5].

31.1What PYNQ is

PYNQ ("Python productivity for Zynq") is an open-source framework from AMD consisting of:

  • a Linux image (Ubuntu-based) for the board's ARM cores, distributed as an SD-card image per board;
  • a Jupyter server (JupyterLab) on the board, so the board is programmed from a browser;
  • the pynq Python package, which loads overlays and provides drivers: MMIO register access, DMA buffers, GPIO, interrupts, clock control, and RFSoC-specific packages xrfdc (RF data converters) and xrfclk (clock chips);
  • example notebooks and a base overlay for each board.

The RFSoC-specific parts (board images, base overlays and notebooks for the 4x2, 2x2 and ZCU111) live in the RFSoC-PYNQ project [1]. The SDR book's Notebook Set A introduces Jupyter, plotting and the PYNQ framework on RFSoC boards [5].

31.2Jupyter in two minutes

A notebook is a document of cells. Code cells run Python on the board when you press Shift+Enter, and their output (text, plots) appears below. Markdown cells hold notes. The kernel is the Python process that keeps your variables between cells; restarting it clears everything, including the connection to the hardware. JupyterLab adds a file browser, terminals (a Linux shell on the board) and text editors in the same browser tab.

Common mistake

Running two notebooks that both create a QickSoc (or load overlays) at the same time. Each one reprograms the PL and expects to own it. Use one notebook per board at a time, or run QICK as a server (Pyro4, Chapter 37) and connect clients to it.

31.3The boot process and the SD card

  1. At power-on, the boot ROM reads the boot mode switch (set to SD) and loads a first-stage boot loader from the SD card's boot partition.
  2. The boot loader configures the PS, loads a default bitstream into the PL (the green DONE LED) and starts U-Boot, which starts the Linux kernel.
  3. Linux mounts the SD card's root file system, starts networking (Ethernet and the USB "gadget" at 192.168.3.1), the Jupyter server and the OLED status display.

The SD card is the board's disk. Keep a spare card with a known-good image, and back up your notebooks regularly: SD cards wear out and can be corrupted by switching power off during writes. Shut the board down cleanly (sudo shutdown -h now in a terminal, or the Jupyter menu) before switching it off.

31.4Networking for a lab

  • USB gadget: plug the micro-USB 3.0 cable into a PC; the board appears as a network adapter and is at 192.168.3.1. Fine for first use.
  • Ethernet with DHCP: the board gets an address from your network; the OLED shows it.
  • Static IP / private network: many labs put instruments on a separate network switch with fixed addresses, connected to the measurement PC through a second network card. This avoids IT restrictions and keeps measurement traffic local. QICK's quick-start guide explains static IP configuration [4].
  • SSH: log in with ssh xilinx@<board-ip> (default user xilinx, password xilinx) for a shell; copy files with scp. Change the default password if the board is on a shared network.

31.5Overlays in practice

An overlay is a .bit plus .hwh (Chapter 27). Loading one in Python takes a few seconds:

from pynq import Overlay
ol = Overlay("base.bit")      # programs the PL with the base design
print(ol.ip_dict.keys())      # names of the IP blocks in the design

PYNQ parses the .hwh and attaches a Python driver to each IP block (generic or specialised), so ol.<block_name> gives you an object with its registers. When QICK starts, it does the same with its own bitstream and builds higher-level objects (generators, readouts, tProcessor) from what it finds [3].

31.6The 4x2 base overlay and its notebooks

The PYNQ image ships a base overlay with the RF data converters, the PL DDR4 controller, two PMOD I/O processors (small MicroBlaze CPUs), and GPIO for the LEDs, buttons, switches and SYZYGY port [1]. Its notebooks are a good first tour:

  • 01_rf_dataconverter_introduction, 02_rf_spectrum_analysis, 03_rf_spectrum_sweep: generate tones, capture ADC data, compute and plot spectra.
  • buttons_leds_switches, pl_ddr4, register_map_intro, syzygy_loopback: board I/O and register access.

Run them before installing QICK: they confirm that your converters, clocks and network work, and they show the same hardware through PYNQ's lower-level API.

31.7Installing software on the board

The board runs a normal Linux with Python and pip, so packages are installed as on any Linux machine (with internet access through your network, or by copying wheel files). QICK is installed with pip from its repository, and its first demo notebook automates this [3]. QICK states which PYNQ image versions it supports; at the time of writing it recommends PYNQ 3.0.1 for the 4x2 and does not yet support PYNQ 3.1 [4]. Check the QICK quick-start page before updating the SD image.

On the 4x2

A clean setup sequence: (1) flash the PYNQ image QICK recommends; (2) boot, connect over USB, run the base-overlay RF notebooks with a DAC looped back into an ADC through a 20 dB attenuator; (3) set up Ethernet and SSH; (4) install QICK and run its first demo. Chapter 34 continues from step 4.

Check yourself

1. Which part of the system answers when you open http://192.168.3.1/lab?

Show answer
The Jupyter server running under Linux on the board's ARM cores (the PS), reached through the USB Ethernet gadget.

2. You restart the Jupyter kernel in the middle of a QICK session. What is lost?

Show answer
All Python variables, including the QickSoc object; you must recreate it (which reloads or reconnects to the firmware). The PL keeps its configuration until reprogrammed, but the Python side forgets it.
Summary
  • PYNQ = Linux image + Jupyter + Python package for overlays and hardware access + example notebooks.
  • Boot from SD; connect at 192.168.3.1 (USB) or the OLED-reported IP (Ethernet); SSH as xilinx.
  • Overlay() programs the PL and maps IP blocks to Python objects.
  • Run the base overlay RF notebooks first; install the QICK-recommended PYNQ image (3.0.1 for the 4x2 at the time of writing).
