Part VIII · PYNQ · Chapter 32

Talking to hardware from Python, and the SDR book labs

Why you need this

QICK hides most hardware details, but when something does not work, or when you want to test the converters directly, you will drop down to PYNQ's lower-level tools: reading registers, capturing raw ADC data, changing converter settings, checking clock lock. This chapter shows those tools with short examples, then maps the AMD SDR book's nine sets of hands-on notebooks onto what a qubit experimentalist should learn from each.

32.1Registers: MMIO

Every AXI-Lite peripheral in the PL appears as a block of 32-bit registers at a physical address (Chapter 25). PYNQ's MMIO class maps such a block into Python:

from pynq import MMIO
regs = MMIO(base_addr, 0x1000)   # base address and size, from the overlay's ip_dict
regs.write(0x10, 12345)           # write register at offset 0x10
value = regs.read(0x14)           # read register at offset 0x14

Overlay drivers do this for you; for example ol.ip_dict lists each block's base address, and many drivers expose a register_map with named fields (the 4x2 base overlay has a register_map_intro notebook) [1]. Each access from Python costs of order a microsecond, so MMIO is for configuration, never for timing.

32.2Bulk data: allocate and DMA

DMA engines need physically contiguous memory that both Linux and the PL can access. PYNQ provides it with allocate, which returns a NumPy array backed by such memory:

import numpy as np
from pynq import allocate
buf = allocate(shape=(16384,), dtype=np.int32)
dma = ol.axi_dma_0                 # a DMA engine in the overlay (name depends on the design)
dma.recvchannel.transfer(buf)      # PL → memory
dma.recvchannel.wait()
data = np.array(buf)               # copy out, then free
buf.freebuffer()

QICK uses this mechanism internally for loading tProcessor programs and envelopes and for reading readout buffers [3].

32.3The RF data converters: xrfdc

The xrfdc driver exposes the RF Data Converter IP as tiles and blocks with properties you can read and set. A few examples:

rf = ol.usp_rf_data_converter_0           # name in QICK's and most designs
dac = rf.dac_tiles[0].blocks[0]           # DAC tile 0 (AMD tile 228), block 0 = DAC_B on the 4x2
print(dac.NyquistZone)                    # 1 or 2 (QICK sets this through set_nyquist)
adc = rf.adc_tiles[0].blocks[0]           # ADC tile 0 (AMD tile 224), block 0 = ADC_D
print(adc.MixerSettings)                  # mixer configuration of the hardened DDC
print(rf.adc_tiles[0].PLLLockStatus)      # 2 means locked in the RFDC driver's convention

Properties correspond to the settings described in AMD's PG269 product guide [46]. With QICK loaded, prefer QICK's own methods, which keep its cached settings consistent (Chapter 26).

32.4The clocks: xrfclk

The xrfclk package programs the LMK and LMX clock chips from configuration files (exported from TI's TICS Pro tool), which is how PYNQ sets up the 4x2's sampling clocks at start-up [2]. QICK calls it when it configures clocks, for example when you request an external reference [3]. You rarely need it directly unless you change sample rates.

32.5A first hardware test without QICK

In the lab

With the base overlay and its RF notebooks: connect DAC_B → 20 dB attenuator → ADC_D. Play a tone at 200 MHz, capture a buffer of ADC samples, plot it and its spectrum. Then sweep the tone from 10 MHz to 2 GHz and record the received power: this is your loopback transfer function, including both baluns. Repeat with the 20 dB attenuator replaced by a known filter to see the effect. Keep the notebook: it is your board's health check.

32.6The SDR book's notebook labs, mapped for qubit work

The AMD SDR book comes with nine sets of notebooks, installable on the 4x2 with pip from the Strathclyde repository (pip install the release archive, then python -m rfsoc_book install) [51]. Notebooks marked "RFSoC" in the book need the board; the rest run anywhere [5]. Not all are equally relevant to qubits:

SetTopicNotebooksValue for qubit work
AJupyter and PYNQjupyter lab, visualisation, PYNQ introduction, overlaysEssential. Do all four first.
BDSP fundamentalssampling, quantisation, ADCs and DACs, filter designEssential. The basis of Chapters 19–21.
CSpectrumexploring the spectrum, RFSoC spectrum analyser, Fourier, DFT, FFTVery useful. The spectrum analyser is a debugging tool you will reuse.
DCommunicationsbaseband modulation, EVM and BER, pulse shapingUseful for pulse shaping and matched filtering (readout); skip BER details.
EComplex frequency domainAM, QAM, complex QAMEssential. I/Q modulation and demodulation (Chapter 20).
FFrequency planningfrequency planning, RFSoC frequency plannerVery useful. Use the planner for your readout and drive frequencies.
GRadio demonstratorradio system, observe the pipeline, "Hello World" transmit/receiveUseful to see a complete DAC→ADC system with FPGA processing.
HForward error correctionSD-FEC hardware blocksNot needed for qubit control.
IOFDMOFDM fundamentals and transceiverOptional; relevant ideas for frequency-multiplexed readout.
Suggested order

Week 1: Sets A and B. Week 2: Sets C and E, plus the 4x2 base RF notebooks. Week 3: Set F with your planned frequencies, Set G to see a full radio pipeline, then install QICK (Chapter 34). This gives you the SDR intuition the QICK documentation assumes.

Check yourself

1. Why does allocate() exist instead of just using a NumPy array?

Show answer
DMA engines need physically contiguous memory at a known physical address; ordinary NumPy arrays live in virtual memory that may be scattered. allocate() provides contiguous, DMA-accessible buffers that still behave like NumPy arrays.

2. Which SDR book notebook sets would you skip if short of time, and why?

Show answer
H (FEC) and most of I (OFDM) and D's BER material: they concern data communications, not qubit control or readout.
Summary
  • MMIO for registers (slow, configuration only); allocate + DMA for bulk data.
  • xrfdc exposes converter tiles and blocks; xrfclk programs clock chips; prefer QICK's methods once QICK is loaded.
  • Build a DAC→ADC loopback test as your board health check.
  • From the SDR book labs, sets A, B, C, E and F matter most for qubit work.

Part IX · QICK and spinQICK · Chapter 33

QICK architecture

Why you need this

QICK turns an RFSoC board into a qubit controller. To write good experiments with it, and to understand its limits on the 4x2, you need a clear picture of its parts: the timed processor that schedules everything, the signal generators that make the pulses, the readouts that demodulate, the buffers that store results, and the Python library that ties them together. This chapter gives that picture, based on the QICK papers, documentation and firmware source [9, 52, 4, 3].

33.1What QICK is

The Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit was developed at Fermilab with Princeton and other partners and published in 2022 [9]. It consists of firmware for the ZCU111, ZCU216 and RFSoC 4x2 boards, the qick Python package, demo notebooks, and an optional custom analog front end. It is open source (MIT licence). As of October 2026, QICK's own list counts 91 papers that used it, 59 of them on superconducting circuits and 4 on quantum dots [4], and several companies sell QICK-based systems.

33.2The tProcessor: a clock for everything

The tProcessor is a small custom processor in the FPGA. Its key idea is the separation of execution from timing: instructions run as fast as the processor can go, but the commands they issue (play this pulse, trigger that readout, set this pin) carry a timestamp and are queued in FIFOs. A dispatcher compares each timestamp with a running time counter and releases the command exactly when its time comes [4]. So you program a timeline, and loops, branches and arithmetic happen "ahead of time", as long as the processor stays ahead of the schedule.

Two generations exist:

tProc v1 (axis_tproc64x32_x8)tProc v2 (qick_processor)
Instructions / data64-bit instructions, 32-bit registers72-bit instructions, 32-bit data; 5-stage pipeline, one instruction per cycle
TimingTime registers per channel48-bit absolute time counter; reference time; signed output times
ExtrasBasic branchingCall stack, pseudo-random number generator (LFSR), ports for readout data and external peripherals
Python APIAveragerProgram, RAveragerProgram, NDAveragerProgramAveragerProgramV2, sweeps with QickSweep1D / QickSpan

The QICK repository provides both tProc v1 and tProc v2 standard firmware for the 4x2 [3]. New work should use tProc v2; spinQICK V2 is built on it [10]. In the 4x2 tProc v2 standard design, the processor is configured with 5 waveform output ports, 14 trigger outputs, 3 input ports, a program memory of \(2^{12}\) = 4096 instructions and a data memory of \(2^{14}\) words [3].

33.3Signal generators

A signal generator turns a timed command (frequency, phase, gain, envelope address, length, mode) into DAC samples. The flagship SG-v6 generator, used for both DACs in the 4x2 standard firmware, has [4, 3]:

  • a 32-bit DDS for frequency and phase, computing 16 samples per fabric clock cycle;
  • envelope memory for complex (I/Q) envelopes of up to 65 536 samples (about 6.7 µs at 9.8304 GSPS on the 4x2);
  • output styles: const (DDS × constant), arb (DDS × stored envelope), flat_top (stored rise and fall around a constant middle), plus a periodic mode for continuous tones;
  • a queue for upcoming pulses, so back-to-back pulses play seamlessly.

Other generator types appear in firmware for larger boards: sg_int4_v2 (4× interpolated, longer envelopes at lower bandwidth), sg_mux8 and sg_mixmux8 (up to 8 simultaneous fixed tones on one DAC, for multiplexed readout) [4].

33.4Readouts and buffers

A readout block takes the full-rate ADC stream, mixes it with its own DDS, filters and decimates (by 8 on the 4x2) [3]. Variants differ in who configures them: axis_readout_v2 is configured from Python before a run; axis_dyn_readout_v1 (in the 4x2 tProc v2 firmware) can be reconfigured by the tProcessor shot by shot, so readout frequency and phase can change during a sequence [4, 3].

After the readout come the buffers [4]:

  • Average buffer: on each trigger, accumulates the samples of the readout window into one I/Q value (the accumulated buffer), and can also store the decimated samples themselves (the decimated buffer).
  • Weighted buffer: applies a weighting function during accumulation (matched filtering, Chapter 23).
  • DDR4 buffer: streams decimated data into the 4 GB PL DDR4 for long records.
  • Multi-rate (MR) buffer: captures short raw records.
  • Time tagger: records the times of threshold crossings (used for photon counting).

33.5Feedback

Each readout's accumulated result can be sent to a tProcessor input port. A program can wait for it, read it into registers (I and Q), compare it with a threshold and jump. The QICK tutorials show conditional pulses and active reset built this way, after measuring the readout latency so that the program waits long enough before reading [4]. The total latency from the end of a readout window to a conditional pulse is a few hundred nanoseconds, set by the readout pipeline and the processor.

33.6The Python side

  • QickSoc (on the board) loads the firmware, configures clocks and converters, and creates drivers for every QICK block. It is also a QickConfig: a description of the firmware (channels, clocks, memory sizes) that can be sent to a remote PC.
  • Program classes such as AveragerProgramV2 describe an experiment: in _initialize() you declare channels and define pulses and readouts; in _body() you write one shot's timeline. Loops and sweeps (add_loop, QickSweep1D) run in hardware.
  • acquire() returns accumulated results (averaged, or per shot with thresholding); acquire_decimated() returns time traces [4].
  • Units are human-friendly: frequencies in MHz, times in µs, phases in degrees, gains from −1 to 1. The library converts and quantises them; get_pulse_param() returns the values actually used.
Check yourself

1. Why can a tProcessor program contain loops and arithmetic without disturbing pulse timing?

Show answer
Because commands carry timestamps and wait in FIFOs; the dispatcher releases them at their scheduled times. The processor only needs to issue each command before its time arrives.

2. What is the difference between the accumulated and decimated buffers?

Show answer
The accumulated buffer stores one integrated I/Q value per readout trigger (per shot); the decimated buffer stores the time-domain I/Q samples within the readout window, for looking at waveforms.
Summary
  • QICK = firmware (tProcessor, generators, readouts, buffers) + Python library + demos, open source.
  • The tProcessor schedules timestamped commands; tProc v2 has a 48-bit time counter, 72-bit instructions, a call stack and an RNG.
  • SG-v6 generators: 32-bit DDS, 16 samples/cycle, 65 536-sample envelopes, const/arb/flat-top pulses.
  • Readouts mix, filter, decimate; buffers accumulate, store traces, or capture long records; results can feed back to the tProcessor.
  • Python describes experiments in _initialize() and _body(), with sweeps in hardware and human units.

Part IX · QICK and spinQICK · Chapter 34

QICK on the 4x2: firmware, channels and numbers

Why you need this

This chapter is the practical bridge between the board and QICK: which firmware to use, how to install the library, what the configuration printout means line by line, which SMA connector is which channel, and the numbers that set the limits of your experiments (sample rates, frequency steps, memory sizes, buffer lengths). All values are from the QICK source and documentation as of October 2026 (software 0.2.436); check your own printout, because they change between firmware builds [3, 4].

34.1Two firmware families

tProc v1 standard firmwaretProc v2 standard firmware
Where to get itBundled with the QICK library (qick_4x2.bit, used by default when you call QickSoc() without a path)Build from firmware/projects/qick_tprocv2_4x2_standard (Vivado 2023.1), or obtain a pre-built file from the QICK team or community
Python APIAveragerProgram, RAveragerProgram, NDAveragerProgram (QICK's tprocv1 tutorials and qick_demos)AveragerProgramV2 (QICK tutorials 00–15, spinQICK V2)
Readoutsaxis_readout_v2, configured from Pythonaxis_dyn_readout_v1, reconfigurable by the tProcessor
Recommended forGetting started immediatelyNew projects, spinQICK, advanced timing

The firmware type bundled with the library was checked from its hardware description, which instantiates the tProc v1 core (axis_tproc64x32_x8) [3]. The QICK tutorials state that the tProc v2 notebooks "must be run with a tProc v2 firmware" [4]. A software emulator of the firmware (QickEmu) is under development on a separate branch of the QICK repository and lets you try the v2 tutorials without a board.

34.2Installing QICK on the board

  1. Flash the PYNQ image QICK supports (for the 4x2, PYNQ 3.0.1; PYNQ 3.1 is not supported at the time of writing) [4].
  2. Copy or clone the QICK repository onto the board (for example into /home/xilinx/jupyter_notebooks/qick).
  3. Open qick_demos/000_Install_qick_package.ipynb and run it. It installs the library with pip3 install --no-index --no-build-isolation -e ../: the options let it work without internet and stop pip from replacing the board's PYNQ library [3].
  4. Restart the kernel, then create the SoC object:
from qick import *
soc = QickSoc()          # default: bundled tProc v1 firmware for this board
# soc = QickSoc('/home/xilinx/firmware/qick_4x2_tprocv2.bit')  # your tProc v2 build
soccfg = soc
print(soccfg)

34.3Reading the configuration printout

This is the printout of the 4x2 standard firmware from QICK's demo notebook (software 0.2.381, tProc v1 firmware), abridged [3]:

QICK running on RFSoC4x2, software version 0.2.381
Firmware configuration (built Mon Dec 15 20:44:36 2025):
  Global clocks (MHz): tProc dispatcher timing 409.600, RF reference 491.520
  Groups of related clocks: [tProc clock, DAC tile 0, DAC tile 2], [ADC tile 0]
  DAC output power mode: 20mA
  2 signal generator channels:
  0: axis_signal_gen_v6 - fs=9830.400 Msps, fabric=614.400 MHz
     envelope memory: 65536 complex samples (6.667 us)
     32-bit DDS, range=9830.400 MHz
     DAC tile 0, blk 0 is DAC_B
  1: axis_signal_gen_v6 - fs=9830.400 Msps, fabric=614.400 MHz
     ...  DAC tile 2, blk 0 is DAC_A
  2 readout channels:
  0: axis_readout_v2 - configured by PYNQ
     fs=4423.680 Msps, decimated=552.960 MHz, 32-bit DDS, range=4423.680 MHz
     axis_avg_buffer v1.2 (has edge counter, no weights)
     memory 16384 accumulated, 4096 decimated (7.407 us)
     triggered by output 7, pin 14, feedback to tProc input 0
     ADC tile 0, blk 0 is ADC_D
  1: ...  ADC tile 0, blk 2 is ADC_C
  8 digital output pins: PMOD0_0 ... PMOD0_7
  tProc: axis_tproc64x32_x8 ("v1") rev 4, program memory 1024 words, data memory 1024 words
     external start pin: PMOD1_0
  DDR4 memory buffer: 1073741824 samples (1.942 sec), 256 samples/transfer
  MR buffer: 8192 samples (1.852 us), wired to readouts [0, 1]

Line by line:

  • tProc dispatcher timing 409.6 MHz: the tProcessor's time grid, 2.44 ns per tick.
  • RF reference 491.52 MHz: the reference the converter tiles multiply (×20 for the DACs, ×9 for the ADCs).
  • Groups of related clocks: the tProcessor and both DAC tiles share one clock group; the ADC tile is in another. Timing between groups has fixed but calibration-dependent offsets.
  • DAC output power mode 20 mA: the RF-DAC current setting (the other legacy option is 32 mA; Gen3 also allows finer VOP control).
  • Generators: two SG-v6 generators at 9830.4 MSPS, 16 samples per 614.4 MHz cycle; 65 536-sample envelopes (6.667 µs); 32-bit DDS spanning the full 9830.4 MHz (both Nyquist zones). Generator 0 is DAC_B, generator 1 is DAC_A.
  • Readouts: two readouts at 4423.68 MSPS, decimated to 552.96 MSPS; each has 16 384 accumulated entries and 4096 decimated samples (7.4 µs); triggered by tProc output pins 14 and 15; their results can feed tProc inputs 0 and 1 for feedback. Readout 0 is ADC_D, readout 1 is ADC_C.
  • Digital outputs: PMOD0_0–PMOD0_7, timed by the tProcessor. External start: PMOD1_0.
  • DDR4 and MR buffers: a 1.07-billion-sample capture (1.94 s) and an 8192-sample raw capture, both wired to the two readouts.

The tProc v2 firmware has a different processor and readout type and somewhat different memory sizes, but the same generator count, DACs and sample rates: its block design contains two SG-v6 generators and three dynamic readouts, with the RF data converter set to 9.8304 GSPS (DAC) and 4.42368 GSPS (ADC) [3].

34.4The connector map

Board SMAQICK channel (standard firmware)Typical use in a spin-qubit setup
DAC_Bgenerator 0Readout carrier (reflectometry)
DAC_Agenerator 1EDSR drive (direct or as IF for a mixer), or a second gate
ADC_Dreadout 0Reflected readout signal
ADC_Creadout 1Second sensor, monitor, or loopback reference
ADC_A, ADC_Bnot used by standard firmwareAvailable for custom firmware
CLK INexternal_clk=True10 MHz lab reference
PMOD0_0–7trigger outputsTrigger AWG, DC source, scope (via level shifter)

34.5The numbers that limit your experiments

QuantityValue on the 4x2 (standard firmware)Consequence
DAC rate, zone 1 limit9830.4 MSPS, 4915 MHzDirect synthesis up to ~4.9 GHz (zone 2 with nqz=2)
ADC rate, Nyquist4423.68 MSPS, 2212 MHzReadout carriers below ~2.2 GHz in zone 1
Generator frequency step2.3 Hz (common step with a readout: 20.6 Hz)Fine enough for any qubit or resonator
Phase resolution360°/232Virtual Z gates with negligible error
Gain resolutionabout 1/32 766Fine amplitude calibration
Time grid2.44 ns (409.6 MHz)Pulse start times on this grid; sample-level detail inside envelopes
Envelope memory65 536 samples = 6.67 µs per generatorLong shaped sequences need loops or constant segments
Accumulated buffer16 384 entries per readoutShots × sweep points per acquisition chunk
Decimated buffer4096 samples = 7.4 µsTrace length for debugging
DDR4 buffer~1.07 × 109 samples = 1.94 sLong continuous records (tunnelling statistics, noise)

The frequency steps are from QICK's frequency-matching documentation for the 4x2 [4]; the others from the firmware printout and documentation [3, 4].

34.6A first loopback test

Connect DAC_B → 20 dB attenuator → ADC_D. The following tProc v2 program (adapted from QICK's basic sequencing tutorial [4]) plays a 100 ns pulse at 200 MHz and records the averaged I/Q trace:

from qick import *
from qick.asm_v2 import AveragerProgramV2
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

soc = QickSoc('qick_4x2_tprocv2.bit')     # path to your tProc v2 firmware
GEN, RO = 0, 0                              # DAC_B and ADC_D on the 4x2

class Loopback(AveragerProgramV2):
    def _initialize(self, cfg):
        self.declare_gen(ch=GEN, nqz=1)
        self.declare_readout(ch=RO, length=cfg['ro_len'])
        self.add_pulse(ch=GEN, name='p', style='const', freq=cfg['f'],
                       ro_ch=RO, length=cfg['len'], phase=0, gain=0.5)
        self.add_readoutconfig(ch=RO, name='ro', freq=cfg['f'], gen_ch=GEN)
        self.send_readoutconfig(ch=RO, name='ro', t=0)
    def _body(self, cfg):
        self.pulse(ch=GEN, name='p', t=0)
        self.trigger(ros=[RO], pins=[0], t=cfg['trig'])

cfg = dict(f=200.0, len=0.1, ro_len=1.0, trig=0.0)     # MHz and µs
prog = Loopback(soc, reps=1, final_delay=1.0, cfg=cfg)
iq = prog.acquire_decimated(soc, rounds=100)
t = prog.get_time_axis(ro_index=0)
plt.plot(t, np.abs(iq[0].dot([1, 1j]))); plt.xlabel('time (µs)'); plt.show()

With the trigger at 0, the pulse appears some hundreds of nanoseconds into the trace: that offset is the time of flight through the converters and cables (Chapter 36). Move trig so that the readout window covers the pulse, then switch to acquire() for one I/Q value per shot.

Common mistake

Copying demo notebooks written for other boards without changing channel numbers. Many QICK demos assume ZCU216 or ZCU111 channel numbers (for example "generator 6"); on the 4x2 standard firmware there are only generators 0 and 1. QICK's quick-start guide warns about this for the 4x2 [4].

Check yourself

1. You want a 6.2 GHz tone from DAC_A. What do you set, and what should you check?

Show answer
Generator 1 with declare_gen(ch=1, nqz=2) and freq=6200. Check the actual output power with a spectrum analyser (it is reduced and frequency-dependent in zone 2), and check images and spurs.

2. A sweep of 101 frequency points with 1000 shots each, using accumulated readout, needs how many accumulated-buffer entries per readout if every shot is stored? What does that imply?

Show answer
101 000, more than the 16 384 entries of the standard firmware's buffer. QICK must split the acquisition into chunks (it reads the buffer as it fills), or you average in hardware and store fewer entries.
Summary
  • The QICK library bundles tProc v1 firmware for the 4x2; tProc v2 firmware must be built or obtained separately and is recommended for new work.
  • Install with the 000_Install_qick_package notebook on PYNQ 3.0.1; QICK does not support PYNQ 3.1 yet.
  • Generator 0 = DAC_B, generator 1 = DAC_A, readout 0 = ADC_D, readout 1 = ADC_C; PMOD0_0–7 triggers.
  • Key limits: 9830.4/4423.68 MSPS, 2.3 Hz frequency steps, 2.44 ns time grid, 6.7 µs envelopes, 16 384-entry accumulated buffers, 1.94 s DDR4 capture.

Part IX · QICK and spinQICK · Chapter 35

Programming QICK with tProcessor v2

Why you need this

This chapter teaches you to write QICK programs for spin-qubit experiments: how a program is structured, how pulses, readouts and triggers are placed on the timeline, how sweeps run in hardware, how data comes back, and how to branch on a measurement. The examples use the tProc v2 API (AveragerProgramV2) of QICK 0.2.436, following the official tutorials [4]. Every example is written for the 4x2's two generators and two readouts.

35.1The shape of every program

from qick.asm_v2 import AveragerProgramV2, QickSweep1D, QickSpan

class MyExperiment(AveragerProgramV2):
    def _initialize(self, cfg):
        # runs once, in Python, when the program is compiled:
        # declare channels, define envelopes and pulses, configure readouts, add loops
        ...
    def _body(self, cfg):
        # describes ONE shot's timeline; the tProcessor repeats it reps × loops times
        ...

prog = MyExperiment(soccfg, reps=1000, final_delay=10.0, cfg=cfg)
data = prog.acquire(soc, rounds=1)
  • _initialize() runs on the Python side; _body() is translated into tProcessor instructions and executed in hardware [4].
  • reps repeats the body inside the tProcessor; rounds repeats the whole program from Python (useful to interleave long acquisitions with drift checks).
  • final_delay (µs) is the idle time added at the end of each shot: for spin qubits this is where you put re-initialisation or waiting for the reservoir, unless your sequence does it explicitly.
  • Units: MHz, µs, degrees, gain in [−1, 1].

35.2Declaring channels

self.declare_gen(ch=0, nqz=1)             # DAC_B, Nyquist zone 1 (readout carrier)
self.declare_gen(ch=1, nqz=2)             # DAC_A, zone 2 (e.g. a 6 GHz EDSR tone)
self.declare_readout(ch=0, length=2.0)    # ADC_D, 2 µs readout window

35.3Envelopes and pulses

self.add_gauss(ch=1, name='g', sigma=0.01, length=0.05)   # 50 ns Gaussian envelope
self.add_pulse(ch=1, name='x90', style='arb', envelope='g',
               freq=cfg['f_q'], phase=0, gain=cfg['g_x90'])
self.add_pulse(ch=1, name='y90', style='arb', envelope='g',
               freq=cfg['f_q'], phase=90, gain=cfg['g_x90'])  # same pulse, 90° phase
self.add_pulse(ch=0, name='ro', style='const', freq=cfg['f_ro'],
               ro_ch=0, length=cfg['ro_len'], phase=0, gain=cfg['g_ro'])
self.add_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='roc', freq=cfg['f_ro'], gen_ch=0)
self.send_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='roc', t=0)

Envelope helpers include add_gauss, add_cosine, add_triangle, add_DRAG and add_envelope (your own I and Q arrays) [3]. Pulse styles are const, arb and flat_top (Chapter 33). Passing ro_ch to the readout pulse and gen_ch to the readout configuration makes their frequencies match exactly (Chapter 36).

35.4Placing events on the timeline

Inside _body(), times are relative to a reference time that you move forward as the shot proceeds:

def _body(self, cfg):
    self.pulse(ch=1, name='x90', t=0)            # at reference time
    self.delay_auto(t=cfg['tau'])                 # move the reference to the end of all
                                                  # pulses so far, plus tau
    self.pulse(ch=1, name='x90', t=0)
    self.delay_auto(t=0.05)
    self.pulse(ch=0, name='ro', t=0)              # readout carrier
    self.trigger(ros=[0], pins=[0], t=cfg['tof']) # start the readout window after the
                                                  # time of flight; also pulse PMOD0_0
  • pulse(ch, name, t) schedules a pulse at time t after the current reference.
  • trigger(ros=[...], pins=[...], t) starts readout windows and pulses PMOD trigger pins.
  • delay(t) moves the reference by t; delay_auto(t) moves it to the end of the last scheduled pulse or readout window, plus t.
  • wait(t) / wait_auto() make the processor pause until a time, needed before reading a measurement result for feedback.

QICK warns if two pulses on one generator overlap; the tips tutorial recommends delay_auto() to space them [4].

35.5Sweeps in hardware

Declare a loop and attach swept parameters to it; the tProcessor runs the loop and updates the parameters without Python [4]:

def _initialize(self, cfg):
    self.add_loop('len_loop', cfg['steps'])            # first loop declared = outermost
    self.add_pulse(ch=1, name='drive', style='const', freq=cfg['f_q'], phase=0,
                   gain=cfg['g'], length=QickSweep1D('len_loop', 0.01, 1.0))  # 10 ns → 1 µs
    ...
# after running:
lengths = prog.get_pulse_param('drive', 'length', as_array=True)   # actual, quantised values

Several loops nest in declaration order; QickSpan('loop', step_total) adds an increment per loop so a parameter can depend on several loops. Times, frequencies, phases and gains can all be swept. Always read back the actual values with get_pulse_param(), because they are quantised.

35.6Getting data back

  • acquire(soc, rounds=...) returns, for each readout, an array with one I/Q pair per sweep point, averaged over reps. With threshold= and angle= it classifies every shot first and returns the fraction above threshold; get_shots() returns per-shot results [4, 3].
  • acquire_decimated(soc, rounds=...) returns time traces; pair with get_time_axis().
  • Data shapes follow the loop order: (reps, outer loop, inner loop, …, I/Q) for raw data.

35.7Feedback: branching on a measurement

def _body(self, cfg):
    self.pulse(ch=0, name='ro', t=0)
    self.trigger(ros=[0], pins=[0], t=cfg['tof'])
    self.wait_auto(cfg['read_wait'])          # processor waits until the result is ready
    self.read_and_jump(ro_ch=0, component='I', threshold=cfg['thr'],
                       test='>=', label='SKIP')
    self.pulse(ch=1, name='x180', t=0)        # only if I < threshold: e.g. active reset
    self.label('SKIP')

The QICK feedback tutorial shows how to measure the needed read_wait by comparing the value read by the processor with the buffered value, and how to rotate the readout phase so the decision is made on one quadrature [4]. Lower-level instructions (read_input, cond_jump, registers, data memory) allow more complex logic such as counters, majority votes or adaptive sweeps.

35.8A spin-qubit example: EDSR Rabi with an external plunger AWG

The 4x2 cannot hold a plunger level (Chapter 29), so here an external DC-coupled AWG plays the plunger pulse (load → manipulate → PSB readout point), started by a PMOD trigger. The 4x2 plays the EDSR burst on generator 1 and the readout carrier on generator 0:

class EDSRRabi(AveragerProgramV2):
    def _initialize(self, cfg):
        self.declare_gen(ch=0, nqz=1)                       # readout carrier, DAC_B
        self.declare_gen(ch=1, nqz=cfg['nqz_q'])            # EDSR drive (or IF), DAC_A
        self.declare_readout(ch=0, length=cfg['ro_len'])    # ADC_D
        self.add_loop('t', cfg['steps'])
        self.add_pulse(ch=1, name='burst', style='const', freq=cfg['f_q'], phase=0,
                       gain=cfg['g_q'], length=QickSweep1D('t', cfg['t0'], cfg['t1']))
        self.add_pulse(ch=0, name='ro', style='const', freq=cfg['f_ro'], ro_ch=0,
                       length=cfg['ro_len'], phase=0, gain=cfg['g_ro'])
        self.add_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='roc', freq=cfg['f_ro'], gen_ch=0)
        self.send_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='roc', t=0)

    def _body(self, cfg):
        self.trigger(pins=[1], t=0)                 # PMOD0_1 starts the AWG plunger sequence
        self.delay(cfg['t_manip'])                  # AWG reaches the manipulation point
        self.pulse(ch=1, name='burst', t=0)         # EDSR burst of swept length
        self.delay(cfg['t_to_readout'])             # AWG moves to the PSB readout point
        self.pulse(ch=0, name='ro', t=0)
        self.trigger(ros=[0], t=cfg['tof'])

The AWG's sequence must be designed to match these delays, and the trigger latency between the 4x2 and the AWG must be measured and compensated (Chapter 30). With DC-coupled outputs (a modified board or a ZCU216), the plunger pulses would simply be a third pulse in the same program, which is what spinQICK does [10].

Common mistake

Reading data shapes wrongly. With nested loops, the outermost declared loop changes slowest. Print the shape of the returned arrays and of get_pulse_param(..., as_array=True) the first time you run any new program.

Check yourself

1. In a Ramsey experiment, how would you implement "virtual detuning" in QICK without changing the drive frequency?

Show answer
Sweep the phase of the second X/2 pulse together with the free-evolution time: phase = 360° × \(f_{\text{virt}}\) × τ. With a loop over τ, use QickSweep1D for both the delay and the second pulse's phase, so the fringes appear at \(f_{\text{virt}}\).

2. Why do you need wait_auto() before read_and_jump() but not before a normal pulse?

Show answer
Normal commands are timestamped and queued; the processor can issue them long before they play. A branch depends on a measurement result that only exists after the readout window ends and the result propagates, so the processor itself must wait until then.
Summary
  • Programs define pulses and readouts in _initialize() and one shot's timeline in _body(); reps and loops run in hardware.
  • Place events with pulse, trigger, delay, delay_auto; wait with wait/wait_auto before reading results.
  • Sweep any parameter with add_loop + QickSweep1D/QickSpan; read back actual values.
  • acquire() for I/Q per point (optionally thresholded), acquire_decimated() for traces.
  • Feedback with read_and_jump; external AWGs are triggered with PMOD pins when baseband pulses are needed.
PreviousChapter 34 · QICK on the 4x2: firmware, channels and numbersNextChapter 36 · Calibrations: loopback, time of flight, frequency and phase

Part IX · QICK and spinQICK · Chapter 36

Calibrations: loopback, time of flight, frequency and phase

Why you need this

Before the qubit can tell you anything, the controller must be calibrated: when does a pulse actually arrive at the ADC, what power comes out of each DAC at each frequency, how do generator and readout phases relate, how large is a pulse at the device, how late is an external instrument. Uncalibrated offsets look like physics (a shifted resonance, a "decay" of contrast, a wrong Rabi frequency). This chapter lists the calibrations an RFSoC-based spin-qubit setup needs, how to do each, and how often.

36.11. Loopback and output power

What: the power each DAC delivers versus frequency and gain, and what each ADC reports for a known input.

How: DAC → spectrum analyser (or power meter) for output power; DAC → known attenuator → ADC for the loopback response. Sweep frequency across your bands, in the Nyquist zones you will use. Record DAC output in dBm versus QICK gain at your working frequencies.

Why: every power budget (Chapter 18) starts from these numbers. Zone-2 power in particular varies strongly with frequency (Chapter 19).

When: once, then after firmware or hardware changes.

36.22. Time of flight

What: the delay between a generator pulse starting and its arrival in the readout data, through converters, FPGA pipelines and cables.

How: play a short pulse and record a decimated trace with the readout triggered at t = 0 (as in Chapter 34's loopback). The pulse appears after a delay: that is the time of flight. Repeat with the real fridge cabling, since metres of cable add 5 ns per metre. Then set your readout trigger time to this delay plus the resonator ring-up time.

When: once per wiring configuration. QICK's documentation includes a dedicated page on timing and the tutorials show how pulse and trigger times relate [4].

36.33. Frequency matching

What: ensuring the readout's demodulation frequency equals the generator's carrier frequency exactly. Generators and readouts run on different clocks, so their frequency grids differ; a mismatch of a few Hz rotates the demodulated phase slowly, making each run's I/Q land at a different angle [4].

How: pass ro_ch to add_pulse() and gen_ch to add_readoutconfig(), or round the frequency first with soccfg.adcfreq(f, gen_ch=..., ro_ch=...). On the 4x2, the generator's own step is 2.3 Hz and the common step 20.6 Hz; without matching, a 100 MHz readout would be off by about 9 Hz, rotating the phase once every 0.1 s [4].

When: always, in every program. It costs nothing.

36.44. Phase offset between generator and readout

What: even with matched frequencies, the demodulated signal has a fixed phase offset that depends on the frequency (through the time of flight: phase = 360° × f × delay) and on the state of the clock dividers after power-up. QICK's older demo describes this as a constant phase difference "randomly determined each time the board clocks are initialized" [3].

How: measure the loopback (or the reflected signal off-resonance) phase versus frequency; the slope gives the electrical delay, the intercept the offset. Subtract it, or simply rotate the IQ plane as part of readout calibration (Chapter 23).

When: after each power cycle if you rely on absolute phase. For charge-state readout, rotating the IQ plane on your measured data (two charge states) does the job automatically.

36.55. Readout working point

What: carrier frequency, power, integration window and IQ rotation that maximise SNR for your sensor.

How: sweep carrier frequency across the tank resonance with the sensor on and off a Coulomb peak; choose the frequency of maximum difference. Sweep power to find where the signal stops growing without heating (Coulomb peaks broaden). Record single-shot data for the two charge states and choose the window length and threshold (Chapter 23).

When: after tuning the sensor; re-check daily, since sensor drift changes the optimum.

36.66. Amplitude at the device

What: the actual voltage a gate sees for a given QICK gain (or AWG amplitude), after attenuation, reflections and frequency-dependent losses.

How, for baseband pulses: apply a square pulse of known nominal amplitude to a plunger and observe how far a charge transition shifts in a CSD measured during the pulse; with the lever arm this gives the real amplitude. For microwaves: photon-assisted tunnelling side-peaks spaced by \(hf/(e\alpha)\) give the amplitude at frequency \(f\) through their strength (Bessel-function dependence), and the measured Rabi frequency versus gain gives the drive's linear range.

When: once per cooldown and per frequency band.

36.77. Channel skew and external trigger latency

What: relative delays between DAC_A and DAC_B outputs (different tiles and paths), and between a QICK PMOD trigger and an external AWG's output.

How: send simultaneous edges on all channels into a fast oscilloscope with matched cables; measure offsets. For the external AWG, trigger it from a PMOD pin and measure the delay from the PMOD edge (or from a reference QICK pulse) to the AWG output. Compensate in the QICK program (shift times) or in the AWG sequence.

When: once per configuration; re-check if you change instruments or cables. Lock everything to the same 10 MHz reference to keep jitter low (Chapter 30).

36.88. IQ mixer calibration (if you upconvert)

What: LO leakage and the unwanted sideband from an external IQ mixer.

How: with a spectrum analyser at the mixer output, adjust small DC offsets on I and Q to minimise LO leakage, then adjust the relative amplitude and phase of I and Q to minimise the image. With a double-sideband mixer and a filter, check the filter's suppression instead.

When: after any change of LO frequency, IF or power; re-check weekly, since offsets drift with temperature.

36.99. Pulse distortion

What: the impulse response of the baseband chain (amplifiers, filters, bias tees, cables), needed for pre-distortion (Chapter 21).

How: measure the step response of the room-temperature chain with a sampling oscilloscope, as HRL did for their spinQICK setup [11]; fit a small number of filter terms; verify on the qubit (for example with exchange-pulse sequences whose result depends on pulse shape).

When: once per hardware configuration.

CalibrationHow oftenTypical time
Loopback / output poweronce; after changes1 hour
Time of flightper wiring setup10 minutes
Frequency matchingevery program (automatic)0
Phase offset / IQ rotationeach boot or each readout calibrationminutes
Readout working pointafter sensor tuning; daily check15–60 minutes
Amplitude at deviceper cooldown and bandhours
Channel skew, trigger latencyper configuration30 minutes
IQ mixerper LO/IF change; weekly15 minutes
Pulse distortionper hardware configurationhours
In the lab

Keep calibrations as code and data, not as notes: a Python file or configuration object with every number (time of flight, phase offsets, gains per dBm, trigger latencies), version-controlled and saved with every dataset. spinQICK uses typed configuration models for this purpose [10]. Six months later, when a result looks strange, you will want to know exactly what the calibration was.

Check yourself

1. Your demodulated phase changes by 36° when you move the readout from 200 MHz to 210 MHz. What electrical delay does that imply?

Show answer
Phase slope = 360° × Δf × τ, so τ = 36°/(360° × 10 MHz) = 10 ns (modulo full turns: the true delay could be 10 ns + n × 100 ns; measure at finer frequency steps to resolve the ambiguity).

2. Why does an unmatched generator/readout frequency pair cause problems only between runs, not within one run?

Show answer
A few-Hz mismatch rotates the phase by only a tiny amount during a µs readout, so within a shot it is invisible, but over seconds between runs it accumulates to large angles, so different runs' I/Q values appear rotated relative to each other.
Summary
  • Calibrate output power, time of flight, frequency matching, phase offsets, readout working point, device amplitudes, channel skew and trigger latency, IQ mixers and pulse distortion.
  • Frequency matching is a one-line habit; phase offsets change at power-up; device amplitudes need the qubit device itself.
  • Store calibrations as versioned data next to your measurements.
