Part IX · QICK and spinQICK · Chapter 37

spinQICK, remote control and lab software

Why you need this

QICK was developed mainly by and for superconducting-qubit groups. HRL Laboratories' spinQICK adds what gate-defined spin qubits need: charge-stability scans, Pauli-blockade readout set-up, single-spin and exchange-only control, exchange calibration, crosstalk compensation, and a configuration system for many gates. Even if your hardware differs from HRL's, its code is the best public reference for how spin-qubit experiments map onto QICK. This chapter describes spinQICK, how a QICK board is run remotely from a lab PC, and how it fits with other lab software [10, 11].

37.1What spinQICK is

spinQICK (version 3.0.0 at the time of writing) is "an open-source extension to QICK designed to control electrostatically confined solid-state spin-qubits", built on QICK's tProc v2 API and some custom low-level QICK assembly [10]. Its experiments cover:

AreaExamples of spinQICK experiments (function names in the code)
Electrostatic tune-upgate_turn_on, gate_action, gate-vs-gate scans with DC sources (gvg_dc), with baseband pulses (gvg_baseband) and photon-assisted tunnelling (gvg_pat), cross-capacitance extraction (get_cross_caps)
Charge sensordcs_stability, retune_dcs, readout noise measurements
PSB readoutpsb_config, measurement-window and idle-cell scans, meashist (single-shot histograms), flush_window_scan
Single-spin (LD) controltime_rabi, amplitude_rabi, rabi_chevron, ramsey_experiment, spin_echo, allxy
Exchange-only controlexchange calibrations (course_cal, fine_cal), fingerprint scans (do_fingerprint), exchange voltage calculations
System calibrationcalibrate_baseband_voltage, measure_bandwidth, ADC trigger offset sweeps
Two-qubit (LD)programs in ld_2_qubit

Its demo notebooks walk through configuration, DC voltage source set-up, charge stability, crosstalk compensation, PSB, coherent LD control and coherent EO control [10].

Structure

  • core: pulse construction for LD and EO qubits, readout utilities, the dot_experiment base class, data handling.
  • experiments: the user-facing experiments listed above.
  • qick_code_v2: the QICK programs (tProc v2) underneath each experiment.
  • models: Pydantic models for hardware and experiment configuration, giving type-checked parameters for every gate and qubit.
  • helper_functions, backends: file management, hardware maps, plotting, analysis, and data back-ends including netCDF4 and QCoDeS.

Hardware it expects

spinQICK targets the ZCU216 (16 DAC outputs), with TI LMH5401 DC-coupled differential amplifiers on the DACs, an LMH6401 variable-gain amplifier for the ADC, optional THS3491 amplifiers, a PMOD level shifter for triggers, and a precision DC source such as a QDevil QDAC or Basel LNHR. Alternatively, Real Digital's QICK Box with "DC Out" and "DC In" modules provides the DC-coupled front end [10]. Its recommended firmware is a ZCU216 tProc v2 build with 16 full-speed outputs and 11-channel crosstalk compensation, which needs HRL's fork of QICK and the XtalkSoc class [10].

On the 4x2

spinQICK is not written for the 4x2, and most of its experiments assume DC-coupled baseband outputs on many gates. What you can reuse on a 4x2:

  • its structure and configuration models, as a template for your own code;
  • its readout and analysis code (histograms, thresholds, noise measurements), which only need a readout channel;
  • its QICK programs as worked examples of PSB, Rabi, Ramsey, echo and AllXY sequences, adapted to two generators plus an external AWG for plunger pulses;
  • everything, if you move to a ZCU216 or a QICK Box later.

37.2Running QICK remotely with Pyro4

In most labs the analysis, plotting and instrument control run on a lab PC, not on the board. QICK supports this with Pyro4 (Python Remote Objects): a name server runs on the PC (or the board), a QICK server runs on the board and publishes the QickSoc, and clients on the PC obtain a proxy object and a copy of the board's configuration [4]:

# on the PC: start a name server
#   python -m Pyro4.naming -n 0.0.0.0 -p 8888
# on the board (in a notebook or service):
from qick.pyro import start_server
start_server(ns_host='<pc-ip>', ns_port=8888, proxy_name='rfsoc4x2')
# on the PC (client):
from qick.pyro import make_proxy
soc, soccfg = make_proxy(ns_host='<pc-ip>', ns_port=8888, proxy_name='rfsoc4x2')
prog = MyExperiment(soccfg, reps=1000, final_delay=10, cfg=cfg)   # compiled on the PC
data = prog.acquire(soc)                                         # run on the board

Programs are compiled on the PC using the configuration copy and executed on the board. The QICK team distinguishes Pyro4 (software, over Ethernet, flexible) from XCOM (hardware, low-latency links between boards) [4]. spinQICK's documentation shows the same pattern with XtalkSoc for its crosstalk firmware [10].

37.3Fitting into lab software

  • QCoDeS (Python measurement framework from Copenhagen/Microsoft) is widely used in spin-qubit labs for instrument drivers and data storage; spinQICK includes a QCoDeS data back-end [10]. A QICK board can be wrapped as a QCoDeS instrument or used alongside one that controls your DC sources and magnet.
  • Qibolab / Qibosoq: an open-source stack that drives QICK boards as part of a hybrid quantum operating system, with calibration routines in Qibocal [4].
  • Your own scripts: many groups write thin Python classes that combine a DC-source driver, the QICK proxy and a data-saving layer. Start simple, and save the full configuration (including calibrations) with every dataset.
Common mistake

Mixing library versions between the PC client and the board server. Pyro sends compiled programs and configuration objects between the two; different QICK versions can produce subtle errors. Pin the same QICK version on both, as spinQICK does by pinning qick[full]==0.2.436 [10].

Check yourself

1. Which spinQICK capabilities depend on DC-coupled baseband outputs and therefore would not work on a stock 4x2?

Show answer
Anything that pulses gates to charge-state points: baseband gate-vs-gate scans, PSB readout pulses (measurement and idle windows), exchange pulses and EO control, LD sequences that move between load/manipulate/readout points, and crosstalk-compensated virtual pulses.

2. In a Pyro4 setup, where is a program compiled and where does it run?

Show answer
Compiled on the PC using a copy of the board's configuration (soccfg); executed on the board by the QICK server through the proxy soc.
Summary
  • spinQICK (HRL) extends QICK with spin-qubit tune-up, PSB readout, LD and EO control, exchange calibration, crosstalk compensation and typed configuration.
  • It targets a ZCU216 (or QICK Box) with DC-coupled amplifiers; on a 4x2 its readout, analysis and program structure are reusable references.
  • Pyro4 runs QICK remotely: name server, board server, PC client; pin library versions.
  • QICK integrates with QCoDeS, Qibolab/Qibosoq and custom lab code.
PreviousChapter 36 · Calibrations: loopback, time of flight, frequency and phaseNextChapter 38 · Planning a spin-qubit setup around a 4x2

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 38

Planning a spin-qubit setup around a 4x2

Why you need this

Every experiment in this part needs a concrete hardware plan: which signal comes from which instrument, through which components, at what power, triggered by what. Because the 4x2 has two AC-coupled outputs, the plan decides what you can do. This chapter gives three architectures, from "use the board as it is" to "move to a larger board", with wiring, frequency plans, power budgets and parts lists, so you can choose consciously and know what each choice costs.

38.1The constraints, restated

  • 2 DAC outputs (DAC_A, DAC_B), 4 ADC inputs (QICK standard firmware reads ADC_C and ADC_D), all AC-coupled via 10 MHz–10 GHz baluns [2].
  • Direct synthesis to ~4.9 GHz (zone 1), with reduced power to ~9.8 GHz (zone 2); ADC zone 1 to ~2.2 GHz [3].
  • 8 timed trigger outputs (1.8 V), external 10 MHz reference input.
  • A Si/SiGe micromagnet device: many DC gates, PSB or Elzerman readout, EDSR at roughly 10–20 GHz at typical fields (Chapter 12).

38.2Architecture A: the 4x2 as readout, microwave and timing engine (no modification)

What it can do

Everything in Chapters 39–42: reflectometry readout, fast charge-stability maps (with the AWG or DC source sweeping and the 4x2 recording), PSB and Elzerman readout (AWG pulses, 4x2 measuring), EDSR spectroscopy, Rabi, Ramsey, echo, AllXY and randomised benchmarking, plus real-time frequency tracking. Two-qubit gates are possible if the AWG has enough channels for plungers and barrier.

What it costs

  • A DC-coupled AWG with 2–4 channels and trigger input (or an integrated controller's baseband channels).
  • A microwave LO and mixer components for EDSR above ~9.8 GHz.
  • Calibration of trigger latency and jitter between the 4x2 and the AWG (Chapter 36).

An example frequency plan

SignalChoiceReason
Readout carrier (DAC_B, ADC_D)≈ 200–400 MHz (set by the tank)Zone 1 of both converters; far from \(f_s/8\) = 553 MHz and \(f_s/4\) = 1106 MHz of the ADC
EDSR IF (DAC_A)1.5 GHzImages of a DSB mixer 3 GHz apart, easy to filter; check that 1.5 GHz and its harmonics do not alias near the readout carrier in the ADC (1.5 GHz is in ADC zone 1, so keep the IF out of the readout input with a low-pass filter)
LOqubit frequency − 1.5 GHz (e.g. 11.5 GHz for a 13 GHz qubit)Upper sideband used; filter the lower

An example power budget for the readout

DAC_B at about −10 dBm; −20 dB at room temperature, −20 dB at 4 K, −10 dB at the still, −20 dB at the mixing chamber and a −20 dB coupler gives −100 dBm at the tank. The reflected signal (−100 dBm or a bit less) passes the coupler's through path, a HEMT (+35 dB), a room-temperature amplifier (+30 dB), and arrives at ADC_D around −35 dBm (Chapter 18). Add a low-pass filter before ADC_D to stop the EDSR IF and other signals from aliasing.

38.3Architecture B: a modified 4x2 for baseband (advanced)

Make one or both DAC outputs DC-coupled (remove the output balun and capacitors and provide correct termination and a DC-coupled differential amplifier, Chapter 29). Then QICK plays plunger pulses directly. Since both DACs are then gate channels, the readout carrier must come from elsewhere: an external RF source locked to the same 10 MHz, with the 4x2's readout block demodulating it. The demodulated phase is then stable but has an arbitrary offset, which the IQ rotation removes. This architecture can run a singlet–triplet qubit (two fast gates plus readout) on a single 4x2. It carries real risk to the board, and none of the sources used for this book documents such a modification of the 4x2's DAC outputs.

38.4Architecture C: grow into a ZCU216 or QICK Box

The ZCU216 has 16 DACs and 16 ADCs on connectors that can be AC- or DC-coupled, and it is the platform of spinQICK and the published RFSoC spin-qubit work [4, 10, 11]. The QICK Box adds a modular front end with RF, balun and DC-coupled modules [44]. In this architecture the 4x2 remains valuable as a development, teaching and test board (same FPGA fabric and the same QICK software model [4]), or as a dedicated readout and microwave unit.

38.5Choosing

GoalArchitecture
Learn QICK/RFSoC, fast readout, CSD mapping, EDSR single-qubit workA
Singlet–triplet qubit on one board, willing to rework hardwareB
Exchange-only or multi-qubit devices, many baseband gatesC
In the lab

Parts list for Architecture A beyond the 4x2: SMA attenuators (3, 10, 20 dB), DC blocks, SMA low-pass and band-pass filters for the readout and IF bands, a room-temperature low-noise amplifier for the readout, a directional coupler and HEMT in the fridge (often already present), a microwave LO, a mixer and filter for EDSR, a PMOD level shifter and BNC adapters for triggers, a 10 MHz distribution amplifier, and short, good-quality SMA cables. Budget time to characterise each component.

Check yourself

1. In Architecture A, why must the EDSR IF be kept out of ADC_D?

Show answer
Any IF leakage into the readout input is digitised; at 1.5 GHz it lies in the ADC's first zone, and its harmonics alias across the band. It can add spurs near the readout carrier or saturate the input. A low-pass filter on ADC_D (cut-off above the readout carrier, below the IF) prevents this.

2. Why does Architecture B need an external readout source?

Show answer
Both DACs are used for DC-coupled gate pulses, leaving no DAC for the readout carrier. The ADC side can still demodulate an external carrier if it is locked to the same reference.
Summary
  • A: unmodified 4x2 for readout, EDSR (direct or via mixer) and timing, with a DC-coupled AWG and DC source triggered by PMOD; the recommended start.
  • B: DC-coupled DAC modification for baseband pulses; readout carrier from an external source; risky.
  • C: ZCU216/QICK Box with spinQICK for EO and multi-qubit work; 4x2 as test or readout unit.
  • Write a frequency plan and a power budget, filter the ADC input, and lock everything to one 10 MHz reference.
PreviousChapter 37 · spinQICK, remote control and lab softwareNextChapter 39 · Experiment: RF reflectometry readout

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 39

Experiment: RF reflectometry readout

Why you need this

This is the first real experiment to run with the 4x2, and the one it does best: fast charge sensing by RF reflectometry. Once it works, every later experiment (charge maps, spin readout, qubit control) is a matter of adding pulses before the readout. This chapter is a step-by-step procedure, from a bench test to single-electron tunnelling events, with QICK code, expected results and what goes wrong. The physics is in Chapter 9 and the signal processing in Chapter 23.

39.1Step 0: practise on the bench

Before using the fridge, build a dummy tank: a chip inductor (for example 820 nH) in series with a small capacitor and a resistor or potentiometer to ground on a small PCB, at room temperature. Its resonance and matching behave like the real thing (with lower Q), and you can change "the sensor resistance" with a screwdriver. Connect DAC_B → 20 dB → directional coupler → dummy tank; coupler output → amplifier → ADC_D. Every step below can be rehearsed this way.

39.2Step 1: find the resonance

Sweep the carrier frequency and record the reflected amplitude and phase. The simplest QICK approach is a Python loop over a short program (adapted from QICK's basic tutorial [4]):

import numpy as np
from qick.asm_v2 import AveragerProgramV2

class ReflPoint(AveragerProgramV2):
    def _initialize(self, cfg):
        self.declare_gen(ch=0, nqz=1)                           # DAC_B
        self.declare_readout(ch=0, length=cfg['ro_len'])        # ADC_D
        self.add_pulse(ch=0, name='c', style='const', freq=cfg['f'], ro_ch=0,
                       length=cfg['ro_len'] + cfg['tof'] + 0.2, phase=0, gain=cfg['g'])
        self.add_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='r', freq=cfg['f'], gen_ch=0)
        self.send_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='r', t=0)
    def _body(self, cfg):
        self.pulse(ch=0, name='c', t=0)
        self.trigger(ros=[0], t=cfg['tof'] + 0.1)              # after time of flight + settling

freqs = np.linspace(150, 350, 401)                              # MHz
S = []
for f in freqs:
    cfg = dict(f=f, g=0.3, ro_len=2.0, tof=0.6)
    iq = ReflPoint(soccfg, reps=200, final_delay=1.0, cfg=cfg).acquire(soc)
    S.append(iq[0][0] + 1j * iq[0][1])                         # averaged I + iQ
S = np.array(S)

Plot \(|S|\) and the unwrapped phase of \(S\) versus frequency. The phase has a linear slope from the cable delay (Chapter 36); subtract it. The resonance appears as a dip in \(|S|\) and a step in phase, as in Figure 9.3. The data structure of acquire()'s return value depends on your QICK version; print it the first time.

In the lab

Typical cold resonances are 100–800 MHz with loaded quality factors of 10–100. If the dip is shallow, the tank is far from matched for the present sensor resistance (Chapter 9). Note the resonance frequency at several sensor settings: the frequency shift with gate voltage tells you how much capacitance the device adds, and some groups use varactor diodes on the PCB to tune the match in situ [29].

39.3Step 2: see the sensor through the resonator

Fix the carrier at the frequency with the largest response, then sweep the sensor's plunger with your DC source and record I/Q at each point. You should see the sensor's Coulomb peaks as peaks or dips in \(|S|\) or as phase changes. Compare with a DC transport measurement of the same sweep: the two must line up, as in the Tohoku group's RFSoC demonstration [31].

To sweep the DC gate fast, let the 4x2 trigger the DC source: each shot, a PMOD pulse advances the DC source one step in a pre-loaded list, and QICK records one point. This "triggered list" mode exists in several multi-channel DC sources.

39.4Step 3: choose the power

Sweep the carrier gain while measuring one Coulomb peak. The signal grows with power until the RF voltage across the sensor becomes comparable to the Coulomb peak width (a few times \(k_BT_e/e\)), after which the peak broadens and the sensitivity drops. Pick the power just below broadening. Record the resulting power at the device from your budget.

39.5Step 4: measure SNR and \(t_{\min}\)

Park the sensor on the steepest flank and prepare two charge states of a nearby qubit dot (for example by stepping its plunger across a transition with the DC source or AWG). For each state record a few thousand single-shot I/Q values (acquire() with per-shot data, or get_shots()), for several integration lengths. Rotate the IQ plane, compute the separation over the standard deviation (SNR) versus integration time \(t\), and fit SNR \(= \sqrt{t/t_{\min}}\) (Chapter 9). Report \(t_{\min}\): it is the figure of merit of your readout chain.

Worked example

You measure SNR = 2.0 at 0.5 µs and 4.0 at 2 µs. Then \(t_{\min} = t/\text{SNR}^2 = 0.5/4 = 0.125\ \mu\)s (and 2/16 = 0.125 µs: consistent with white noise). SNR 6 then needs \(36\times0.125 = 4.5\ \mu\)s.

39.6Step 5: watch single electrons tunnel

Tune a qubit dot to a charge transition with a reservoir, so that an electron tunnels in and out randomly. Record a long, continuous demodulated trace: on the 4x2 the DDR4 buffer can capture about 1.94 s of decimated data [3], which you can filter and downsample afterwards. The trace shows a random telegraph signal between two levels. The histograms of the dwell times in each level are exponential; their means are the tunnel-in and tunnel-out times. Changing the plunger shifts the ratio (the Fermi function, Chapter 7), and changing the barrier changes the rates exponentially. This measurement calibrates tunnel rates for Elzerman readout and loading (Chapter 41).

39.7What goes wrong

SymptomLikely causes
No resonance anywhereWrong frequency range (parasitics differ from design); broken bond or inductor; a line not connected; HEMT not biased
Resonance present but no response to the sensorSensor not conducting; match far from the sensor's resistance; carrier power too high (peaks washed out)
Phase of the data rotates between runsFrequency matching not used; external source not locked
Sharp lines in the spectrum, or "noise" at fixed frequenciesSpurs or aliases (Chapter 22); EDSR IF leaking into the ADC; ground loops
Very noisy, broad spectrumHEMT or room-temperature amplifier oscillating; missing attenuation; too little integration
Signal saturates or clipsToo much gain after the HEMT; check ADC input level against full scale
On the 4x2

Reflectometry uses exactly one DAC and one ADC, leaving DAC_A free for EDSR or for a second sensor's carrier (frequency multiplexing two tanks with two tones requires the tones on one line, which would need a multiplexed generator or a combiner of DAC_A and DAC_B outputs). ADC_C can read a second sensor or monitor the incident carrier for reference.

Check yourself

1. Your resonance dip is only 1 dB deep. What does that tell you and what can you change?

Show answer
The tank is far from matched for the current sensor resistance (or the sensor is not in the circuit). Change the sensor's working point (lower its resistance), change the inductor, or tune the match with a varactor; also check that you measure at the right frequency and that the sensor is connected.

2. Why record tunnelling events with the DDR4 buffer rather than with many short readouts?

Show answer
Tunnelling is random and continuous; a long unbroken record lets you measure dwell-time distributions without dead time between shots. The DDR4 buffer stores about 1.94 s continuously at the decimated rate.
Summary
  • Rehearse with a room-temperature dummy tank; then find the cold resonance by sweeping the carrier.
  • Confirm sensor response with gate sweeps (DC source triggered by PMOD), choose power below broadening.
  • Measure SNR versus integration time to get \(t_{\min}\), the figure of merit of the readout.
  • Use the DDR4 buffer for long tunnelling records to calibrate tunnel rates.
PreviousChapter 38 · Planning a spin-qubit setup around a 4x2NextChapter 40 · Experiment: fast charge-stability maps and pulsed-gate spectroscopy

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 40

Experiment: fast charge-stability maps and pulsed-gate spectroscopy

Why you need this

Charge stability diagrams are the map you navigate by (Chapter 8), and you will take thousands of them. With DC readout each takes minutes; with RF readout and fast scanning, a map can refresh several times per second, so you can tune gates while watching ("video mode"). Pulsed-gate spectroscopy then adds time resolution: it measures tunnel rates and excited-state energies by pulsing a gate during the scan. This chapter shows how to build both with the 4x2 as the measuring and timing engine, and an AWG or a triggered DC source doing the sweeping.

40.1Three ways to scan

MethodWho sweepsSpeedNotes
Point by pointDC source steps both gates; 4x2 measures one point per stepms per point (DC-source settling)Simplest; slow but reliable
Triggered rasterDC source runs a pre-loaded list, advanced by 4x2 PMOD triggers; 4x2 measures between triggers~10–100 µs per pointLimited by DC source update rate and line filtering
Video modeAWG sweeps the fast axis (sawtooth) through a bias tee; DC source or AWG steps the slow axis; 4x2 records continuously, synchronised by triggerµs per point, full maps in 10–100 msNeeds fast lines and bias tees; most powerful

40.2Video mode in detail

Design rules:

  • Ramp rate versus bandwidth: each pixel needs a dwell time longer than the readout's response time (tank ring-down plus filtering). For a 100-pixel row with 2 µs per pixel, the ramp lasts 200 µs (5 kHz). A 100-row map then takes 20 ms.
  • AC coupling of the fast axis: a sawtooth at 5 kHz passes a PCB bias tee (with a sub-Hz corner) almost undistorted but does not pass the 4x2's 10 MHz baluns. So the fast axis comes from a DC-coupled AWG, not from the 4x2's DACs.
  • Hysteresis and latency: charge transitions lag the gate slightly (tunnel times), and the readout chain delays the signal. Sweep in both directions or calibrate the pixel offset.
  • Recording: either one QICK readout per pixel (accumulated mode, one trigger per pixel, clean timing), or one long decimated record per row into the DDR4 buffer, binned in software.
Worked example: how fast can a map be?

With \(t_{\min} = 0.125\ \mu\)s (Chapter 39), a pixel SNR of 3 needs \(9\times0.125 \approx 1.1\ \mu\)s. A 128 × 128 map has 16 384 pixels: about 18 ms of integration. Overheads (ramp flyback, settling) may double it: about 25 maps per second. The same map with DC current readout at 10 ms per point would take 2.7 minutes.

40.3Turning maps into virtual gates

Fast maps make it practical to calibrate the virtual-gate matrix automatically: detect transition lines in the image (edge detection or a Hough transform), fit their slopes, build the lever-arm matrix (Chapter 8), and rescan in virtual coordinates to check that dot-1 lines are vertical and dot-2 lines horizontal. Machine-learning classifiers that identify charge states and transitions from such images are reviewed by Zwolak and Taylor [27]. spinQICK includes cross-capacitance extraction and gate-vs-gate scan routines [10].

40.4Pulsed-gate spectroscopy

Add a square-wave pulse of amplitude \(V_p\) to a plunger during a 1D or 2D scan. When the pulse frequency is low compared with the tunnel rate, a charge transition appears twice, split by \(V_p\) (the dot sees two gate voltages alternately). As the pulse frequency approaches the tunnel rate, the split lines fade, because the electron cannot follow: the fading frequency measures the tunnel rate. Excited orbital or valley states appear as extra lines between the split copies, because during the high half of the pulse an electron can tunnel into an excited state if it is below the reservoir's Fermi level; their position gives the excitation energy [18]. This is how valley splittings of individual dots are often first estimated.

On the 4x2

Square pulses at kHz–MHz on a plunger need a DC-coupled source (AWG), because the 4x2's outputs only pass edges. A useful variant that the 4x2 can do itself is photon-assisted tunnelling: a microwave tone (hundreds of MHz to GHz) from DAC_A, through a bias tee onto a plunger, creates side-peaks of charge transitions spaced by \(hf/(e\alpha)\). Measuring the spacing versus frequency calibrates the lever arm, and the side-peak strength calibrates the microwave amplitude at the gate (Chapter 36). spinQICK has a dedicated routine (gvg_pat) for this [10].

Check yourself

1. Your video-mode map shows transitions shifted between left-to-right and right-to-left sweeps. Why?

Show answer
Finite tunnel rates and the readout chain's response time make the measured transition lag the gate voltage. The lag reverses with sweep direction. Sweep slower, average both directions, or calibrate and correct the pixel offset.

2. In pulsed-gate spectroscopy, the split transition lines fade when the pulse period drops below 20 µs. What is the tunnel rate, roughly?

Show answer
Each half-period is 10 µs; the electron can no longer follow when the tunnel time is comparable, so \(\Gamma \sim 1/(10\ \mu\text{s}) = 100\) kHz (to within a factor of order one; fit the fading curve for a precise value).
Summary
  • Scan point by point, by triggered raster, or in video mode; the 4x2 measures and triggers, an AWG or DC source sweeps.
  • Video mode with RF readout gives full maps in tens of milliseconds; design pixel dwell time from \(t_{\min}\).
  • Fast maps enable automated virtual-gate calibration and machine-learning tuning.
  • Pulsed-gate spectroscopy measures tunnel rates and excited states; photon-assisted tunnelling (doable from the 4x2) calibrates lever arms and microwave amplitudes.
PreviousChapter 39 · Experiment: RF reflectometry readoutNextChapter 41 · Experiment: spin readout, single shots and T1

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 41

Experiment: spin readout, single shots and T1

Why you need this

Single-shot spin readout is the milestone that turns a charge device into a spin device: from here on, every experiment ends with "measure the spin". This chapter sets up energy-selective (Elzerman) and Pauli-blockade (PSB) readout with the 4x2 measuring the sensor and a DC-coupled AWG pulsing the plungers (Architecture A), then measures readout fidelity and the spin relaxation time \(T_1\). The physics is in Chapter 11.

41.1Common building block: several readout windows per shot

Spin readout signals evolve during the read phase (a blip in Elzerman readout, relaxation in PSB). Recording the sensor in several consecutive windows per shot gives you a coarse trace of every shot with the efficient accumulated readout. In QICK tProc v2, every trigger() of a readout inside _body() is counted, and the returned data has one entry per trigger per shot [3]:

class SpinReadout(AveragerProgramV2):
    def _initialize(self, cfg):
        self.declare_gen(ch=0, nqz=1)
        self.declare_readout(ch=0, length=cfg['win'])               # one window, e.g. 2 µs
        total = cfg['n_win'] * cfg['win'] + cfg['tof'] + 0.2
        self.add_pulse(ch=0, name='c', style='const', freq=cfg['f_ro'], ro_ch=0,
                       length=total, phase=0, gain=cfg['g_ro'])
        self.add_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='r', freq=cfg['f_ro'], gen_ch=0)
        self.send_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='r', t=0)
    def _body(self, cfg):
        self.trigger(pins=[1], t=0)                    # AWG: start the plunger sequence
        self.delay(cfg['t_read'])                      # AWG has reached the read level
        self.pulse(ch=0, name='c', t=0)                # one long readout carrier
        for k in range(cfg['n_win']):                  # unrolled at compile time
            self.trigger(ros=[0], t=cfg['tof'] + k * cfg['win'])

With 20 windows of 2 µs you get a 40 µs coarse trace per shot. Keep the number of unrolled triggers moderate (the tProc v2 program memory holds about 4096 instructions [4]). For long Elzerman reads (hundreds of µs to ms), use fewer, longer windows, or record whole traces with the DDR4 buffer.

41.2Elzerman readout

Set-up

  1. Tunnel rates: from a telegraph-signal measurement (Chapter 39), set the dot–reservoir barrier so the tunnel time is 10–100 µs: slow enough for the sensor to resolve, fast compared with \(T_1\).
  2. Field: choose \(E_Z\) well above \(k_BT_e\) (Chapter 11), for example 0.4–0.6 T in silicon.
  3. Pulse: AWG plays empty → load → read → empty on the plunger (Figure 11.2), with the read level positioned so the Fermi level sits between \(E_\downarrow\) and \(E_\uparrow\).
  4. Find the read level: sweep the read-level voltage; the probability of a blip during the read window rises from zero (both levels below \(E_F\)), peaks where only spin-up can leave, and rises again to one when both levels are above \(E_F\) (any electron leaves). The plateau or peak between is the spin-selective window.

Analysis

For each shot, low-pass filter the window sequence and check whether the signal crosses a blip threshold in the read phase. The fraction of shots with a blip is \(P_\uparrow\) (with errors). Plot histograms of the maximum signal per shot for prepared states to choose the threshold; the spin-down histogram is a single peak, the spin-up histogram a peak at the blip level plus a tail of shots that relaxed before tunnelling.

T1

Load with both levels below \(E_F\) (random spin, roughly 50% up), wait a time \(\tau\) at that level, then read. The blip fraction decays as \(P_\uparrow(\tau) = A\,e^{-\tau/T_1} + B\). Repeat versus magnetic field: \(T_1\) falls steeply with field and dips at the spin–valley hot spot, which gives the valley splitting (Chapter 10) [17, 18].

41.3Pauli spin blockade readout

Set-up

  1. Find the \((1,1)\)–\((2,0)\) transition in a fast CSD (Chapter 40), in virtual coordinates.
  2. Sequence: (a) initialise in \(S(2,0)\) by waiting deep in \((2,0)\); (b) pulse into \((1,1)\) and wait long enough for the micromagnet field difference to mix \(S\) and \(T_0\) (tens of ns to µs), giving a mixed spin state; (c) pulse to a candidate readout point just across the interdot line into \((2,0)\); (d) read the sensor. As a reference, run the same sequence without the wait in \((1,1)\), so the state stays a singlet.
  3. Map the readout window: scan the readout point over a 2D region near the transition and plot the difference between the mixed and singlet-reference signals. The PSB triangle (Figure 11.4) is where they differ. spinQICK has routines for this (measurement-window and idle-cell scans) [10].
  4. Choose the integration window from single-shot data: separation grows with integration, but triplets relax to the singlet during readout (Chapter 11).
In the lab

HRL's spinQICK exchange-only work made every PSB measurement relative to a reference measurement immediately before each shot (initialise a singlet, measure at the readout window), to cancel slow drifts of the sensor. They reached SNR of 5–6 and a singlet assignment of 98.9% for prepared singlets [11]. Reference measurements cost time but make long experiments robust against sensor drift.

41.4Readout and initialisation fidelity

From histograms of prepared states, extract the overlap error and the relaxation tail. A common model fits each histogram with two Gaussians plus a "relaxation bridge" between them. Separate readout errors from initialisation errors by repeating readout twice in one shot (if the readout is non-destructive enough) or by preparing states with different methods. Report readout visibility and the conditions (integration time, field, temperature) clearly.

41.5Real-time thresholding

For single-shot data, QICK's acquire(..., threshold=, angle=) classifies shots after rotating the IQ plane [4]. For feedback (for example, re-initialising until the readout says "spin down"), the tProcessor reads the result and branches (Chapter 35). Elzerman readout has the useful property that after a spin-up blip a spin-down electron reloads the dot, so readout also re-initialises.

On the 4x2

In this chapter the 4x2 does the readout and triggers; the AWG does the plunger pulses. The accumulated buffer (16 384 entries per readout on the standard firmware) holds shots × windows; for 20 windows per shot that is 819 shots per buffer fill, which QICK reads out in chunks during long acquisitions [3]. For millisecond Elzerman reads, the 1.94 s DDR4 buffer can record hundreds of complete shot traces in one go.

Check yourself

1. In an Elzerman read-level sweep, the blip probability is 0 at low read voltage, 0.4 in a middle range, and 1 at high voltage. What is happening in each range?

Show answer
Low: both spin levels below \(E_F\), no electron can leave. Middle: only spin-up above \(E_F\), so only spin-up electrons leave: spin-selective readout, with ~40% of loaded spins up (plus errors). High: both levels above \(E_F\), every electron leaves.

2. Why does PSB readout often use a reference measurement in every shot?

Show answer
The sensor's working point drifts (charge noise, temperature). Comparing each measurement with a reference taken moments earlier removes slow drifts, keeping the threshold valid over long experiments.
Summary
  • Record several readout windows per shot; QICK returns one value per trigger.
  • Elzerman: set tunnel rates and field, find the spin-selective read level, detect blips; measure \(T_1\) and its field dependence.
  • PSB: initialise S(2,0), mix in (1,1), pulse to the readout window, compare with a singlet reference; map the PSB triangle.
  • Extract fidelities from prepared-state histograms; threshold in software or in the tProcessor for feedback.
PreviousChapter 40 · Experiment: fast charge-stability maps and pulsed-gate spectroscopyNextChapter 42 · Experiment: a micromagnet EDSR qubit, from spectroscopy to benchmarking

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 42

Experiment: a micromagnet EDSR qubit, from spectroscopy to benchmarking

Why you need this

This chapter runs your Si/SiGe micromagnet qubit: find the EDSR resonance, calibrate Rabi oscillations, measure \(T_2^*\) and \(T_2\), calibrate gates with AllXY and benchmark them. It is the sequence every single-spin qubit paper reports. The 4x2 generates the microwave drive (directly or as an IF for a mixer) and the readout; plunger pulses for initialisation and PSB or Elzerman readout come from the AWG of Architecture A (Chapter 38). The physics is in Chapters 3–5 and 12.

42.1The microwave chain

Pick the option that matches your field (Chapters 12 and 20):

Qubit frequencyChain from DAC_ANotes
< 4.9 GHzdirect, nqz=1 → attenuators → bias tee on an EDSR gateRequires a total field at the dot below ~0.175 T; check the micromagnet is magnetised
4.9–9.8 GHzdirect, nqz=2 → band-pass filter → lineCheck output power per frequency; filter images
> 9.8 GHzIF (0.5–2 GHz) → mixer with LO (locked to 10 MHz) → band-pass filter → amplifier if needed → lineTypical for micromagnet devices at 0.3–0.6 T (10–20 GHz)

Power: aim for a few millivolts of amplitude at the gate (Chapter 12). For example, −10 dBm out of the mixer chain with 30 dB of fridge attenuation gives −40 dBm at the gate line (about 3 mV amplitude in 50 Ω, up to twice that at an open gate).

Common mistake

Leaving the microwave on between experiments, or driving continuously at high power while searching for the resonance. Microwaves heat the device and the mixing chamber, which shifts qubit frequencies and broadens charge transitions. Use pulsed drive with a low duty cycle, and watch the mixing-chamber temperature and the sensor's Coulomb peak width while you increase power.

42.2Step 1: find the resonance

Sequence per shot: initialise (PSB: singlet in (2,0), then adiabatic separation to \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) or \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\); Elzerman: load spin-down), apply a long, strong microwave burst (several µs) at frequency \(f\), read out. Sweep \(f\) and the applied field. Resonances appear as lines with slope \(g\mu_B/h \approx 28\) GHz/T, offset by the micromagnet's field at each dot (Chapter 12).

Searching GHz with MHz-wide lines takes many points. Speed it up with frequency chirps: a burst whose frequency sweeps over, say, 50 MHz adiabatically inverts any spin whose resonance lies inside the sweep, so each point covers 50 MHz. With QICK, a chirp can be built from an envelope with a phase ramp or from a sequence of short pulses at stepped frequencies.

42.3Step 2: Rabi oscillations and the chevron

class RabiChevron(AveragerProgramV2):
    def _initialize(self, cfg):
        self.declare_gen(ch=0, nqz=1)                     # readout carrier (DAC_B)
        self.declare_gen(ch=1, nqz=cfg['nqz'])            # EDSR drive or IF (DAC_A)
        self.declare_readout(ch=0, length=cfg['ro_len'])
        self.add_loop('f', cfg['nf'])                      # outer loop: frequency
        self.add_loop('t', cfg['nt'])                      # inner loop: burst length
        self.add_pulse(ch=1, name='mw', style='const',
                       freq=QickSweep1D('f', cfg['f0'], cfg['f1']),
                       length=QickSweep1D('t', 0.01, cfg['tmax']), phase=0, gain=cfg['g'])
        self.add_pulse(ch=0, name='ro', style='const', freq=cfg['f_ro'], ro_ch=0,
                       length=cfg['ro_len'] + cfg['tof'], phase=0, gain=cfg['g_ro'])
        self.add_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='r', freq=cfg['f_ro'], gen_ch=0)
        self.send_readoutconfig(ch=0, name='r', t=0)
    def _body(self, cfg):
        self.trigger(pins=[1], t=0)                       # AWG: initialise and move to manipulation point
        self.delay(cfg['t_manip'])
        self.pulse(ch=1, name='mw', t=0)
        self.delay(cfg['t_to_ro'])                        # AWG: move to readout point
        self.pulse(ch=0, name='ro', t=0)
        self.trigger(ros=[0], t=cfg['tof'])

With an external mixer, the swept frequency is the IF, and the qubit frequency is LO + IF. Expect a chevron like Figure 3.3: the centre gives the qubit frequency, the period gives the π time. Then fix the frequency and sweep the amplitude at fixed length to calibrate gain for X and X/2 pulses with Gaussian envelopes.

42.4Step 3: Ramsey and echo

  • Ramsey: X/2 – τ – X/2 with a virtual detuning (advance the second pulse's phase by 360° × \(f_{\text{virt}}\) × τ, Chapter 35). Fit fringes for the precise qubit frequency and \(T_2^*\) (Chapter 4). In purified silicon expect up to ~20 µs; in natural silicon about 1 µs [13, 20].
  • Hahn echo and CPMG: X/2 – τ/2 – X – τ/2 – X/2, and versions with more π pulses. Their decays give \(T_2\) and, with different pulse numbers, the noise spectrum (Chapter 4).

All three need only the microwave channel and readout from the 4x2, plus the AWG's fixed plunger sequence.

42.5Step 4: gate calibration and benchmarking

  • AllXY (Chapter 5): 21 pulse pairs; corrects amplitude, detuning and phase errors at a glance. spinQICK implements it [10].
  • Randomised benchmarking: random Clifford sequences of increasing length, built from X/2, Y/2 and virtual Z (phase updates); fit the decay (Figure 5.2). Generate sequences in Python and compile one QICK program per sequence, or store pulse indices in data memory and loop (Chapter 5).

42.6Two qubits under one magnet

With both resonances known, address each qubit at its own frequency. On the 4x2, either retune DAC_A's frequency between pulses (keeping separate phase bookkeeping for each qubit, Chapter 3) or, with an IQ mixer or a wide IF band, place both IFs within the mixer's band and play them on the same generator in sequence. Calibrate crosstalk (driving Q1 slightly rotates Q2) and AC Stark shifts with Ramsey on the idle qubit while the other is driven [14].

42.7Keeping the qubit calibrated

The qubit frequency drifts with charge noise and with microwave heating. Typical practice: repeat a short Ramsey every few minutes and correct the drive frequency; keep the average microwave power constant (add off-resonant "dummy" pulses when the qubit is idle) to stabilise heating [16]. Real-time tracking, where the FPGA estimates the frequency from a burst of Ramsey shots and updates it immediately, is discussed in Chapter 44.

Check yourself

1. Your Rabi chevron is centred at an IF of 812 MHz with an LO of 12.4 GHz (upper sideband). What is the qubit frequency? What field does that correspond to for a dot whose micromagnet adds 0.12 T?

Show answer
\(f_q = 12.4 + 0.812 = 13.212\) GHz. Total field \(= 13.212/27.99 = 0.472\) T, so the applied field is about 0.352 T.

2. Why use Gaussian rather than square pulses for X/2 when two qubits are 40 MHz apart and the Rabi frequency is 5 MHz?

Show answer
A square pulse's sinc spectrum has side lobes that still carry power 40 MHz away, slightly driving the other qubit. A Gaussian's spectrum falls off much faster, reducing crosstalk (Chapter 21).
Summary
  • Choose the microwave chain by qubit frequency: direct (zone 1 or 2) or IF + mixer + LO; keep a few mV at the gate and watch heating.
  • Find resonances with field–frequency spectroscopy (chirps speed it up); calibrate with a Rabi chevron and amplitude Rabi.
  • Measure \(T_2^*\) (Ramsey with virtual detuning) and \(T_2\) (echo, CPMG); calibrate with AllXY; benchmark with RB.
  • Address two qubits by frequency, calibrate crosstalk and Stark shifts, and recalibrate against drift.

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 43

Experiment: singlet–triplet and exchange-only qubits

Why you need this

Singlet–triplet and exchange-only qubits are controlled entirely by baseband pulses (Chapter 13), so they are the hardest fit for the 4x2's AC-coupled outputs and the clearest test of what your setup can do. This chapter describes the standard experiments for both encodings, what each requires from the hardware, and what part a 4x2 can play: full control in a modified two-channel configuration for S–T₀, readout and calibration support for exchange-only devices run from a larger controller.

43.1Singlet–triplet qubit experiments

Hardware needs

  • Two fast, DC-coupled baseband channels: P1 and P2 (detuning control) or a plunger and the barrier (symmetric exchange), with sub-ns timing and ~ns rise times.
  • PSB readout: a sensor carrier and receiver.
  • A stable field difference \(\Delta B_z\) between the dots (micromagnet in Si).

With the 4x2, use Architecture A (AWG for P1/P2 with the 4x2 reading out) or Architecture B (DC-coupled DAC_A and DAC_B, readout carrier from an external source) (Chapter 38).

The experiments

  1. S–T₀ precession (ΔBz oscillations): initialise \(S(2,0)\), pulse quickly (diabatically with respect to \(\Delta E_Z\)) deep into \((1,1)\) where \(J\approx0\), wait \(\tau\), return and read. The singlet probability oscillates at \(\Delta E_Z/h\), giving the field difference and, from the decay, \(T_2^*\) of the S–T₀ qubit.
  2. Exchange oscillations: prepare \(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) (adiabatic separation), apply an exchange pulse of amplitude \(\varepsilon\) and duration \(\tau\), reverse the adiabatic ramp, read. The outcome oscillates at \(\sqrt{J^2+\Delta E_Z^2}/h\). A 2D map versus pulse amplitude and duration is the "fingerprint" from which \(J(\varepsilon)\) is calibrated [19, 11].
  3. Exchange echo: a π pulse about \(\Delta B_z\) in the middle of an exchange evolution refocuses slow detuning noise, measuring charge-noise-limited coherence of the exchange axis.
  4. Two-axis gates: combine exchange pulses and \(\Delta B_z\) evolution for arbitrary rotations; benchmark with RB.
Worked example: timing resolution

At the top of the fingerprint, \(J/h \approx 150\) MHz: a full oscillation every 6.7 ns. The 4x2's DAC sample period is 0.1 ns, and QICK envelopes are sample-accurate, so a pulse's duration can be set in 0.1 ns steps inside an envelope even though the tProcessor's scheduling grid is 2.44 ns. A 0.1 ns error is then a 5° rotation error at 150 MHz, acceptable for calibration scans and improvable with smaller \(J\) for precise gates.

43.2Exchange-only qubit experiments

HRL's RFSoC-based work on a triangular EO qubit is the reference for this encoding on QICK hardware [11]. The sequence of experiments was:

  1. Tune a triple dot to the \((1,1,1)\) region with PSB readout on one pair.
  2. Exchange oscillations on each axis (\(J_{12}\), \(J_{23}\), and \(J_{13}\) for the triangle), with crosstalk-compensated pulses so that pulsing one barrier does not shift the dots. Reported: \(J/h\approx 75\)–78 MHz and 21–35 oscillations before 1/e decay.
  3. Fingerprint plots versus exchange-pulse amplitude and detuning for each axis, to set the symmetric exchange operating point.
  4. Pre-distortion of 10 ns exchange pulses using a measured response of the amplifier chain, and a calibrated 40 ns gap between pulses.
  5. Exchange-angle calibration, then dynamical-decoupling sequences (NZ1 and the new NZM1 enabled by the triangular geometry) to separate hyperfine and charge-noise contributions.

Hardware: a ZCU216 with 14 baseband channels and 2 DDS channels, DC-coupled LMH5401 and THS3491 amplifiers, an 11 × 11 crosstalk matrix in firmware and a 20-bit DC source [11].

On the 4x2

An EO qubit needs at least two exchange (barrier) channels and usually plunger channels for initialisation and readout, all DC-coupled: more than the 4x2's two AC-coupled outputs. Use a ZCU216-based system (or a commercial controller) for EO control. A 4x2 can still serve as a dedicated readout unit, a calibration instrument (photon-assisted tunnelling, sensor characterisation, noise spectroscopy with its ADCs and DDR4 buffer), or a development platform for QICK programs before running them on the larger board, since QICK's programming model is the same across boards [4].

Check yourself

1. In the S–T₀ precession experiment, why must the pulse into (1,1) be fast compared with \(h/\Delta E_Z\)?

Show answer
So that the singlet state is preserved as it enters (1,1) and then precesses towards T₀ under \(\Delta E_Z\). A slow (adiabatic) pulse would instead map the singlet onto an eigenstate of \(\Delta E_Z\) (\(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}\) or \(\ket{\downarrow\uparrow}\)), and no precession would be seen.

2. Why does an EO qubit benefit so much from crosstalk compensation in firmware?

Show answer
Each exchange pulse on a barrier also shifts neighbouring dot potentials (and other exchange couplings) through cross-capacitance, changing the qubit's operating point during the pulse. Compensating pulses on neighbouring gates, computed from a crosstalk matrix, keep the pulse acting only on the intended exchange axis. Doing it in firmware keeps programs simple and timing exact.
Summary
  • S–T₀ experiments: ΔBz precession, exchange oscillations and fingerprints, exchange echo, two-axis gates; they need two fast DC-coupled channels plus PSB readout.
  • EO experiments (HRL/spinQICK): crosstalk-compensated exchange on each axis, fingerprints, pre-distorted 10 ns pulses, exchange calibration and decoupling sequences, on a ZCU216 with 14 baseband channels.
  • The 4x2 can run S–T₀ control only with an AWG or a DC-coupling modification; for EO it is a readout, calibration or development unit.

Part X · Experiments with the 4x2 · Chapter 44

Experiment: two-qubit gates, feedback and stabilisation

Why you need this

The last group of experiments goes beyond single qubits: entangling gates between two spins, and closed-loop experiments where the controller reacts to measurement results in real time. Two-qubit gates need more channels than a 4x2 has, so here the board shares the work with an AWG. Real-time feedback, on the other hand, is something an FPGA-based controller does better than a rack of separate instruments, and several useful feedback experiments fit the 4x2 well. This chapter covers both.

44.1Two-qubit gate experiments

Requirements for two LD qubits (Chapter 14): EDSR drive for both qubits (one microwave channel, frequency-multiplexed), a DC-coupled barrier pulse for exchange with plunger compensation, plunger pulses for initialisation and PSB readout, and the readout. In Architecture A the AWG provides barrier and plunger pulses (3–4 channels), the 4x2 provides the microwave drive, readout and master timing.

Calibration sequence

  1. Exchange spectroscopy: with a barrier pulse on during a long, weak EDSR burst, the qubit lines split by \(J/h\) (Figure 14.1). Measure \(J\) versus barrier voltage; expect an exponential dependence.
  2. CROT: choose a J-split line and calibrate a selective π pulse whose Rabi frequency satisfies the synchronisation condition (Chapter 14).
  3. CZ: run a Ramsey experiment on the target qubit with a shaped barrier pulse inserted between the X/2 pulses, once with the control qubit up and once down. The difference between the two fringe phases is the conditional phase; adjust the pulse amplitude or duration until it is 180°, then correct each qubit's single-qubit phase with virtual Z gates [14, 15, 22].
  4. Bell states and tomography: prepare, apply the gate, measure in several bases with single-qubit pre-rotations, reconstruct the two-qubit density matrix.
  5. Benchmarking: two-qubit RB or gate set tomography.

Timing between the 4x2's microwave pulses and the AWG's barrier pulse must be known to within a fraction of a nanosecond, because the CZ phase depends on the overlap of pulses and the qubits' free evolution in between. Measure the trigger latency carefully (Chapter 36).

44.2Real-time feedback with the 4x2

QICK's tProcessor can read a measurement result, compare it with a threshold, and choose the next pulse, all within the same shot (Chapters 33 and 35). Several useful experiments only need the 4x2's two outputs:

1. Repeat-until-success initialisation

After initialising, measure; if the result indicates the wrong state, re-initialise and measure again, up to N times, before starting the experiment. This filters out initialisation errors. It needs a readout that does not itself spoil the state you keep, which is natural for Elzerman readout (a spin-down result leaves a spin-down electron) [17].

2. Real-time qubit-frequency tracking

Charge noise moves the qubit frequency on time scales of seconds to hours (Chapter 4). A feedback loop can track it:

  1. run a short burst of Ramsey shots at a fixed delay \(\tau\) and two phases of the second pulse (±90°), which gives the sign and size of the detuning;
  2. compute a frequency correction (a proportional–integral update, or a Bayesian estimate);
  3. update the drive frequency for the following experiment shots.

The first version can run with Python updating the QICK program between short acquisitions (latency of tens of ms, enough for slow drift). A faster version computes the update in the tProcessor using its integer registers and updates the DDS frequency register directly, giving sub-millisecond response. Both use only DAC_A (drive), DAC_B and ADC_D (readout).

3. Adaptive readout

Integrate in several short windows and stop as soon as the accumulated signal is clearly on one side of the threshold. Shots that are easy to classify finish early, saving time on average. With QICK this is a loop of short readouts with a conditional jump.

4. Charge-jump detection

Monitor a reference measurement each shot (as in HRL's PSB work [11]); if it jumps beyond a tolerance, flag the data and trigger a recalibration routine. Detecting such events on the FPGA and pausing the experiment avoids collecting hours of useless data. QICK has been used with on-FPGA neural networks for similar real-time detection in superconducting qubits [4].

5. Electrostatic stabilisation (needs a DC path)

Bryan, Wilson and Jiang stabilised a silicon double dot against 1/f charge noise with FPGA-based gradient-descent feedback, using fast RF reflectometry to compute gradients and updating gate voltages continuously, reaching better than −6 dB of noise suppression up to 5 kHz [21]. They used a commercial controller with DC-coupled outputs. With a 4x2, the measurement and computation fit, but applying the correction needs a DC-coupled output (a modified DAC, an external fast DC source with a digital interface, or an AWG whose offset can be updated quickly).

Worked example: latency budget

A conditional π pulse after a 2 µs readout: the readout window ends; the readout pipeline and accumulation deliver the result to the tProcessor after a few hundred nanoseconds (measure your firmware's value with the latency method of QICK's feedback tutorial [4]); the jump and pulse issue take tens of nanoseconds. Total decision delay: well under 1 µs, small compared with spin \(T_1\) (ms) and comparable to the readout itself. Feedback on spin qubits is limited by readout time, not by the controller.

Check yourself

1. Which feedback experiments in this chapter can run on an unmodified 4x2 with no other pulse instrument?

Show answer
Those whose actions are microwave pulses or readout decisions: frequency tracking, adaptive readout, charge-jump detection (with a fixed plunger configuration), and repeat-until-success schemes whose re-initialisation does not need baseband pulses. Anything requiring plunger or barrier pulses needs the AWG or a DC-coupled output.

2. Why does the CZ calibration need a Ramsey experiment on the target with two different control states?

Show answer
The CZ gate's essence is a phase on the target that depends on the control's state. Ramsey measures the target's phase; the difference between control-up and control-down Ramsey phases is the conditional phase, which must be 180°.
Summary
  • Two-qubit gates (CROT, CZ) need EDSR, barrier and plunger pulses and readout, synchronised to sub-ns; the 4x2 provides drive, readout and timing, an AWG the baseband pulses.
  • Feedback that fits the 4x2: repeat-until-success initialisation, real-time frequency tracking, adaptive readout, charge-jump detection.
  • Electrostatic stabilisation needs a DC-coupled actuator.
  • Controller decision latency (well under 1 µs) is short compared with spin readout times.

Part XI · Capability map and roadmap · Chapter 45

What the 4x2 can and cannot do

Why you need this

This chapter collects the whole book into one answer to your original question: of everything that semiconductor spin-qubit research groups do, what can the RFSoC 4x2 do, what can it do with help, and what needs different hardware? Use the tables to plan experiments and to explain your hardware choices to your group.

45.1The short answer

The RFSoC 4x2 with QICK is an excellent readout, microwave and timing engine. It does RF reflectometry readout, real-time demodulation, single-shot classification, microwave EDSR drive (directly up to a few GHz, via a mixer above), precise sequencing and real-time feedback, at a small fraction of the cost of commercial controllers. It is not a baseband gate-pulse instrument: its two outputs are AC-coupled through 10 MHz–10 GHz baluns, so it cannot produce the DC levels and µs–ms pulses that spin-qubit initialisation, readout, exchange and charge-state manipulation need, and two outputs are too few for multi-gate control anyway. Paired with a DC-coupled AWG and a DC source, it supports most single-qubit spin experiments; for exchange-only qubits and multi-qubit devices, groups use larger RFSoC systems (ZCU216, QICK Box, spinQICK) or commercial controllers.

45.3What leading groups have that the 4x2 lacks

  • Channel count: tens to hundreds of synchronised DC-coupled baseband channels, several microwave channels and many readout channels.
  • DC-coupled, low-noise, crosstalk-compensated pulsing: integrated in commercial systems and in spinQICK's ZCU216 firmware [11].
  • Built-in upconversion to 10–20 GHz with calibrated IQ mixing.
  • Mature software stacks with calibration libraries, scheduling and databases.
  • Cryogenic electronics and superconducting amplifiers (parametric amplifiers for readout), which are independent of the controller but often present.

45.4What the 4x2 offers that racks do not

  • Cost: $2,499 academic for 2 DACs, 4 ADCs and an FPGA with full open-source control [1], versus tens of thousands of dollars per commercial channel group.
  • Openness: firmware and software can be read and changed; new ideas (custom filters, on-FPGA machine learning, new feedback schemes) can be implemented directly.
  • Phase coherence by construction: all channels from one clock tree; no external triggering between source and digitiser.
  • A path to larger systems: the same QICK programming model runs on ZCU216-based systems [4], so code and skills transfer.
Summary
  • Alone: reflectometry readout, single-shot analysis, microwave drive (direct to a few GHz), timing and feedback.
  • With a DC-coupled AWG, DC source and LO/mixer: most single-spin experiments, including PSB/Elzerman readout, EDSR control and benchmarking; S–T₀ control.
  • Exchange-only and multi-qubit work needs ZCU216-class systems or commercial controllers.
  • Its value lies in low cost, openness, phase-coherent readout and a direct path to larger QICK systems.

Part XI · Capability map and roadmap · Chapter 46

Your roadmap with the board

Why you need this

A plan turns this book into results. This chapter lays out a realistic sequence of stages, from reading to a working qubit measurement, with clear goals and checks for each stage, and a list of projects that suit the 4x2 and could become research contributions in their own right.

46.1Stage 0: before (or while) the board arrives

  • Read Parts I–III of this book; then Hanson et al. and Burkard et al. for depth [18, 7].
  • Read the QICK documentation's getting-started and tutorial pages; if available, try the tProc v2 tutorials on the QICK emulator branch [4, 3].
  • Read the SDR book's Chapters 4, 7, 9, 11 and 12 (sampling, quadrature, RF converters, figures of merit) [5].
  • Check: you can explain Figure 1.2, a Rabi chevron, a charge stability diagram, a Nyquist zone and an I/Q demodulator without notes.

46.2Stage 1: board bring-up (week 1–2)

  • Flash the QICK-recommended PYNQ image, boot, connect, run the base-overlay RF notebooks (Chapter 31).
  • Install the SDR book notebooks; work through sets A, B, C, E, F (Chapter 32).
  • Record your board's DAC output spectra and a DAC→ADC loopback transfer function (Chapters 29 and 36).
  • Check: a saved "board health" notebook with plots you can compare against later.

46.3Stage 2: QICK on the bench (week 3–4)

  • Install QICK; run the bundled tProc v1 demos; build or obtain tProc v2 firmware and run tutorials 00–04 (Chapter 34).
  • Do the bench calibrations: time of flight, frequency matching, phase versus frequency, trigger latency to an AWG (Chapter 36).
  • Lock the board to a 10 MHz reference together with an LO; build and characterise your EDSR upconversion chain into a spectrum analyser (Chapters 20, 30, 42).
  • Check: loopback pulses at the expected times, stable I/Q phase across runs, a clean upconverted tone with image and LO leakage measured.

46.4Stage 3: reflectometry rehearsal (month 2)

  • Build a room-temperature dummy tank and run the full Chapter 39 procedure on it: resonance, matching, power, SNR versus integration time.
  • Write your frequency plan and power budget for the real fridge (Chapters 18, 22, 38).
  • Check: a measured \(t_{\min}\) on the dummy tank and a written plan reviewed by a senior lab member.

46.5Stage 4: on the device (month 3 onward)

  • Connect to the fridge with conservative attenuation; find the cold resonance; read the sensor dot; measure Coulomb peaks by reflectometry and compare with DC (Chapter 39).
  • Fast charge stability maps with the AWG or DC source sweeping (Chapter 40); calibrate virtual gates.
  • Tunnelling records with the DDR4 buffer; tunnel rates.
  • Check: a sub-second CSD of the qubit dots in the few-electron regime.

46.6Stage 5: spins

  • PSB or Elzerman readout with the AWG for plunger pulses (Chapter 41); single-shot fidelity; \(T_1\) versus field.
  • EDSR spectroscopy, Rabi, Ramsey, echo, AllXY, RB (Chapter 42).
  • Check: a calibrated single-spin qubit with reported \(T_1\), \(T_2^*\), \(T_2\), readout and gate fidelities.

46.7Stage 6: decide how to grow

With a working single-qubit setup, decide whether you need DC-coupled channels on the RFSoC itself (modification, ZCU216/QICK Box with spinQICK) or a commercial controller for multi-qubit and encoded-qubit work (Chapters 38 and 45). Keep the 4x2 as a readout or development unit.

46.8Projects that suit the 4x2

ProjectUsesWhy it is interesting
Real-time qubit-frequency tracking in the tProcessorDAC_A, readout, tProc arithmeticFights 1/f drift; directly improves \(T_2^*\)-limited gates
Matched-filter spin readout with the weighted bufferReadout, weighted buffer, single-shot dataBetter fidelity for free; publishable comparison with boxcar
Adaptive (early-stopping) readoutReadout, conditional logicShorter average readout time
ML classification of video-mode CSDs, possibly on the FPGAFast maps, Python or HLSAutomated tuning [27]
Automated tank-circuit matching with a varactorReflectometry, DC sourceSolves the most common reflectometry problem [31, 53]
Sensor noise spectroscopy from DDR4 recordsLong records, FFTCharacterises charge noise in your heterostructure
DC-coupled ADC input modification (following QICK-DAWG)Hardware rework, LMH5401Enables lock-in style kHz–MHz sensing on the board [41]
Porting spinQICK readout and analysis routines to 4x2 configurationsspinQICK code, Architecture AUseful to other groups with 4x2 boards [10]
In the lab

Keep a lab notebook (electronic) for every session with: firmware and software versions, calibration values, wiring changes, device state and what you tried. Commit your measurement code to version control. Share results with the QICK and spinQICK communities: they are small, active and helpful, and your experience with the 4x2 on spin qubits is exactly what they lack.

Summary
  • Stage 0–2: learn, bring up the board, run QICK on the bench with calibrations.
  • Stage 3: rehearse reflectometry at room temperature; plan frequencies and power.
  • Stage 4–5: readout, fast maps, spin readout and single-qubit control on the device.
  • Stage 6: choose how to scale; meanwhile, pursue 4x2-friendly projects like real-time frequency tracking and optimal readout.

Appendix A: Mathematics refresher

The mathematics used in this book, in one place, with the identities you will reach for most often.

A.1 Complex numbers and phasors

  • \(z = x + iy = re^{i\theta}\), with \(r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)\).
  • Euler: \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\); so \(\cos\theta = (e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta})/2\), \(\sin\theta = (e^{i\theta}-e^{-i\theta})/2i\).
  • Multiplying complex numbers multiplies magnitudes and adds angles: rotating a phasor by \(\phi\) means multiplying by \(e^{i\phi}\).
  • A sinusoid \(A\cos(\omega t+\phi) = \Re\{Ae^{i\phi}e^{i\omega t}\} = I\cos\omega t - Q\sin\omega t\) with \(I + iQ = Ae^{i\phi}\).

A.2 Trigonometric identities used for mixing and the RWA

\[ \cos A\cos B = \tfrac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)],\quad \sin A\sin B = \tfrac12[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)],\quad \sin A\cos B = \tfrac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]. \]

A.3 Fourier transforms

\(X(f) = \int x(t)e^{-i2\pi ft}dt\), \(x(t) = \int X(f)e^{i2\pi ft}df\). Useful pairs:

TimeFrequency
Rectangle of width \(T\)\(T\operatorname{sinc}(fT)\), \(\operatorname{sinc}(u) = \sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)\)
Gaussian \(e^{-t^2/2\sigma^2}\)Gaussian of width \(1/(2\pi\sigma)\)
Decaying exponential \(e^{-|t|/\tau}\)Lorentzian of half-width \(1/(2\pi\tau)\)
\(\cos(2\pi f_0t)\)Two delta functions at \(\pm f_0\)
Convolution \(x * h\)Product \(X\cdot H\)
Product \(x\cdot m\)Convolution \(X * M\) (this is why mixing shifts spectra)

A.4 Linear algebra for qubits

  • Hermitian: \(H = H^\dagger\) (real eigenvalues, observables). Unitary: \(U^\dagger U = I\) (evolutions, gates).
  • Pauli matrices: \(\sigma_i^2 = I\), \(\sigma_x\sigma_y = i\sigma_z\) (cyclic), \(\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\} = 2\delta_{ij}I\).
  • \(e^{-i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2} = \cos(\theta/2)I - i\sin(\theta/2)\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma\).
  • Tensor products: \((A\otimes B)(\ket a\otimes\ket b) = A\ket a\otimes B\ket b\); two-qubit basis \(\ket{00},\ket{01},\ket{10},\ket{11}\).
  • Second-order perturbation theory (used for exchange): \(E_n^{(2)} = \sum_{m\ne n}|V_{mn}|^2/(E_n - E_m)\).

A.5 Statistics

  • Binomial estimate of a probability from \(N\) shots: \(\sigma = \sqrt{P(1-P)/N}\).
  • Gaussian overlap error with threshold midway, SNR = \(\Delta\mu/\sigma\): \(\epsilon = \tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(\text{SNR}/2\sqrt2)\).
  • Averaging \(N\) independent samples reduces white noise by \(\sqrt N\).
  • Gaussian average: \(\ev{\cos(\delta\omega\,\tau)} = e^{-\sigma^2\tau^2/2}\) for \(\delta\omega\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\).

A.6 Decibels

  • Power ratio: \(10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1)\); voltage ratio: \(20\log_{10}(V_2/V_1)\).
  • dBm: \(10\log_{10}(P/1\ \text{mW})\); in 50 Ω, 0 dBm = 0.224 V RMS = 0.316 V amplitude.
  • Thermal noise: \(-174\) dBm/Hz at 290 K; add \(10\log_{10}B\) for bandwidth \(B\).

A.7 Constants and conversions

QuantityValue
Planck constant \(h\)\(6.626\times10^{-34}\) J s = 4.136 µeV/GHz
Elementary charge \(e\)\(1.602\times10^{-19}\) C
Boltzmann constant \(k_B\)86.17 µeV/K (1 K ↔ 20.8 GHz)
Bohr magneton \(\mu_B\)57.88 µeV/T; \(\mu_B/h\) = 13.996 GHz/T
Electron spin in Si (\(g\approx2\))≈ 28.0 GHz/T
Electron spin in GaAs (\(|g|\approx0.44\))≈ 6.2 GHz/T
1 µeV241.8 MHz, 11.6 mK
Resistance quantum \(h/e^2\)25.81 kΩ
Signal speed in typical coax≈ 5 ns/m

Appendix B: Handling, safety and protecting the board

A checklist of rules that protect the board, your device and you. Most of them come from experience of things going wrong.

B.1 Protecting the RFSoC 4x2

  • Attenuate first. Never connect a signal of unknown power to an ADC input. Start with 20 dB of attenuation and remove it only after measuring. Respect the maximum input ratings in AMD's DS926 [45].
  • No DC on the SMA ports. Use DC blocks when connecting to anything that may carry DC (bias tees, amplifier outputs during power-up, fridge lines with bias).
  • ESD. Wear a grounded wrist strap when touching the board or connecting cables; discharge cables before connecting. QICK's quick-start guide warns that touching exposed components with metal tools can cause immediate, permanent damage [4].
  • Power and cooling. Use the supplied 12 V, 10 A supply; never block the fan; watch the FAIL and OVER TEMP LEDs [2].
  • Logic levels. PMOD pins are 1.8 V logic; use level shifters, never connect 3.3 V or 5 V outputs to them [2].
  • Shut down cleanly before switching off, to protect the SD card; keep a spare, imaged card.
  • Network security. Change the default xilinx password if the board is on a shared network.

B.2 Protecting the quantum device

  • Gate limits. Set software voltage limits and ramp rates on every gate; log the maximum each gate has seen.
  • Grounding. Ground all device lines (with a breakout box or grounding caps) when connecting or disconnecting anything; un-ground only when everything is connected.
  • Ground loops. Connect instrument grounds at one point; use isolation where needed (Chapter 16).
  • Microwave power. Increase EDSR and readout power gradually while watching mixing-chamber temperature and sensor peak width.
  • Pulse amplitudes. Before applying a new pulse sequence, check its amplitude at room temperature with an oscilloscope and compute the amplitude at the device from your attenuation.

B.3 Around the cryostat

  • Superconducting magnets store large energies; follow your lab's procedures for ramping and quench protection, and keep magnetic tools away.
  • Cryogens and pressurised gas: dry dilution refrigerators still contain helium mixtures and cold surfaces; follow the manufacturer's and your lab's safety training.
  • Vibration and cables: secure cables so they do not move with the pulse tube; moving cables generate noise.

B.4 Before every new experiment

  1. Is the frequency plan written, and are filters in place for every converter input?
  2. Is the power budget computed from DAC to device and from device to ADC?
  3. Are all instruments locked to the same 10 MHz reference?
  4. Are trigger latencies and time of flight calibrated?
  5. Is the configuration (firmware, software versions, calibrations) saved with the data?
